guides.title: Rocks, Minerals & the Rock Cycle
guides.summary: What minerals and rocks actually are, how to identify them by hardness, streak, cleavage and acid fizz, the three rock families, and how the rock cycle continuously converts each into the others.

sections.heading: First principles: element, mineral, rock
sections.body: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered internal atomic arrangement, meaning a crystal lattice. All four conditions must hold simultaneously, and testing a candidate against each one in turn settles most arguments. Glacier ice qualifies on every count. Liquid water fails because it has no lattice. Coal fails because it is organic. Steel fails because it is manufactured. A rock, by contrast, is a naturally occurring aggregate of one or more minerals, sometimes with volcanic glass or organic matter mixed in. Granite is a rock because it is built from at least three separate minerals, typically quartz, feldspar and mica, each visible as a distinct grain. Quartz is a mineral: silicon dioxide, one composition, one structure, everywhere on Earth. Crustal abundance explains why the mineral kingdom is so lopsided. By mass the crust is roughly 46.6 percent oxygen, 27.7 percent silicon, 8.1 percent aluminium, 5.0 percent iron, 3.6 percent calcium, 2.8 percent sodium, 2.6 percent potassium and 2.1 percent magnesium. Because oxygen and silicon together account for nearly three-quarters of the mass, about 92 percent of crustal minerals are silicates, all built from a single repeating unit: the silica tetrahedron, one silicon ion surrounded by four oxygen ions in a pyramid, carrying a net charge of minus four. Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms, and the number of corners shared is what defines each silicate class. Share no corners and the tetrahedra stay isolated, giving olivine. Share two and they form single chains, giving the pyroxenes such as augite. Share between two and three in a staggered arrangement and they form double chains, giving the amphiboles such as hornblende. Share three and they form sheets, giving the micas biotite and muscovite along with the clay minerals. Share all four and they form a three-dimensional framework, giving quartz and the feldspars. This progression is not a filing convenience but a predictor: more sharing means a higher silicon-to-oxygen ratio, which in turn means a lighter-coloured, lower-density mineral with a lower melting temperature. Knowing where a mineral sits on that scale tells you roughly how hot it formed and how it will behave when heated again. Beyond the silicates, six non-silicate classes matter in the field: carbonates such as calcite and dolomite; oxides such as hematite and magnetite; sulphides such as pyrite and galena; sulphates such as gypsum; halides such as halite, ordinary rock salt; and native elements including gold, graphite and diamond. Between them these classes account for most ore deposits and most economically useful rock. Two boundary cases are worth knowing because they come up constantly. Opal has the right composition for a mineral but lacks a proper lattice, being an ordered packing of silica spheres, so it is called a mineraloid rather than a true mineral; obsidian is glass and fails the same test outright. Amber and pearl are excluded on the organic criterion despite being solid, natural and beautiful. This is not pedantry: a repeating lattice is what gives a mineral its predictable hardness, cleavage, density and optical behaviour, the properties every identification method depends on.

sections.heading: Identifying a mineral: seven field tests in order
sections.body:
Mineral identification is a sequence, not a guess, and running the tests in a fixed order matters because each one narrows the field before the next is applied. Always work on a fresh, unweathered surface: a weathered rind is chemically altered and will lie to you about colour, hardness and lustre alike, so break a face first.

Lustre comes first because it is the single biggest split. A mineral either looks like polished metal, as pyrite, galena and magnetite do, or it does not. Non-metallic lustres subdivide into glassy or vitreous like quartz, pearly like mica, earthy like limonite, resinous, and silky. Streak comes second: drag the specimen hard across the unglazed tile and read the colour of the powder, which is far more reliable than the colour of the lump because powder removes the optical effects of grain size and surface film. Hematite may look silver-black or red as a lump but always streaks red-brown. Pyrite looks convincingly gold but streaks greenish-black, while gold streaks golden yellow, so this one test separates fool's gold from the real thing in seconds. Minerals harder than about seven will not streak at all; they scratch the plate instead, which is itself information.

Hardness is third, measured on the Mohs scale: talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase feldspar 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, diamond 10. The scale is ordinal, not linear — diamond is roughly four times harder than corundum by absolute indentation, though they sit one step apart. Useful field references are a fingernail at about 2.5, a copper coin about 3.5, a steel knife or nail and window glass both about 5.5, a steel file about 6.5. Try to scratch the unknown with a known material, then reverse the test, and always wipe the mark to confirm you cut a groove rather than leaving a smear of soft metal.

Fourth is cleavage against fracture. Cleavage is breakage along planes of weak atomic bonding and produces flat, repeatable, reflective faces; count the directions and measure the angles between them. Mica has one direction and peels into sheets. Feldspar has two at about ninety degrees. Pyroxene has two at roughly eighty-seven and ninety-three degrees, while amphibole has two at about fifty-six and one hundred twenty-four, and that angle is the classic way to separate hornblende from augite in hand specimen. Halite and galena cleave three ways at ninety degrees into cubes; calcite cleaves three ways but not at ninety degrees, giving rhombs. Fracture means no planar weakness at all, and quartz shows the curved, shell-like conchoidal fracture of glass.

The last three tests are quick. A drop of dilute hydrochloric acid or strong vinegar makes calcite fizz vigorously as carbon dioxide is released; dolomite fizzes only when powdered or warmed, and nothing else common fizzes at all, so this identifies limestone and marble instantly. Magnetite is strongly magnetic and pyrrhotite weakly so. Finally, heft the specimen: quartz has a specific gravity near 2.65 and feels normal, whereas galena at 7.6 and gold at 19.3 feel startlingly heavy for their size.

sections.heading: Igneous rocks: crystallised melt
sections.body:
Igneous rocks solidify from molten silicate liquid, called magma while it is below ground and lava once it reaches the surface. They are classified on two independent axes, and you must read both to name a rock; either alone gets you only halfway.

The first axis is texture, which records cooling rate. Slow cooling at depth gives atoms time to migrate and organise, growing large interlocking crystals visible to the naked eye; this is phaneritic texture, and such rocks are intrusive or plutonic. Granite, diorite and gabbro are the standard examples. Fast cooling at the surface leaves crystals too small to resolve without a lens; this is aphanitic texture, and the rocks are extrusive or volcanic, giving rhyolite, andesite and basalt. Instantaneous quenching, as when lava hits water, freezes the melt before any lattice forms, producing obsidian, a true glass with no crystal structure. Lava frothed by escaping gas produces vesicular rocks: pumice, so full of bubbles that its bulk density falls below water's and it floats, and the denser, darker scoria. Two-stage cooling leaves a diagnostic signature called porphyritic texture, in which large crystals called phenocrysts sit in a fine-grained groundmass. That combination tells a specific story: the magma sat in a chamber long enough to grow big crystals, then erupted. Explosive fragmentation welds shattered ash and pumice into pyroclastic tuff.

The second axis is composition, tracked by silica content, which controls colour, density and viscosity together. Felsic rocks carry sixty-five to seventy-five percent silica, are pale, rich in quartz and potassium feldspar, and have densities near 2700 kilograms per cubic metre; slow-cooled they are granite, fast-cooled they are rhyolite. Intermediate rocks at fifty-five to sixty-five percent give diorite and andesite. Mafic rocks at forty-five to fifty-five percent are dark, dominated by pyroxene, calcium-rich plagioclase and olivine, with densities near 3000 kilograms per cubic metre; these are gabbro and basalt. Below forty-five percent lies ultramafic peridotite, the rock of the mantle itself. Silica content also governs eruption style, because silica-rich melts polymerise into viscous liquids that trap gas and erupt explosively, whereas mafic melts are runny and erupt as flows. That single variable is why Hawaiian basalt produces rivers of lava you can outwalk while a rhyolitic volcano produces a column of ash and pyroclastic density currents that nothing outruns. The pairing of textures and compositions is deliberate: granite and rhyolite are chemically the same rock cooled at different rates, as are diorite and andesite, and gabbro and basalt. Naming an unknown igneous rock is therefore a two-question procedure. Ask first whether you can see individual crystals with the unaided eye or a hand lens, which fixes the texture and says whether the rock cooled at depth or at the surface. Ask second how dark it is, since colour index, the percentage of dark ferromagnesian minerals present, tracks silica content closely enough for field use: under about fifteen percent dark minerals suggests felsic, forty-five or more suggests mafic. The caveat is that colour index fails on glassy and very fine-grained rocks, where iron oxidation state rather than composition controls the shade; obsidian is typically black yet chemically rhyolitic, the felsic end of the scale.

sections.heading: Sedimentary rocks: the archive of the surface
sections.body:
Sedimentary rocks form at ordinary surface temperatures and pressures, and because they form where life and water are, they hold essentially all the fossils and all the fossil fuel. They come in three genetically distinct kinds, and separating them is the first move in the field.

Clastic or detrital rocks are made of transported fragments and are named by grain size on the Wentworth scale. Clay is finer than 0.004 millimetres and lithifies to claystone or shale; silt spans 0.004 to 0.0625 millimetres and gives siltstone; sand spans 0.0625 to 2 millimetres and gives sandstone; anything coarser than 2 millimetres gives conglomerate if the clasts are rounded and breccia if they are angular. Two textural properties let you read the transport history directly off the rock. Roundness increases with distance travelled, because protruding corners abrade first, so angular clasts mean a short journey. Sorting is the spread of grain sizes present: a well-sorted sandstone in which all grains are alike implies a persistent, selective agent such as wind or surf that repeatedly removed everything outside a narrow size band, whereas a poorly sorted jumble of clay through boulders implies a non-selective dump such as a glacier depositing till or a debris flow. Combine the two and the interpretation is immediate: an angular, poorly sorted breccia says local and fast, while a rounded, well-sorted quartz sandstone says long journey, high energy, repeatedly reworked.

Chemical rocks precipitate directly from solution rather than being carried as grains: limestone from calcium carbonate, rock salt from halite, gypsum, and chert from microcrystalline silica. When seawater evaporates, minerals precipitate in a fixed order as concentration rises, because each has its own solubility limit. Calcite comes out first at roughly fifty percent volume loss, gypsum at about eighty percent, halite at about ninety percent, and the bitter potassium and magnesium salts only at the very end. Finding that exact sequence stacked in a drill core is strong evidence that a sea basin dried up, and the thickness of each layer estimates how much water was lost.

Biochemical and organic rocks are built by living things. Most limestone is accumulated shell and coral debris rather than inorganic precipitate; chalk is a limestone made almost entirely of microscopic coccolith plates; coal is compressed plant matter that passes through peat, lignite and bituminous stages to anthracite as burial drives off water and volatiles and carbon content climbs from roughly sixty percent to over ninety.

Lithification converts loose sediment into rock by two processes. Compaction is burial pressure squeezing out pore water, which reduces the porosity of mud from around sixty percent to under ten. Cementation is groundwater precipitating calcite, silica or iron oxide into whatever pore space remains. Only sedimentary rocks preserve bedding, cross-bedding that records current direction, ripple marks, mud cracks, raindrop impressions, burrows and body fossils, which makes them the only direct archive of past surface conditions.

sections.heading: Metamorphic rocks: solid-state rebuilding
sections.body:
Metamorphism is the transformation of a pre-existing rock, called the protolith, into a new one by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids, while remaining solid throughout. That last condition is what separates it from igneous processes and it sets the temperature window. The lower bound is roughly 150 to 200 degrees Celsius, below which the changes are called diagenesis rather than metamorphism. The upper bound is around 850 degrees, above which the rock begins to melt partially, producing the mixed igneous-metamorphic rock called migmatite and eventually true magma. Pressure is quoted in kilobars, where one kilobar is about 100 megapascals and corresponds to the weight of roughly 3.5 kilometres of overlying crust, so the pressures involved in mountain-belt metamorphism represent burial of tens of kilometres.

Several distinct settings produce distinct results. Contact or thermal metamorphism is high temperature at low pressure in a halo around an intruding body of magma; because the stress is not directional, it produces non-foliated rocks such as hornfels and marble, and the halo's width, often a few metres to a few hundred, scales with the size of the intrusion. Regional or dynamothermal metamorphism combines high temperature with high directed pressure across entire mountain belts and produces foliated rocks. Burial, hydrothermal and shock metamorphism, the last from meteorite impact, make up the remainder.

Foliation is the parallel alignment of platy or elongate minerals perpendicular to the direction of maximum compressive stress, and its progressive development defines the classic grade sequence starting from a shale protolith. At about 200 degrees, shale becomes slate, very fine-grained and splitting into flat sheets along a cleavage that ignores the original bedding. Near 300 degrees, growing micas give phyllite its silky sheen. Near 450 degrees the micas are individually visible and aligned, producing schist. Near 650 degrees, minerals segregate into coarse light and dark bands, producing feldspar-rich gneiss. Where the protolith contains nothing platy to align, the products are non-foliated regardless of stress: limestone becomes marble, and quartz sandstone becomes quartzite, which breaks straight through the grains rather than around them, a reliable and quick field test.

Index minerals pin down the conditions numerically because each is stable only inside a known window of temperature and pressure. Running from low grade to high, the standard sequence in aluminium-rich rocks is chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite. The three polymorphs of aluminium silicate are the neatest illustration of the principle: andalusite, kyanite and sillimanite share an identical chemical formula but crystallise in three different structures, andalusite at low pressure, kyanite at high pressure and moderate temperature, sillimanite at high temperature. Identify which one is present and you have read the depth and heat the rock endured.

sections.heading: The rock cycle as a mass-balance system
sections.body:
The rock cycle is the statement that all three rock families are interconvertible and that no path through the system is one-way. Magma cools and crystallises into igneous rock. Any rock at the surface is weathered, eroded, transported, deposited and lithified into sedimentary rock. Any rock subjected to heat and pressure while staying solid becomes metamorphic rock. Any rock heated above its solidus melts back into magma. The point most often missed is that shortcuts exist everywhere: an igneous rock can become metamorphic without ever passing through a sedimentary stage, a metamorphic rock can be weathered straight into sediment, and a sedimentary rock can melt directly. The cycle is a network of possible transitions, not a circle that must be travelled in order.

Two energy sources drive the whole loop, and they power opposite halves of it. Earth's internal heat, from radioactive decay of uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40 together with residual heat from accretion, delivers about 47 terawatts through the surface and powers melting, metamorphism and the plate motion that buries rock in the first place. Solar energy, of which roughly 174,000 terawatts is intercepted, powers the water cycle, the wind and therefore the entire weathering and erosion half. The vast disparity between those two numbers is why surface processes are so much faster than deep ones.

Residence times make the abstraction concrete. Oceanic crust is created at spreading ridges and destroyed at trenches on a cycle of roughly 100 to 200 million years, which is why no seafloor older than about 180 million years exists anywhere on the planet. Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct wholesale and therefore survives: the oldest intact rocks, the Acasta Gneiss in northern Canada, are about 4.03 billion years old, and the oldest known mineral grains, detrital zircons from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old. Those zircons have been recycled through successive sandstones many times while the rock that originally contained them has vanished completely. Volumetrically, sedimentary rocks make up only about five to eight percent of the crust yet cover roughly seventy-five percent of the land surface: a thin veneer over an igneous and metamorphic basement.

Follow a single silicon atom to see the whole system operate. It crystallises into a quartz grain in a granite pluton five kilometres down. Uplift and erosion expose the granite; the surrounding feldspar weathers to clay and frees the grain. A river carries it four hundred kilometres, rounding it slightly, and deposits it on a beach. Burial to two kilometres and silica cementation turn the sand into sandstone. Continental collision drives the sandstone to twenty kilometres depth and 500 degrees, recrystallising it into quartzite. Fifty million years of erosion strip the mountain belt, exposing the quartzite, which weathers and releases the same grain to a new river. Several hundred million years have passed, the atom has occupied all three rock families, and it has never changed element.

sections.heading: Practical uses, common mistakes and safety
sections.body:
Knowing the rock beneath your feet predicts water, ground stability and resources, which is why geology was a practical trade long before it was an academic subject. Limestone and other carbonates dissolve in slightly acidic rainwater to form karst terrain, with caves, sinkholes and rapid, unfiltered groundwater flow through open conduits. The practical consequence is important: a spring in limestone country can carry surface bacteria kilometres underground in hours and arrive looking perfectly clear, so clarity is no guide to safety there. Shale and clay-rich rock hold water but transmit it poorly, make weak slopes and slide readily when saturated, which is why so many landslides follow prolonged rain on shale hillsides. Granite and quartzite make strong, low-permeability foundations, with water available only from fractures, so a well in granite either hits a fracture and produces or misses and does not. Sandstone with fifteen to twenty-five percent porosity is the classic aquifer and petroleum reservoir rock. For construction, quartzite and granite make excellent aggregate while shale is unsuitable because it slakes and crumbles through repeated wetting and drying. For a fire ring, never use river cobbles, sandstone or any porous stone that has been sitting in water: trapped pore water flashes to steam and can spall a rock violently, throwing fragments several metres. Use dry, dense, non-porous stone and keep people back.

Five mistakes account for most misidentifications. The first is identifying minerals by colour, when quartz alone occurs clear, white, pink, purple, smoky and black; streak and hardness are the reliable properties. The second is testing a weathered surface instead of breaking a fresh face. The third is confusing cleavage with crystal faces, distinguished by the fact that cleavage repeats indefinitely as you keep breaking the sample while a crystal face is a one-off growth surface. The fourth is calling any layered rock sedimentary, when gneiss is conspicuously banded and thoroughly metamorphic; foliation commonly cuts across bedding, whereas bedding is depositional and laterally continuous. The fifth is quoting a Mohs number as though the scale were linear.

Safety deserves genuine attention because rock work injures people. Wear eye protection whenever you strike a rock, since quartz and obsidian throw glass-sharp flakes at speed. Never hammer directly on another hardened steel face, because steel spalls. Treat road cuts and quarry faces as unstable, never work directly beneath an overhang or a fresh vertical face, and be especially wary after rain or a freeze-thaw night, when loose blocks fall without warning. Use only dilute acid, five percent hydrochloric or household vinegar, carried in a dropper bottle, and rinse skin immediately and generously if splashed. Avoid inhaling rock dust: crystalline silica causes silicosis, an irreversible lung disease, so break rock outdoors, work downwind, and wet the surface if you are doing it repeatedly. Some minerals warrant specific care. Galena is lead sulphide, so wash your hands and never taste a specimen. Cinnabar contains mercury. Asbestiform amphiboles must never be crushed or inhaled. Finally, check the law, because collecting is prohibited in most national parks and on much protected and private land.

sections.heading: Crystal Systems: Why a Mineral's Shape Isn't an Accident
sections.body:
Every mineral is a crystal at heart, even one that never grew a single flat face, because its atoms are locked into a repeating three-dimensional lattice. That internal geometry is what mineralogists call a crystal system, and there are seven of them: isometric or cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal, monoclinic and triclinic. They are distinguished by the relative lengths of the unit cell's crystallographic axes and the angles between them, running from the cubic case where all three axes are equal and mutually perpendicular, to the triclinic case where all three differ in length and no angle is a right angle. The system is a property of the atomic arrangement alone and does not depend on whether the specimen ever had room to grow visible faces.

Halite, ordinary rock salt, crystallises in the isometric system because its sodium and chlorine ions pack into a perfect alternating cube. That is exactly why a chunk of rock salt cleaves into smaller and smaller perfect cubes no matter how many times you split it: you are not cutting the crystal but finding a plane of weakest bonding that was always present, and the same planes exist at every scale down to the lattice itself. Quartz sits at the other extreme. It is trigonal, with silicon and oxygen spiralling around a threefold axis, which is why well-formed natural quartz shows a six-sided prism capped by pyramidal points, and why quartz has no cleavage at all. The silicon-oxygen bonds in its framework structure are so uniformly strong in every direction that there is no preferred plane of failure, so it breaks with the curved, glassy conchoidal fracture that ordinary glass also shows for the same structural reason.

Mica occupies the opposite corner of the same principle. Its sheet-silicate structure bonds atoms tightly within each sheet but only weakly between sheets, where large, loosely held cations sit. The result is one perfect cleavage direction so pronounced that a single crystal peels into flexible, paper-thin sheets under a fingernail, which is why mica was once used for stove windows. Calcite's rhombohedral cleavage, three directions with not one of them at ninety degrees, comes directly from the geometry of its trigonal carbonate lattice, and is distinctive enough that examining a broken calcite fragment through a hand lens usually settles the identification on sight.

The general rule worth carrying into the field is that cleavage planes always lie parallel to the weakest bonds in the lattice. Once you know roughly how a mineral's atoms are stacked, you can predict how it will break before you touch it with a hammer, and conversely, the way an unknown breaks is direct evidence about a structure you cannot see. The one honest caveat is that cleavage quality is graded rather than binary, from perfect through good to poor, and a poorly developed cleavage in a small or fractured specimen can be genuinely hard to distinguish from irregular fracture.

sections.heading: Bowen's Reaction Series: Why Granite and Basalt Never Mix
sections.body:
In the 1910s and 1920s the petrologist Norman L. Bowen melted rock powders in a furnace, cooled them slowly under controlled conditions, and watched under a microscope which minerals crystallised first and which came last. The pattern he documented, now called Bowen's Reaction Series, is one of the most useful single diagrams in geology because it explains both what forms and what cannot coexist.

The series has two branches running in parallel as the melt cools from about 1250 degrees Celsius to roughly 650. The discontinuous branch produces a sequence of chemically distinct minerals: olivine first, near 1200 degrees, then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite mica. It is called discontinuous because each mineral forms by the earlier one reacting with the remaining melt and being restructured, rather than simply ceasing to grow while the next starts. The chemical driver is the progressive linking of silica tetrahedra, from isolated units in olivine to single chains in pyroxene, double chains in amphibole and sheets in biotite. The continuous branch crystallises plagioclase feldspar, whose composition slides smoothly from calcium-rich to sodium-rich as temperature falls, with no abrupt change of mineral. Both branches converge at the bottom on the last phases to appear: potassium feldspar, then muscovite mica, then quartz, which simply fills whatever space remains between everything else.

One consequence is a rule of thumb that saves field time. Olivine and quartz almost never appear together in the same igneous rock, because if silica-rich melt is still present after olivine has formed, it reacts with the olivine to produce pyroxene instead of allowing both to persist. Finding them as genuine neighbours is a real geological oddity worth recording carefully, usually indicating that two magmas mixed too quickly for equilibrium to be reached.

The larger consequence is magmatic differentiation, which explains how one parent magma can generate a whole family of rocks. Early-formed crystals such as olivine and pyroxene are denser than the melt around them, so given time they sink and are removed from further reaction. This is fractional crystallisation, and it drives the residual liquid steadily toward the quartz-and-feldspar end of the series. A single basaltic parent magma can therefore yield gabbro at the base of a chamber, diorite in the middle and granite from the last residual melt. The series read backwards also predicts weathering: minerals that crystallised hottest and furthest from surface conditions break down fastest, which is the Goldich stability series, and it is precisely why olivine rots quickly in soil while quartz survives to dominate beach and desert sand.

Two honest limits apply to the series. It describes equilibrium crystallisation of a cooling melt in a closed system, and real magma chambers are neither closed nor at equilibrium: they are recharged with fresh magma, they assimilate the country rock they intrude, and they erupt before the process finishes. Fractional crystallisation alone also cannot produce the volume of granite in continental crust, because turning basalt into granite by crystal removal discards roughly nine parts in ten of the melt. Most granite is now understood to form instead by partial melting of existing crustal rock.

sections.heading: Putting a Clock on the Cycle: Radiometric Dating in Outline
sections.body:
The rock cycle describes a direction of change, but it took radioactivity to attach real numbers to it, and before that geologists could only order events relatively. Unstable isotopes decay to a daughter isotope at a fixed statistical rate, described by an exponential law in which the remaining parent equals the original amount multiplied by e raised to minus lambda times time, where lambda is the decay constant. Rearranged around the half-life, which equals the natural logarithm of two divided by lambda, this becomes the workhorse dating equation. The rate is genuinely fixed, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state within any geologically realistic range, which is what makes the method trustworthy.

Different parent-daughter pairs suit different timescales, and choosing the wrong one wastes the sample. Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of 4.47 billion years, which suits the oldest rocks on Earth. Potassium-40 decays to argon-40 with a half-life of 1.25 billion years and is the standard for volcanic rocks, since argon is a gas that escapes from a melt and therefore starts from zero when the rock solidifies. Rubidium-87 decays to strontium-87 over 48.8 billion years, suiting ancient continental crust. Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 with a half-life of only 5,730 years, which makes it useless for rocks but invaluable for organic material up to roughly 50,000 years old, beyond which too little parent remains to measure reliably.

A crucial catch limits what any date means. A radiometric age records the last time a mineral cooled below its closure temperature, the point at which the crystal lattice becomes tight enough to stop the daughter isotope diffusing out. Closure temperature is a property of the mineral and the isotope pair, not of the rock as a whole, which is why a single sample can yield several different but equally correct ages. Zircon retains lead above 900 degrees, so a zircon uranium-lead date usually marks original crystallisation. Mica loses argon below about 300 degrees, so a mica potassium-argon date can instead mark a much later metamorphic event that reset the clock. Reporting an age without naming the mineral and method is therefore incomplete.

This closure problem also explains why sedimentary rocks are almost never dated directly. Their grains were recycled from older rocks of mixed and unrelated ages, so a bulk date would average meaningless numbers. Instead, geologists date volcanic ash layers interbedded within a sedimentary sequence, since each ash bed crystallised at the instant it fell, and then bracket the enclosing rock between the ash above and the ash below. That bracketing method is exactly how boundaries such as the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction horizon were pinned to 66 million years. Precision is better than most people expect: modern uranium-lead work on zircon routinely resolves ages to a tenth of a percent, meaning plus or minus about 100,000 years on a 100-million-year date, which is fine enough to test whether a mass extinction and a volcanic episode were genuinely simultaneous.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: A basic mineral-identification kit costs less than a good field guide and turns a set of abstract diagnostic properties into something you can actually measure on a kitchen table. What follows is worth understanding rather than just buying, because each item isolates one physical property and knowing why it works tells you when it will mislead you. The streak plate must be unglazed, because glaze is harder than most minerals and would be scratched rather than dusted; whiteness matters so faint powder colours show, and it works only for minerals softer than about seven on the Mohs scale, above which the specimen cuts the plate instead. The scratch-hardness tools are fixed reference points on that scale, and the improvised set of fingernail near 2.5, copper coin near 3.5, steel knife and window glass both near 5.5 covers most common minerals for nothing. Always reverse a test to confirm the result, and wipe the mark before judging it, because soft metal leaves a grey smear that looks convincingly like a scratch until you rub it away. A hardness pick set adds precision between six and nine, where the improvised references run out. The magnet distinguishes magnetite, strongly attracted, from other black opaque minerals; a small neodymium disc also reveals the weak response of pyrrhotite. Dilute hydrochloric acid at around ten percent tests for carbonates by liberating carbon dioxide, and the reaction is vigorous on calcite but needs powdering or gentle warming on dolomite, itself a diagnostic difference. Acid demands respect: work outdoors or with ventilation, keep safety glasses on, and flush skin contact immediately with plenty of water. A ten-power hand lens is the highest-value item in the kit, because grain texture, crystal faces and the difference between cleavage and fracture often become obvious at that magnification and stay ambiguous without it. A notebook and separate bags matter more than they sound: unlabelled specimens become worthless.
ingredients: An unglazed white porcelain streak plate (the back of a bathroom tile works if a proper one isn't at hand) — a hardware store or hobby/rock shop
A steel pocketknife or a geologist's rock pick with a hardened tip, for scratch-hardness testing — a hardware or outdoor-gear store
A small piece of ordinary window glass (hardness ~5.5) and a copper penny (hardness ~3.5), both useful fixed points on the Mohs scale
A strong magnet (a small neodymium disc magnet works well) to test for magnetite and other magnetic minerals — an electronics or hardware store

Dilute hydrochloric acid (about 10%) in a small dropper bottle, for the carbonate fizz test — a rock-and-mineral or science-supply shop; always pair with safety glasses and use outdoors or in ventilated space, since it irritates skin and eyes on contact
A 10x hand lens or jeweler's loupe for examining crystal faces and grain texture — an optics, hobby, or rock-and-mineral shop

A basic Mohs hardness pick set (points of known hardness from 2 to 9) — a rock-and-mineral or geology-supply shop, though the improvised scale of fingernail, penny, knife, and glass covers most everyday identification
A field notebook and small sample bags or an egg carton for keeping specimens separated and labeled

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Identify Five Unknown Specimens Like a Field Geologist
sections.body: Diagnostic tests only build real skill once you run them on specimens whose answers you do not already know, and a yard, streambed or gravel driveway supplies plenty of genuine unknowns for nothing. The exercise below turns on one discipline: record each observation before forming an opinion, because the commonest failure in mineral identification is deciding what a specimen is at first glance and then reading every later test as confirmation. Writing colour and lustre down first, knowing colour is the least reliable property of all, forces the evidence to accumulate independently of the guess. Order matters for a practical reason as well as a psychological one. Streak is taken early because it barely marks the specimen and immediately separates the metallic-looking minerals, several of which are otherwise easily confused. Hardness is worked upward from softest tool to hardest so the specimen is damaged as little as possible and the first tool which succeeds gives a genuine bracket rather than an unrepeatable gouge. Cleavage is assessed on a freshly broken face, because a rolled streambed cobble has had its flat faces abraded away, and counting cleavage directions on a weathered surface is close to guesswork. The acid test comes near the end because it etches a mark and leaves residue that interferes with later observation, so confine it to an inconspicuous spot. The final judgement, whether a specimen is a single mineral or a rock built from several minerals grown together, is the step most beginners skip and the one that teaches most: writing a single sentence of reasoning for each call, naming the evidence rather than the conclusion, makes a wrong answer instructive instead of merely wrong.
steps: Collect five different-looking rock or mineral specimens, at least fist-sized if possible, ideally from different locations (a streambed, a gravel driveway, a road cut, a garden bed).
For each specimen, first record color and luster (metallic, glassy, pearly, dull) in your notebook before testing anything — color alone is often misleading, so note it but don't rely on it.
Run the streak test: scrape the specimen firmly across the unglazed porcelain plate and record the color of the powder left behind, not the color of the specimen itself.

Test hardness by attempting to scratch the specimen with your fingernail, then a penny, then the knife blade, then the glass plate, working up in order and recording the highest material that successfully scratches it.

Check for cleavage versus fracture: look for flat, repeating, reflective planes (cleavage) versus curved or irregular broken surfaces (fracture), and count how many distinct cleavage directions you can see.
Apply a single drop of dilute acid to an inconspicuous spot and watch for fizzing, which indicates a carbonate mineral such as calcite; wipe it off afterward and wash your hands.
Test with the magnet to rule in or out magnetite or other strongly magnetic minerals.
Cross-reference your recorded properties against a mineral identification chart or field guide to reach a tentative ID.

Decide whether each specimen is a single mineral or a rock made of several minerals grown together — if you see multiple distinct minerals with your hand lens, classify it as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic and write a one-line reasoning for your call.

guides.title: Plate Tectonics, Earthquakes & Volcanoes
guides.summary: Earth's interior structure, the mechanics of plate motion, the three boundary types, how earthquakes are measured and how to survive one, and why different volcanoes erupt in fundamentally different ways.

sections.heading: Earth's interior: the layers and how we know
sections.body:
Earth can be divided twice over, and the two divisions do not line up, which is the first thing to get straight. Divided by chemistry, the outermost shell is the crust: oceanic crust is basaltic, 5 to 10 kilometres thick, with a density near 3,000 kilograms per cubic metre and an age nowhere greater than about 180 million years, while continental crust averages granitic, runs 30 to 50 kilometres thick and up to 70 under Tibet, has a density near 2,700, and includes rock up to 4.0 billion years old. Beneath it the mantle, made of peridotite, a mixture of olivine and pyroxene, extends to 2,890 kilometres and accounts for 84 per cent of Earth's volume and roughly 67 per cent of its mass. It is solid rock that nonetheless flows plastically over geological time at strain rates around ten to the minus fourteen or fifteen per second; the useful mental image is extremely stiff toffee, not liquid. The core is an iron-nickel alloy with about ten per cent light elements such as sulphur, oxygen and silicon, running from 2,890 kilometres to the centre at 6,371. Its outer part is genuinely liquid, while the inner core below 5,150 kilometres is solid despite being hotter, near 5,400 degrees Celsius, because the pressure there exceeds 330 gigapascals and pressure raises the melting point.

Divided instead by how the rock deforms, which is the division that governs tectonics, the outer layer is the lithosphere: crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, zero to 100 kilometres thick under oceans and thickening as it ages, up to 200 to 250 kilometres under ancient continental cratons. This is the layer that breaks into plates. Below it the asthenosphere, from roughly 100 to 350 kilometres, is weak and ductile, close enough to its melting point to hold perhaps 0.1 to 1 per cent partial melt, and it is on this that plates slide. Deeper still lie the stiffer lower mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.

All of this was mapped with earthquake waves. P-waves are compressional, with particle motion parallel to travel, moving about 6 kilometres per second in crust and 13 near the base of the mantle, and they pass through solids and liquids alike. S-waves are shear waves with particle motion perpendicular to travel, roughly 0.58 times P-wave speed, and they cannot propagate through liquid because a liquid has zero shear modulus. Speeds follow the square root of the bulk modulus plus four-thirds the shear modulus, divided by density, for P-waves, and the square root of shear modulus over density for S-waves. The S-wave shadow zone, in which no S-waves arrive beyond 103 degrees of arc from an earthquake, is direct proof that the outer core is liquid, while the P-wave shadow between 103 and 143 degrees comes from refraction at the core-mantle boundary. Sharp velocity jumps mark the Moho at the base of the crust, found in 1909, mineral phase changes at 410 and 660 kilometres, and the Gutenberg discontinuity at 2,890.

sections.heading: Plate tectonics: the engine
sections.body:
The lithosphere is broken into about seven major plates — Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic — plus a dozen or so minor ones including the Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Philippine, Arabian, Juan de Fuca and Scotia plates. They move between 1 and 15 centimetres per year, roughly the speed at which fingernails grow, which is slow enough to be invisible in a human lifetime and fast enough to rearrange a planet. Since the 1990s these rates have been measured directly by satellite positioning, and they agree with the far older estimates derived from seafloor magnetic stripes.

The historical case was built piece by piece. Alfred Wegener assembled the continental fit, matching Permian Glossopteris flora and Mesosaurus fossils across the Atlantic and matching mountain belts such as the Appalachians and Caledonides. Palaeomagnetism then showed that apparent polar wander paths measured on different continents can only be reconciled if the continents moved rather than the pole. In 1963 Vine, Matthews and Morley demonstrated that the symmetric magnetic stripes flanking mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth's magnetic field, yielding both direction and rate of spreading. Seafloor age and sediment thickness both increase away from ridges, and no seafloor anywhere is older than about 180 million years, which is impossible on a static Earth. Finally the Wadati-Benioff zone, a plane of earthquakes deepening inland from a trench at 30 to 60 degrees and traceable to 700 kilometres, images the subducting slab itself.

What actually drives the motion is now reasonably well understood, and the ranking matters because the intuitive answer is wrong. Slab pull supplies roughly 90 per cent of the driving force: cold, dense subducted lithosphere sinks under its own negative buoyancy and drags the trailing plate behind it. Oceanic lithosphere becomes denser than the underlying asthenosphere at about 30 million years old, which explains why old, cold plates such as the Pacific move fastest. Ridge push contributes less; despite the name it is not a shove from below but a body force arising as the elevated, thickening, cooling lithosphere slides gravitationally away from the ridge. Basal drag from mantle convection contributes something and can equally resist motion where the mantle flows against the plate.

The energy behind all of it is Earth's internal heat, about 47 terawatts leaving the surface, roughly half from radioactive decay of uranium-238, uranium-235, thorium-232 and potassium-40, and roughly half residual heat left from accretion and core formation. Mantle convection cells transport that heat outward. The crucial conceptual point is that plates are not passengers riding on convection; they are the cold, rigid top thermal boundary layer of the convection itself, and their sinking is a principal part of the circulation.

sections.heading: The three plate boundaries and what each builds
sections.body:
Where plates move apart, new lithosphere is created. Under the oceans this produces mid-ocean ridges, a single connected mountain system some 65,000 kilometres long. Melting there happens without any added heat, by decompression: mantle rises, pressure falls, and because a rock's melting point drops as pressure drops, the rising material crosses its solidus and partially melts. Slow-spreading ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic open at 2 to 5 centimetres per year and carry a deep axial rift valley, while fast-spreading ridges such as the East Pacific Rise open at 6 to 16 centimetres per year and show a smooth axial high instead. Earthquakes there are shallow, under 20 kilometres, and rarely exceed magnitude 6; volcanism is basaltic and effusive. On continents the same process makes rift valleys, of which the East African Rift is the active example and the Red Sea the completed one.

Where plates converge, lithosphere is destroyed or thickened, and the outcome depends on what collides. When ocean meets continent the denser oceanic plate subducts, producing a trench and a continental volcanic arc 100 to 200 kilometres inland, as in the Andes and the Cascades. The magma there is generated by flux melting: water driven out of the descending slab at 80 to 120 kilometres depth lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge, producing wet, silica-rich, gas-rich andesitic magma that erupts explosively. When ocean meets ocean the older, colder plate subducts and an island arc forms, as with Japan, the Aleutians and the Marianas, where Challenger Deep reaches 10,935 metres. When continent meets continent neither subducts, because both are too buoyant, so the crust thickens and shortens instead; India still drives north into Asia at roughly 5 centimetres per year, having closed the Tethys Ocean over the last 50 million years, and Everest at 8,849 metres continues to rise a few millimetres annually.

Where plates slide past one another, along transform boundaries, lithosphere is neither made nor destroyed and motion is horizontal. Most transforms are short segments offsetting mid-ocean ridges; the famous continental examples are the San Andreas, along which the Pacific plate moves northwest relative to North America at about 3.5 centimetres per year, and the North Anatolian Fault. Their earthquakes are shallow and can reach magnitude 7 to 8, and shallowness makes them disproportionately destructive because little rock lies between the rupture and the buildings. There is no volcanism.

Hotspots are the exception that proves the boundary rule. These are stationary or slowly moving mantle plumes unconnected to any plate margin, and as a plate slides overhead the plume burns an age-progressive chain of volcanoes into it. The Hawaiian-Emperor chain is the type example: Kilauea is active now, Kauai is about 5 million years old, and the pronounced bend at roughly 47 million years records a change in Pacific plate motion. Yellowstone is a continental hotspot, and Iceland is a plume sitting directly on a ridge, which is why it is so extraordinarily productive.

sections.heading: Earthquakes: mechanics and measurement
sections.body:
The governing model is elastic rebound, formulated by Harry Fielding Reid in 1910. Tectonic stress strains rock elastically along a locked fault; when accumulated shear stress exceeds frictional strength the fault ruptures, the rock snaps back past its former position, and the stored elastic strain energy radiates away as seismic waves. The focus, or hypocentre, is the point at depth where rupture begins, and the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it. Shallow events between the surface and 70 kilometres account for about 75 per cent of all earthquakes and most of the damage; intermediate events run to 300 kilometres and deep ones to 700, occurring only within subducting slabs, because below about 700 kilometres rock is too ductile to fail brittlely at all.

Waves arrive in a fixed order. P-waves come first at roughly 6 kilometres per second in crust, felt as a sharp bang. S-waves follow at about 3.5, shearing side to side with stronger shaking. Last come surface waves: Love waves shearing horizontally and Rayleigh waves rolling elliptically. Surface waves are slowest but carry the largest amplitude and do most structural damage.

That ordering also locates the epicentre. The lag between P and S arrivals grows with distance, and distance equals the lag multiplied by the product of the two speeds divided by their difference. With 6.0 and 3.5 kilometres per second the factor is 21 divided by 2.5, or 8.4 kilometres per second of lag. If a station records the S wave 20 seconds after the P wave, the source lies about 168 kilometres away, defining a circle of that radius around the station; three stations' circles intersect at a single point, which is how epicentres were found before computers.

Magnitude and intensity are routinely confused and are not the same quantity. Magnitude is one number describing energy released at the source. The modern standard is moment magnitude, two-thirds of the base-ten logarithm of the seismic moment minus 10.7, where seismic moment is the shear modulus times rupture area times average slip. Because it is logarithmic, each whole step multiplies ground-motion amplitude by ten and energy by about 31.6, so a magnitude 7 releases roughly a thousand times the energy of a magnitude 5, and the magnitude 9.5 Chilean event of 1960 released more than every other twentieth-century earthquake combined. Intensity, on the Modified Mercalli scale from one to twelve, measures observed shaking and damage at a particular place, so a single earthquake has many intensities that fall with distance and vary with ground conditions.

Secondary hazards often outweigh the shaking. In liquefaction, saturated loose sand loses all strength as shaking raises pore water pressure until effective stress, the total stress minus the pore pressure, reaches zero, and buildings sink or float. Fire from ruptured gas mains caused about 80 per cent of the destruction in San Francisco in 1906. Tsunami speed is the square root of gravity times water depth: over 4,000 metres of ocean that is roughly 198 metres per second, while the wave may stand under a metre high with a 200 kilometre wavelength and pass beneath a ship unnoticed.

sections.heading: Volcanoes: why some ooze and some explode
sections.body:
The single most important variable is magma viscosity, which is set by silica content, temperature and dissolved gas. Silica tetrahedra polymerise into chains and networks, so more silica means more polymerisation, higher viscosity, and gas that cannot escape; higher temperature breaks those bonds and thins the melt. Basaltic magma carries 45 to 55 per cent silica at 1,000 to 1,200 degrees Celsius, with viscosity around a hundred to a thousand pascal seconds, so gas escapes freely and eruptions are effusive, producing fluid flows in Hawaiian or Strombolian style and building broad shield volcanoes with slopes of only 2 to 10 degrees; Mauna Loa is 120 kilometres across and 9 kilometres tall from its seafloor base. Andesitic magma at 55 to 65 per cent silica and 800 to 1,000 degrees alternates between explosive and effusive behaviour, building steep composite cones of 30 to 35 degrees from interlayered lava and fragmental debris, as at Fuji, Rainier, Vesuvius and Mayon. Rhyolitic magma at 65 to 75 per cent silica and only 650 to 800 degrees reaches viscosities of a million to a million million pascal seconds, traps gas at high pressure, and erupts catastrophically in Plinian style, building lava domes and calderas tens of kilometres across such as Yellowstone, Toba and Campi Flegrei.

The trigger itself is exsolution. Dissolved water and carbon dioxide come out of solution as magma rises and pressure falls, because solubility is proportional to pressure. In fluid basalt the bubbles simply rise out. In viscous rhyolite they cannot, so gas pressure builds until the magma fragments explosively, which is precisely the mechanism of a shaken carbonated drink opened suddenly. The Volcanic Explosivity Index scales logarithmically with erupted volume, from under ten thousand cubic metres at index zero through a billion at index four, as at Eyjafjallajokull in 2010, ten billion at index five for St Helens in 1980 and Vesuvius in 79, a hundred billion at index six for Pinatubo and Krakatoa, a trillion at index seven for Tambora in 1815, and ten trillion at index eight for Toba and Yellowstone.

Ranked by lethality, lava flows sit near the bottom because they are usually slow enough to walk away from. The deadliest hazard is the pyroclastic density current, a ground-hugging avalanche of gas and ash at 100 to 700 degrees moving 100 to 700 kilometres per hour, which is unsurvivable and cannot be outrun; such currents killed Pompeii, Herculaneum and the 28,000 people of Saint-Pierre in 1902. Lahars, volcanic mudflows with the consistency of wet concrete, travel 50 to 100 kilometres per hour down valleys for tens of kilometres, and a small eruption at Nevado del Ruiz in 1985 melted a summit glacier and buried Armero, killing about 23,000 people 50 kilometres away. Ash fall collapses roofs above roughly 100 kilograms per square metre, about 10 centimetres of wet ash, and is abrasive angular glass rather than soft like wood ash. Carbon dioxide, denser than air, pools invisibly in hollows, as at Lake Nyos in 1986. Sulphur dioxide injected into the stratosphere cools climate: Tambora produced the year without a summer in 1816.

sections.heading: Practical survival: earthquake, tsunami and volcano
sections.body:
The evidence-based action during shaking is to drop, cover and hold on. Drop to hands and knees before the shaking drops you, take cover under a sturdy table or, failing that, against an interior wall away from windows while covering head and neck, and hold on to the furniture so you move with it rather than losing it. Do not run outside while the ground is moving: most injuries come from debris falling at building exteriors, and doorways in modern buildings are no stronger than any other wall. Do not use lifts. In bed, stay there and cover your head with a pillow unless a heavy light fitting hangs above you. Outdoors, move to open ground away from buildings, power lines and free-standing walls. Driving, pull over clear of overpasses, bridges and wires, stay in the vehicle and set the handbrake. Afterwards expect aftershocks; the largest is typically about 1.2 magnitude units below the mainshock and their frequency decays roughly as one over elapsed time, a pattern known as Omori's law. Shut off gas only if you smell or hear a leak, wear sturdy shoes against broken glass, and text rather than call to keep networks clear. Preparation is cheap: bolt tall furniture and water heaters to studs, store four litres of water per person per day for seven days, and keep shoes and a torch beside the bed.

For tsunami the natural warning signs are the instruction to evacuate, and waiting for an official alert can be fatal because a local source may arrive in minutes. If you are near the coast and feel an earthquake strong enough to make standing difficult, or one lasting more than about 20 seconds; or if the sea withdraws and exposes the seafloor, leave at once. Move on foot, because roads jam, to at least 30 metres above sea level or 3 kilometres inland, and stay there. The first wave is often not the largest and the sequence can run 8 to 12 hours with waves 10 to 60 minutes apart. A 30 centimetre flow can knock an adult over.

Around volcanoes, exclusion zones are drawn around the reach of pyroclastic flows and lahars rather than lava, so obey them absolutely. Never enter a valley draining a snow-capped or erupting volcano, and if you feel shaking or hear a roar in such a valley, climb sideways to high ground immediately, since 20 to 30 metres of vertical elevation out of the channel survives most lahars. In ash fall stay indoors with windows and vents closed, wear an N95 or P2 respirator, choose goggles over contact lenses because ash beneath a lens abrades the cornea, sweep roofs before accumulation exceeds about 10 centimetres given that wet ash weighs roughly twice dry ash, and do not drive.

Several widespread beliefs are wrong. The triangle of life advice is discredited; do not lie beside furniture. Small earthquakes do not relieve pressure, since about 32,000 magnitude 4 events equal one magnitude 7. Animals give no reliable warning, and river valleys near a coast are not safe from tsunami, which run far up channels.

sections.heading: Paleomagnetism and the Seafloor Stripes That Proved It All
sections.body:
Plate tectonics moved from fringe idea to established science largely because of rock magnetism. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and was dismissed for decades, not because his evidence was weak but because he could offer no mechanism, and his proposed one, continents ploughing through oceanic crust, was physically impossible. The decisive evidence came from the ocean floor half a century later.

The physics underneath is straightforward. As basaltic lava cools through its Curie point, around 580 degrees Celsius for magnetite, its magnetic minerals lock into alignment with Earth's field as it stands at that moment, like a compass needle frozen mid-swing. This is remanent magnetism, and it persists for hundreds of millions of years unless the rock is reheated. Earth's field has reversed polarity hundreds of times across geological history at irregular intervals averaging a few hundred thousand years, with the most recent reversal about 780,000 years ago, and every reversal is written into whatever rock happens to be cooling at the time.

In the early 1960s magnetometers towed behind ships crossing mid-ocean ridges revealed bands of alternating normal and reversed polarity running parallel to the ridge crest, and crucially symmetric on both sides, like a barcode mirrored about its centre line. Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews at Cambridge, and independently Lawrence Morley in Canada, recognised in 1963 that this was precisely what seafloor spreading must produce: new crust wells up at the ridge axis, splits in two, and rafts away in both directions at a steady rate, so each half records the same sequence of reversals as it cools. Morley's paper was rejected by two journals before Vine and Matthews published, a reminder that priority in science is partly an accident of editorial nerve.

The power of the result is that it converts a pattern into a measurement. Match the width of each stripe against the independently dated reversal timescale, worked out from lava flows on land whose ages came from potassium-argon dating, and you obtain a spreading rate directly. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads at roughly 2 to 5 centimetres per year, about the rate fingernails grow, while the East Pacific Rise reaches 15. Where the stripes are wide the ridge spread fast; where narrow, slow. The same data explain why no seafloor anywhere is older than about 180 million years: ocean crust is continuously created and continuously consumed at trenches, so the ocean floor is a conveyor belt rather than an archive. This single dataset did more than any other to make plate tectonics a measured fact, giving geologists a clock and a ruler for something that had been inferred only from the jigsaw fit of coastlines.

sections.heading: Hotspots and Mantle Plumes: Volcanoes That Don't Follow the Boundary Rule
sections.body:
Almost all volcanism happens at plate boundaries, which makes Hawaii a genuine anomaly. The islands sit near the dead centre of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometres from the nearest margin, and are among the most productive volcanoes on Earth. The explanation, proposed by J. Tuzo Wilson in 1963, is a hotspot: a plume of unusually hot rock rising from deep in the mantle that stays essentially fixed in position while the plate above it drifts overhead. The plate does the moving, so the plume burns a chain of volcanoes into the seafloor much as a blowtorch held steady beneath a sheet of paper dragged across it leaves a line of scorch marks. Each island is therefore progressively older, more eroded and more subsided the farther it lies from the currently active vent.

The Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain is the textbook case and the numbers are checkable. Kilauea sits over the hotspot today, with the submarine seamount Loihi already growing to the southeast as the next island. Kauai, at the northwestern end of the main islands, is about 5 million years old. The chain continues as drowned seamounts for more than 5,800 kilometres to the Aleutian Trench, with ages rising systematically past 80 million years. Divide distance by age difference and you recover the Pacific Plate's velocity independently of any other method, which is why hotspot tracks became a reference frame for plate motion in the first place.

A striking bend of roughly 60 degrees at about 47 million years has been debated for decades. The traditional reading is that the Pacific Plate changed direction. Palaeomagnetic sampling of the Emperor seamounts, however, shows their latitude of formation shifted, implying the plume itself drifted southward at several centimetres per year during that period. The honest position is that both plate motion change and plume drift probably contributed, and that fixed hotspots are an approximation rather than a law. Whether deep plumes exist at all in the form Wilson imagined remains contested; seismic tomography now images low-velocity columns beneath Hawaii and Iceland reaching toward the core-mantle boundary, but the resolution is imperfect and alternative shallow-mantle explanations have serious advocates.

Not every hotspot is oceanic. Yellowstone sits beneath thick continental crust, and the Snake River Plain preserves a matching age-progressive trail of ancient calderas leading back toward it across Idaho. The same mechanism erupting through continental crust behaves very differently, because rising basalt melts and assimilates silica-rich continental rock, producing viscous rhyolite and eruptions vastly more violent than anything Hawaii produces. The Iceland case is different again: a plume sitting directly beneath a spreading ridge, so plume heat and ridge decompression melting reinforce one another and build enough crust to lift the ridge above sea level, which is why Iceland exists as dry land at all when the rest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge lies two kilometres underwater.

sections.heading: Historical Earthquakes and Eruptions That Rewrote Hazard Science
sections.body:
Several individual disasters did more than cause damage; they changed how the science is done, and tracing that is the quickest route to understanding why current hazard practice looks the way it does. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake gave Harry Fielding Reid the dataset he needed. Surveying ground displacement along the San Andreas Fault, he found offset greatest immediately at the fault and tapering with distance on either side, exactly as if the crust had been sheared elastically for decades and then released. From that he formulated elastic rebound theory in 1910, still the core model of earthquake generation: rock stores strain energy as tectonic stress slowly builds, then snaps back past its original position when frictional strength is exceeded, radiating the stored energy as seismic waves. Everything from recurrence-interval estimation to fault-slip budgets rests on that picture.

The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile, moment magnitude 9.5, remains the largest ever instrumentally recorded and exposed a measurement problem. The Richter scale and other amplitude-based magnitudes saturate: above roughly magnitude 8 the seismometer readings they depend on stop growing with the true size of the rupture, so genuinely enormous events all report about the same number. Valdivia ruptured roughly 1,000 kilometres of fault with up to 20 metres of slip, and no amplitude scale could express that. Moment magnitude, built directly from rupture area, average slip and rock rigidity, was developed to fix exactly this and does not saturate.

The 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens rewrote volcanic hazard mapping. The volcano's north flank had been visibly bulging outward for weeks as magma intruded; when a magnitude 5.1 earthquake destabilised it, the entire flank slid away in the largest landslide in recorded history, instantly unroofing the pressurised magma system. The result was a lateral blast that flattened forest 30 kilometres away in a sector no hazard plan had drawn, because plans assumed eruptions go upward and then downslope. Modern maps include lateral blast sectors and edifice-collapse scenarios because of that morning.

The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo, forecast well enough to evacuate tens of thousands, injected roughly 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. That gas converted to a global sulphate aerosol haze that reflected sunlight and cooled global mean surface temperature by about 0.5 degrees Celsius for more than a year before the aerosols settled out. It was the first such event observed by comprehensive satellite instrumentation, and it provided a natural experiment against which climate models could be tested; models that had predicted the cooling correctly gained considerable credibility. The same mechanism underlies proposals for deliberate stratospheric aerosol injection, and the same eruption is the standard cautionary reference for their side effects.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
You do not need a seismic network to start observing plate tectonics directly. A surprising amount is within reach with basic field gear plus disciplined attention to freely published data, and the central skill is not equipment handling but knowing what a given observation can and cannot establish.

Two measurements dominate structural fieldwork: strike and dip. Strike is the compass bearing of a horizontal line drawn on an inclined rock surface, and dip is the angle that surface descends from horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike. Together they define the orientation of any planar feature — a bedding plane, a fault surface, a dyke — in three dimensions with two numbers. A smartphone clinometer is adequate to a degree or two, which is enough to distinguish a gently tilted sedimentary sequence from a steeply overturned one, though metal in the phone and nearby ironwork can deflect the compass badly, so cross-check against a known bearing before trusting a reading.

Public earthquake catalogues are the single most powerful free resource. Every significant national survey publishes near-real-time location, depth and magnitude. Plotting a month of events against a plate-boundary map makes the theory visible in a way no textbook figure does: depths stay shallow along ridges and transforms, and deepen systematically inland from trenches along the inclined plane of the subducting slab. Depth is the variable most people ignore and the one that carries the most information.

A word on hazards, because geological fieldwork injures people in mundane ways. Quarry and roadcut faces shed rock without warning, especially after rain or frost; stay back from the base by at least the height of the face where you can. Fresh volcanic ash is not soot but microscopically angular glass shards that scour lung tissue and scratch corneas, so a fitted particulate respirator and sealed goggles are genuine protective equipment rather than caution theatre. Hammering rock without eye protection is how geologists lose eyes, and struck flakes leave a hammer face at speeds that ordinary spectacles will not stop.
ingredients: A topographic or geologic map of your region (many national geological surveys publish these freely) to locate nearby faults, volcanic fields, or uplifted terrain
A compass and clinometer, or a smartphone compass/clinometer app, for measuring strike and dip of exposed rock near a fault
A basic rock hammer and hand lens for examining volcanic or fault-zone rock samples up close
Sturdy closed-toe boots, work gloves, and safety glasses for any visit to a fault scarp, quarry, or volcanic outcrop
A dust mask or respirator rated for fine particulates if visiting any site with volcanic ash — ash is sharp-edged glass shards microscopically and genuinely damaging to lungs with prolonged exposure
Simple building materials (a wooden board, string, a heavy weight such as a fishing sinker or metal washer, a pen, and a roll of paper) to build a basic pendulum seismometer
Access to a public earthquake catalog (most national geological surveys publish free, real-time earthquake location and magnitude data) for plotting recent seismicity against a plate boundary map

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build a Simple Pendulum Seismometer and Record Real Ground Motion
sections.body:
A device that registers footsteps or a passing truck can be built on a kitchen table in under an hour, on the same principle as a professional instrument. That principle is inertia. A seismometer measures relative motion between the ground and a suspended mass that resists being moved: when the ground shifts, the frame moves with it while the mass briefly stays behind.

The key parameter is the pendulum's natural period, which for a simple pendulum is two pi times the square root of length over gravitational acceleration. A 40 centimetre string gives a period near 1.3 seconds. This matters because a pendulum responds strongly near its own natural frequency and poorly to motion much slower. Distant large earthquakes arrive dominated by surface waves of 10 to 30 seconds, which a short tabletop pendulum barely notices; real instruments therefore use suspensions engineered for periods of many seconds.

The second limitation is damping. A pen dragging on paper is heavily damped by friction, so the trace dies out almost immediately and small motions never register. Real instruments aim for about 70 per cent of critical damping, enough to stop the mass ringing without suppressing the signal, and they use electromagnetic sensing because friction cannot be tuned. Expect honestly that this will never record a real earthquake: distant ground motion is measured in micrometres.
steps: Fix a sturdy board or heavy frame to a solid surface (a table pressed against a wall, or a shelf bolted to a stud) so it won't wobble independently of the ground.
Hang a weight (200–500 g, such as a padlock or a bag of washers) from a length of string about 30–40 cm long, tied to the fixed frame, forming a simple pendulum.
Tape a pen or fine marker to the bottom of the hanging weight, pointing straight down, with the tip just barely touching a horizontal surface below.

Place a long strip of paper on that surface, positioned so the pen tip rests near one end, and set up a way to draw the paper under the pen over several minutes — even manually, at a slow steady rate — as your recording drum.
Let the pendulum settle to a full stop before starting a recording so your baseline is a straight line.

Generate a test disturbance — have someone jump near the table, or gently tap the frame — and watch the pen trace deviate from the straight line; note the amplitude and how long the oscillation takes to die out.

Compare traces from different disturbances (a light tap vs. a heavy footstep vs. a nearby door slam) and record which produces the largest amplitude — this mirrors how a real seismogram distinguishes a small local event from a larger, more distant one.

Look up a recent moderate earthquake in a public earthquake catalog and note its magnitude and distance from a seismic station, then consider why your tabletop pendulum, unlike a real seismometer, is far too damped and insensitive to register any actual earthquake — real instruments use a near-frictionless suspended mass and electromagnetic sensors because distant ground motion is measured in micrometers.

guides.title: The Water Cycle & Hydrology
guides.summary: Where Earth's water is, the physics that moves it, how rivers and groundwater actually work, how to read a catchment, and how to find, judge and treat water in the field.

sections.heading: The global water budget: where the water actually is
sections.body:
Earth holds roughly 1.386 billion cubic kilometres of water, and its distribution is startlingly lopsided. The oceans account for 1,338,000,000 cubic kilometres, or 96.5 per cent of the total, and all of it is saline. Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow hold 24,064,000 cubic kilometres, 1.74 per cent. Groundwater holds 23,400,000 cubic kilometres, 1.69 per cent, though only about 10,530,000 of that, some 0.76 per cent of the world total, is fresh. Below those three reservoirs the numbers fall away sharply: ground ice and permafrost 300,000 cubic kilometres, lakes 176,400 (of which 91,000 is fresh), soil moisture 16,500, the entire atmosphere 12,900, swamps and marshes 11,470, all the world's rivers together just 2,120, and the water inside every living organism on the planet 1,120.

Fresh water is therefore only about 2.5 per cent of the total, and roughly 69 per cent of that fraction is locked in ice, 30 per cent is underground, and well under 1 per cent sits in the accessible surface water on which nearly all terrestrial life depends. The rivers are the most striking case. They contain less than one part in 650,000 of Earth's water, a rounding error in the global ledger, yet they carry the overwhelming bulk of the flux and do most of the work of moving water, sediment and dissolved chemistry across continents. Volume stored and volume transported are entirely different quantities, and confusing them is the commonest error in reading a water budget.

The annual fluxes close the system. About 505,000 cubic kilometres evaporate each year, 434,000 from the ocean surface and 71,000 from land, and the same total returns as precipitation, 398,000 over the ocean and 107,000 over land. Land therefore receives 36,000 cubic kilometres more than it loses to the air, and exactly that surplus flows back to the sea as river discharge and groundwater seepage. This equality is the closure condition of the water cycle: over any long averaging period, global evaporation must equal global precipitation, because there is nowhere else for the water to go.

Residence time makes the whole structure intuitive. It is defined as the stored volume divided by the flux through the reservoir, and it tells you how long a typical water molecule stays put. The atmosphere holds water for about nine days, which is precisely why weather forecasting has a useful horizon of roughly a week and no more. Rivers hold it two to six months, soil moisture one to two months, lakes 50 to 100 years, shallow groundwater 100 to 200 years, deep groundwater as long as 10,000 years, the oceans about 3,200 years, and Antarctic ice up to 800,000. The atmospheric figure is worth dwelling on: a reservoir of only 12,900 cubic kilometres cycles 505,000 cubic kilometres per year, meaning the entire water content of the sky is replaced about 39 times annually. That rapid turnover is what makes the atmosphere a conveyor rather than a store, and it is why a drought is never caused by the air running out of water.

sections.heading: The physics: why water moves at all
sections.body:
Water is driven around the planet by exactly two energy sources, sunlight lifting it into the air and gravity pulling it back down, and its unusual molecular properties account for nearly everything else. Because the water molecule is bent and its oxygen pulls electrons away from its hydrogens, each molecule is electrically lopsided and forms hydrogen bonds with its neighbours. From that one fact follow a specific heat capacity of 4184 joules per kilogram per kelvin, the highest of any common liquid, which is why oceans moderate climate and coastal towns have milder winters than inland ones; a latent heat of vaporisation of 2.26 million joules per kilogram at 100 degrees C, rising to about 2.45 million at 20 degrees C, meaning evaporating one kilogram of water absorbs as much energy as heating that same kilogram by 540 degrees would; a latent heat of fusion of 334,000 joules per kilogram; and a density maximum at 4 degrees C rather than at freezing, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down, leaving liquid water and living things beneath.

Evaporation requires both an energy supply and a vapour-pressure deficit, meaning the air must be able to accept more water than it currently holds. Saturation vapour pressure climbs roughly exponentially with temperature, and the Clausius-Clapeyron relation gives about 7 per cent more capacity per degree of warming. A workable approximation is e_s(T) = 0.6108 x exp(17.27 x T / (T + 237.3)), with e_s in kilopascals and T in degrees C. At 20 degrees the saturation pressure is about 2.34 kPa; at 30 degrees it is 4.24 kPa, nearly double. Relative humidity is the actual vapour pressure divided by that saturation value, expressed as a percentage, and the dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins. The dew point, not the relative humidity, is the number that actually tells you how muggy the air feels, because relative humidity changes through the day merely because the temperature does.

Evapotranspiration combines evaporation from surfaces with transpiration through the pores in plant leaves, and over vegetated land transpiration usually dominates. A single large oak can move 150 to 400 litres a day, and a hectare of maize about 40,000 litres a day at peak growth.

Precipitation begins when air rises, expands against falling pressure, and cools without exchanging heat with its surroundings.
