The dry adiabatic lapse rate is 9.8 degrees C per kilometre of ascent; once the parcel saturates, the latent heat released by condensation slows cooling to a saturated rate of about 4 to 7 degrees per kilometre. At the dew point, water condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei such as dust, sea salt, sulphates and pollen, typically 0.2 to 2 micrometres across. Cloud droplets are only about 20 micrometres and fall far too slowly to reach the ground; they must grow to roughly 500 to 1000 micrometres, either by collision and coalescence or by the Bergeron process, in which ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets because saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over liquid water. Four mechanisms lift the air in the first place: convective heating producing thunderstorms, orographic forcing over mountains giving a wet windward slope and a dry rain shadow behind it, frontal lifting as warm air rides over cold, and convergence into a low-pressure zone. The Atacama, Death Valley and the Tibetan Plateau are all rain shadows.

sections.heading: Catchments, runoff and the water balance
sections.body:
A CATCHMENT (watershed, drainage basin) is the entire area of land whose precipitation drains to one common outlet. Catchments are separated by DIVIDES — the ridge lines. Every point on Earth is in exactly one catchment at every scale, nested like a tree. Stream ORDER (Strahler) formalises the tree: a headwater stream with no tributaries is order 1; two order-1 streams join to make an order 2; two order-2s make an order 3; an order-1 joining an order-3 leaves it order 3. The Amazon is order 12. Each order up, the number of streams falls by roughly a factor of 3–5 and the average length rises by a similar factor.
The WATER BALANCE EQUATION is the master accounting identity for any catchment over any period:
P = Q + ET + ΔS
where P = precipitation (mm), Q = runoff/streamflow leaving the basin (mm), ET = evapotranspiration (mm) and ΔS = change in storage (soil moisture + groundwater + snowpack + surface water, mm). All terms are usually expressed as a depth of water over the whole catchment area. Over a long enough period (many years) ΔS ≈ 0, so P ≈ Q + ET.
WORKED EXAMPLE. A catchment of 250 km² receives 900 mm/yr of precipitation. Measured streamflow at the outlet averages 4.0 m³/s. Convert flow to a depth: annual volume = 4.0 m³/s × 31,557,600 s = 1.262 × 10⁸ m³. Divided by the area, 250 km² = 2.5 × 10⁸ m², gives 0.505 m = 505 mm. So Q = 505 mm. Assuming ΔS ≈ 0, ET = P − Q = 900 − 505 = 395 mm/yr. The RUNOFF COEFFICIENT is Q/P = 505/900 = 0.56, meaning 56% of rainfall leaves as streamflow — typical of a temperate, moderately vegetated basin. A forested tropical basin might be 0.2; a paved urban basin 0.8–0.95.
When rain falls it partitions: INTERCEPTION (caught on leaves, 10–40% of small rainfalls in forest, mostly re-evaporated), INFILTRATION into soil, and OVERLAND FLOW when rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration capacity (Hortonian) or when the soil saturates from below (saturation-excess). Infiltration capacity is high at the start of a storm and decays toward the soil's saturated hydraulic conductivity — sand 20–100 mm/hr, silt loam 5–20 mm/hr, clay 0.1–1 mm/hr. This is why the same 30 mm/hr downpour runs straight off clay and vanishes into sand.
The STORM HYDROGRAPH plots discharge against time: a rising limb, a peak, then a long recession limb, with LAG TIME between the rainfall centroid and the peak. Urbanisation, deforestation, steep slopes, thin soils and antecedent wetness all shorten lag time and raise the peak — this is precisely the mechanism of flash flooding. BASE FLOW, the discharge sustained between storms, is groundwater seeping into the channel; a river that keeps flowing in drought is being fed by its aquifer.

sections.heading: Rivers: how channels do their work
sections.body:
DISCHARGE is the fundamental measurement: Q = A × v, where Q is discharge in m³/s (cumecs), A the cross-sectional area of flow in m², and v the mean velocity in m/s. To measure it in the field: stretch a tape across the channel, divide the width into 10–20 segments, at each segment measure depth and measure velocity at 0.6 of the depth from the surface (that single point closely approximates the depth-averaged velocity), then sum A_i × v_i over all segments. A rough float method: time a floating object over a measured 10 m reach, take the mean of at least 3 trials, and multiply the surface velocity by 0.85 to estimate the mean.
MANNING'S EQUATION predicts velocity from channel geometry:
v = (1/n) · R^(2/3) · S^(1/2)
where v is mean velocity (m/s), n is Manning's roughness coefficient (dimensionless: 0.010 for smooth concrete, 0.030 for a clean natural earth channel, 0.040 for a gravel-bed stream with weeds, 0.070–0.15 for a heavily vegetated floodplain), R is the hydraulic radius = A/P with P the wetted perimeter (m), and S is the energy slope (m/m, approximated by the water-surface slope). WORKED EXAMPLE: a channel 8 m wide and 1.2 m deep has A = 9.6 m², wetted perimeter P = 8 + 2(1.2) = 10.4 m, so R = 0.923 m. With a gravel bed (n = 0.040) and a slope of 0.002, v = (1/0.040) × 0.923^0.667 × 0.002^0.5 = 25 × 0.948 × 0.0447 = 1.06 m/s. Discharge Q = 9.6 × 1.06 ≈ 10.2 m³/s.
SEDIMENT AND ENERGY. A river transports material as dissolved load, suspended load (which makes it look brown and is usually the largest fraction by mass), and bed load (rolling, sliding and saltating grains). The HJULSTRÖM CURVE captures a counterintuitive fact: the velocity needed to ERODE a particle is not a simple function of grain size. Sand around 0.2–0.5 mm is entrained at the lowest velocity, about 20–30 cm/s. Coarser gravel needs more velocity because it is heavier; but fine clay ALSO needs more velocity (up to 100 cm/s) because electrostatic cohesion binds the platelets. Once moving, however, clay stays in suspension almost indefinitely — it only settles below about 0.1 cm/s. This is why muddy water clears so slowly, and why a dredged clay bank resists re-erosion.
CHANNEL FORMS. Steep headwaters are straight and boulder-choked with a V-shaped valley, high gradient, and erosion dominant. Middle reaches MEANDER: flow spirals helically, eroding the outside of a bend (the cut bank, deep, fast) and depositing on the inside (the point bar, shallow, slow). Meander wavelength is empirically about 10–14 times the channel width. Necks eventually cut through, abandoning an OXBOW LAKE. Lower reaches are low-gradient, deposit-dominated, and build floodplains, levees and finally a DELTA where the current dies at the sea. The GRADED PROFILE — steep at the head, concave, near-flat at the mouth — is a river's equilibrium form, adjusting toward the minimum work needed to transport its sediment load.
FLOODS are described by RECURRENCE INTERVAL: T = (n + 1)/m, where n is the number of years of record and m is the rank of the flood by size. A "100-year flood" has a 1% chance of being exceeded in any given year — it is a probability, not a schedule, and two can occur in consecutive years. The probability of at least one T-year flood in N years is 1 − (1 − 1/T)^N; over a 30-year mortgage, the chance of at least one 100-year flood is 1 − 0.99³⁰ = 26%.

sections.heading: Groundwater: the invisible reservoir
sections.body:
Rain that infiltrates percolates down through the UNSATURATED (vadose) zone, where pores hold both air and water, to the WATER TABLE — the surface below which every pore is full. Below that is the SATURATED zone. The water table is not flat; it is a subdued replica of the topography, higher under hills and intersecting the surface at springs, lakes and perennial streams.
TWO PROPERTIES govern everything. POROSITY (n) is the percentage of a rock's volume that is void space — gravel 25–40%, sand 25–50%, clay 40–70%, fractured basalt 5–50%, unfractured granite under 1%. PERMEABILITY (hydraulic conductivity, K, in m/day) is the ability to TRANSMIT water, which depends on whether the pores connect and how large they are. Clay has enormous porosity but almost no permeability, because its pores are microscopic and water is held by surface tension — this is the crucial distinction and the most common misunderstanding in hydrogeology. Typical K: gravel 100–1000 m/day, coarse sand 10–100, fine sand 1–10, silt 0.001–0.1, clay 10⁻⁶–10⁻³.
DARCY'S LAW governs groundwater flow:
Q = −K · A · (dh/dl)
where Q is volumetric flow (m³/day), K hydraulic conductivity (m/day), A cross-sectional area (m²), and dh/dl the hydraulic gradient (the drop in head per unit distance, dimensionless). The negative sign means flow goes from high head to low head. WORKED EXAMPLE: an aquifer of coarse sand (K = 30 m/day) is 10 m thick and 200 m wide (A = 2000 m²), and the water table falls 4 m over 800 m of distance (gradient = 0.005). Q = 30 × 2000 × 0.005 = 300 m³/day. The actual water velocity is much slower than this bulk flux suggests: seepage velocity v = K·(dh/dl)/n = 30 × 0.005 / 0.30 = 0.5 m/day. Groundwater typically moves centimetres to a few metres per day — a contaminant plume may take decades to reach a well, and an aquifer polluted today may not be recognised as polluted for a generation.
AQUIFER TYPES: an UNCONFINED aquifer has the water table as its upper surface and is recharged directly from above (and is therefore vulnerable to surface pollution). A CONFINED aquifer is sandwiched between AQUITARDS (low-permeability layers) and is under pressure; drilling into one produces an ARTESIAN well, where water rises above the top of the aquifer, and sometimes flows at the surface without pumping. A PERCHED aquifer sits on a local impermeable lens above the regional water table.
Pumping creates a CONE OF DEPRESSION around a well; over-pumping causes wells to go dry, land SUBSIDENCE (California's San Joaquin Valley has sunk over 8.5 m in places), and SALTWATER INTRUSION at coasts. The Ghyben-Herzberg relation quantifies the last: because fresh water (1000 kg/m³) floats on salt water (1025 kg/m³), z = 40h, meaning for every 1 m the water table sits above sea level, the fresh-water lens extends about 40 m below sea level. Drop the water table 1 m by pumping and the salt interface rises 40 m — which is why small-island and coastal aquifers fail so abruptly.

sections.heading: Finding water in the field: reading the landscape
sections.body:
The hydrological principles above translate directly into where to look when you need water and have no map.
1. FOLLOW GRAVITY AND GREEN. Water collects in the lowest point of any drainage. Trace valleys and gullies downhill; walk toward converging contours. Vegetation is the best indicator: a distinct line or clump of greener, denser, broadleaf growth in dry country marks shallow water. Willows, cottonwoods, sycamores, cattails, reeds, sedges and rushes are phreatophytes — their roots reach the water table, so they mark it. A band of them across a dry hillside marks a seep line.
2. READ THE GEOLOGY. Springs emerge where a permeable layer sits on an impermeable one and the contact is exposed — look along the base of a sandstone or limestone cliff where it meets shale, along fault traces, and at the foot of talus slopes. In limestone country, look for resurgences at the base of hills. At the toe of any large debris or scree slope, water that sank into the coarse material often reappears.
3. DIG, DON'T DESPAIR. In a dry sandy or gravelly streambed, dig on the OUTSIDE of the last bend (the deepest scour, the cut bank), on the downstream side of any obstruction, or at the lowest point. Dig a hole 30–60 cm across and go down 30–100 cm; let it fill and settle for 30+ minutes so silt drops out. This is a seepage well, and it also filters the water through sand, though it does NOT make it microbiologically safe.
4. COASTS AND DUNES. Fresh rainwater floats as a thin lens on salt water. Dig behind the first dune line, above the high-tide mark, only until water appears — dig deeper and you break into salt. Skim the top of the water.
5. COLLECT DIRECTLY. Rainfall from a tarp or poncho funnel is the cleanest source available and needs no treatment if the collecting surface is clean. Dew: drag an absorbent cloth over grass before dawn and wring it out; a person can gather 0.5–1 litre per hour on a heavy dew. Snow and ice: always melt before drinking — eating snow costs 334 kJ per kg of body heat and accelerates hypothermia. Melt old, compacted snow or ice, which yields far more water per volume than fresh powder.
6. TRANSPIRATION BAG. Tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy, non-toxic branch in sun with a weighted low corner; transpired vapour condenses and collects. Yield is modest — 50–250 mL per bag per day — and you must verify the plant is not toxic (avoid oleander, yew, poison ivy/oak/sumac and any milky-sapped plant). A SOLAR STILL dug in soil is usually not worth the calories: typical yield is under 500 mL/day for hours of digging, less than the sweat spent.
WHAT TO AVOID: stagnant water with no outlet, no insects and no green plants around it; water with a chemical or petroleum sheen (a bacterial iron sheen breaks into plates when poked, an oil sheen swirls back together); water downstream of mines, tailings, farms, feedlots or industry; and alkali flats where salt crusts show at the edges. Never drink seawater or urine — both raise your osmotic load and dehydrate you faster.

sections.heading: Making water safe: treatment methods with real numbers
sections.body:
Water carries three hazard classes and no single field method removes all three. PATHOGENS: protozoan cysts (Giardia 8–12 µm, Cryptosporidium 4–6 µm — the latter highly chlorine-resistant), bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae, 0.2–5 µm), and viruses (hepatitis A, rotavirus, norovirus, 0.02–0.1 µm). CHEMICALS: arsenic, nitrate, fluoride, lead, pesticides, industrial solvents. TURBIDITY: suspended sediment, which is not itself dangerous but shields pathogens from disinfection and consumes chemical disinfectant.
STEP 1 — CLARIFY FIRST, ALWAYS. Every disinfection method works far better on clear water. Let sediment settle for several hours; decant the clear top. Then filter through tightly woven cloth folded 4–8 times, or through a simple gravity column: a container with a small hole, packed bottom-up with cloth, then 10 cm of clean coarse gravel, 10 cm of coarse sand, 15–20 cm of fine sand, and optionally 5 cm of crushed charcoal from a hardwood fire (charcoal adsorbs some organics, tastes and odours — it does NOT disinfect and it exhausts within days). Discard the first litre through a new column.
STEP 2 — DISINFECT. Choose by hazard:
• BOILING — the gold standard, kills everything biological. Bring to a rolling boil and hold 1 minute at sea level; hold 3 minutes above 2000 m (water boils at about 93 °C at 2000 m and 80 °C at 6000 m, but pasteurisation still occurs at 70 °C given time). Boiling does NOT remove chemicals, salts or heavy metals — it concentrates them.
• CHLORINE (unscented household bleach, sodium hypochlorite). For 5–6% bleach: 2 drops per litre of clear water, 4 drops per litre if cold or cloudy. For 8.25% bleach: 2 drops per litre. Stir, wait 30 minutes (60 minutes if the water is below 10 °C or cloudy). The water should have a faint chlorine smell; if not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. Kills bacteria and viruses reliably; kills Giardia given time; does NOT reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Use only plain bleach — no scent, no detergent, no thickener — and note bleach loses roughly half its strength per year.
• IODINE (2% tincture): 5 drops per litre clear, 10 drops per litre cloudy, wait 30 minutes (longer when cold). Not for pregnant women, people with thyroid disorders, or continuous use beyond a few weeks. Ineffective against Cryptosporidium.
• SODIS (solar disinfection) — fill a clear PET plastic bottle (max 2 L, max 10 cm diameter) with clear water, lay it on its side on a reflective or dark surface, and expose to full sun for 6 hours (or 2 consecutive days if overcast). UV-A plus heat inactivates bacteria, viruses and protozoa. It requires genuinely clear water (you must be able to read text through the filled bottle) and does not work in glass, which blocks UV-A.
• FILTERS — a filter rated at 1 µm absolute removes protozoa and most bacteria but NOT viruses; a 0.2 µm filter removes bacteria too. Only a purifier rated to 0.02 µm or a chemical/UV step handles viruses. In a wilderness setting where viral contamination is unlikely, a good filter alone is usually sufficient; downstream of human habitation, always add a chemical or boiling step.
• DISTILLATION is the only field method that removes salt, heavy metals and most chemicals — condense steam on a cool surface and collect it. It is slow and fuel-expensive but it is the answer for seawater or chemically contaminated sources.
SAFETY AND COMMON MISTAKES. Do not assume clear, cold, fast-moving mountain water is safe — Giardia is common in pristine-looking streams. Do not rely on charcoal or a cloth filter as disinfection. Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids. Do not over-chlorinate hoping for extra safety. Store treated water in a clean, covered container and do not re-contaminate it with dirty hands or a dirty scoop. Rehydrating: an adult at rest in a temperate climate needs about 2–3 litres a day, rising to 4–6+ litres with heat and exertion; dark, scanty urine is the practical warning sign. If severe diarrhoea occurs after drinking suspect water, oral rehydration matters more than the underlying infection in the short term — the WHO oral rehydration formula is roughly 6 level teaspoons of sugar plus half a level teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water. This is general education, not medical advice; seek professional medical care for persistent illness, bloody stools, high fever or signs of severe dehydration.

sections.heading: Stream Discharge and the Hydrograph: Reading a River's Pulse
sections.body:
The single most useful number in hydrology is discharge, the volume of water passing a point per unit time, written Q and measured in cubic metres per second. In principle it is trivial: Q equals cross-sectional area multiplied by average velocity. In practice both quantities are awkward to measure honestly. Velocity is not uniform across a channel. It is fastest just below the surface in mid-stream, where neither the bed nor the air is dragging on the water, and it falls to nearly zero at the bed and along the banks, where friction dominates. Area changes constantly with stage, the height of the water surface, so a measurement is only valid for the moment it was taken.

Hydrologists therefore measure velocity at a series of verticals spaced across the channel, conventionally taking a single reading at 0.6 of the depth measured down from the surface, which for a typical logarithmic velocity profile is a good approximation of the depth-averaged velocity in that vertical. Where more accuracy is needed, readings at 0.2 and 0.8 of depth are averaged instead. Each vertical is treated as representing a strip of the channel, its own area multiplied by its own velocity, and the strips are summed. This is the mid-section method, and it remains the reference technique against which modern acoustic instruments are checked.

Plotted against time, discharge traces a hydrograph: a rising limb as runoff reaches the channel, a peak, then a longer falling limb called the recession. The shape of that curve is genuinely diagnostic of the landscape upstream. A small, paved urban catchment produces what hydrologists call a flashy hydrograph, with a short lag time between rainfall and peak and a high, sharp crest, because impervious surfaces shed water almost instantly into drains that deliver it to the channel by the most direct route available. A large, forested or wetland-rich catchment produces a damped hydrograph, with a long lag and a lower, broader peak, because soil, leaf litter, vegetation and groundwater storage intercept the water, delay it, and release it along many paths of differing length.

The discharge that persists through dry weather, when no rain has fallen for weeks, is baseflow, and it is groundwater slowly draining into the channel through the bed and banks. A stream with strong baseflow is fed by an aquifer and will keep flowing through a drought; a stream that is almost entirely stormflow will go dry between rains. The ratio of stormflow to baseflow is one of the clearest available fingerprints of how heavily a landscape has been paved, drained or farmed. It is also why urbanisation is one of the most direct and measurable causes of increased downstream flooding, entirely independently of any change in how much rain falls: the same storm delivered to the same catchment produces a far higher peak once the water has been given a fast, smooth route to the river.

sections.heading: Water Quality Beyond Potability: Dissolved Oxygen and Eutrophication
sections.body:
Whether water is safe to drink and whether it is healthy for the ecosystem living in it are two different questions answered by almost entirely different numbers. A stream can be biologically dying while remaining perfectly drinkable after boiling, and a chemically pristine spring can be lethal if it carries a single pathogen. The key ecological metric is dissolved oxygen, measured in milligrams per litre. Most fish require at least 4 to 5 mg/L to thrive, trout and other cold-water species needing the higher end of that; levels below about 2 mg/L constitute hypoxia, the condition of a dead zone in which most aquatic animals suffocate or flee. Cold water holds substantially more dissolved oxygen than warm water, roughly 14 mg/L at saturation near freezing against about 8 mg/L at 25 degrees C, which is why thermal pollution from a power station outfall or from removing shade trees along a bank can suppress oxygen without adding any pollutant at all.

The more dramatic mechanism is eutrophication. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus arriving from agricultural runoff, sewage discharge or phosphate detergents act as fertiliser and fuel explosive growth of algae. The bloom itself is not the damage. The damage comes when that algal mass dies and sinks, and the bacteria decomposing it consume oxygen far faster than diffusion and photosynthesis can replace it. The standard way to quantify that impending demand is biochemical oxygen demand, the amount of oxygen a water sample's own microbial community consumes over five days held in the dark at 20 degrees C. A high BOD reading is a warning about the future rather than a description of the present: the water may still test adequate for oxygen today while carrying the load that will crash it next week.

The textbook large-scale case is the Gulf of Mexico dead zone, which forms most summers where the Mississippi River delivers a nitrogen- and phosphorus-rich plume from the agricultural interior of a continent. The resulting bloom and subsequent decomposition regularly produce a hypoxic area of several thousand square miles, persisting until autumn storms mix the water column and re-oxygenate it. The pattern repeats at every scale, from a farm pond to the Baltic Sea.

Turbidity compounds all of this. It is cloudiness caused by suspended sediment, measured formally in nephelometric turbidity units or estimated in the field with a Secchi disk, a weighted black-and-white disc lowered on a marked cord until it disappears from view. Suspended sediment blocks sunlight from reaching submerged plants, which are themselves a major oxygen source for the water column, so a turbid stream loses oxygen production at exactly the moment that decomposition is consuming it. Sediment also abrades fish gills and smothers the gravel beds in which many species spawn, so its effects run well beyond the oxygen budget.

sections.heading: Floods, Droughts, and the Return-Period Statistics Behind the Headlines
sections.body:
When a report describes something as a hundred-year flood, it is stating a probability, not promising a spacing, and the confusion between those two readings lies behind some of the most consequential misunderstandings in applied hydrology. A flood's return period, written T, is estimated from a record of annual peak discharges using a plotting-position formula. The commonest is Weibull's, T = (n + 1) / m, where n is the number of years of record and m is the rank of a given year's peak when all the peaks are sorted from largest to smallest. The largest flood in a 49-year record therefore receives an estimated return period of 50 years, the second largest 25 years, and so on.

A hundred-year flood is thus the discharge level with an estimated one-in-a-hundred chance of being equalled or exceeded in any given year. Nothing prevents two from occurring in consecutive years, any more than flipping heads twice running contradicts a fair coin, and the arithmetic of repeated exposure is more alarming than the label suggests. Over a thirty-year mortgage, the cumulative probability of experiencing at least one is 1 minus 0.99 raised to the thirtieth power, which is about 26 per cent, better than one chance in four. Expressed that way, the same statistic that sounds reassuringly rare on a single-year basis becomes a serious planning consideration over the life of a building.

Drought resists this kind of crisp definition because it is a sustained deficit rather than a threshold crossing, and there is no single moment at which a drought can be said to have begun. Hydrologists therefore use indices, of which the Standardized Precipitation Index is the most widely used. It compares accumulated precipitation over a chosen window, commonly 3, 6 or 12 months, against the long-term historical distribution for that location and season, and expresses the shortfall in standard deviations. An SPI of minus 2.0 means precipitation fell in roughly the driest 2 to 3 per cent of the historical record. The choice of window matters enormously and is not a technicality: a 3-month SPI captures agricultural drought affecting a growing season, while a 12-month or 24-month SPI captures hydrological drought affecting reservoirs and aquifers, and a region can easily be in one and not the other.

Both statistics share a caveat that deserves stating plainly. They are only as good as the record they are built on. A fifty-year gauge record gives a poor estimate of a hundred-year event by definition, since it extrapolates beyond anything observed. And a genuinely changing climate undermines the stationarity assumption on which the whole method rests, so return periods estimated from twentieth-century data can materially understate twenty-first-century risk. That gap catches infrastructure planners off guard more often than any single storm does, and it is why modern practice increasingly reports return periods with explicit confidence bounds rather than as single numbers.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
Real stream and rainfall measurements do not require a hydrology laboratory. A rain gauge and a stopwatch will produce genuine, useful numbers, and the equipment that matters costs very little. What separates a real measurement from an impression is mostly siting and consistency rather than instrument quality.

The rain gauge illustrates this best. Any straight-sided clear cylinder with graduated markings works, because rainfall depth is independent of the collector's diameter as long as the sides are vertical: a wider gauge catches proportionally more water into a proportionally wider column, and the depth reading is identical. A tapered container, by contrast, gives a systematically wrong reading and cannot be corrected without knowing its exact geometry. Siting matters far more than the gauge itself. Mount it in the open with the rim level and roughly 30 cm above ground, well clear of overhanging trees, eaves and walls. A useful rule is to keep the gauge at least twice as far from any obstruction as that obstruction is tall, since a nearby building both shelters the gauge and generates wind eddies that carry raindrops past it. Under-catch in windy conditions is the dominant error in amateur rainfall records, and it can easily reach 10 to 20 per cent for light rain.

Depth measurement in a stream needs a rod rather than a tape, because a flexible tape bows downstream in current and reads long. A straight stick marked in centimetres is entirely adequate and considerably safer than wading with a hand at the bed.

For velocity timing, choose a float that sits mostly submerged rather than riding high. An orange is the traditional choice precisely because it floats with only a small cap above the surface, so it samples water speed rather than being pushed by wind. A tennis ball is lighter and more wind-affected, and a light plastic object is nearly useless on a breezy day.

Finally, use pencil rather than pen in the notebook. Ink runs when the page gets wet, and field pages always get wet.
ingredients: A simple rain gauge (a clear straight-sided cylinder with graduated markings, or a purpose-built plastic gauge) mounted in an open spot away from overhanging trees or eaves — a garden center or hardware store
A stopwatch or any phone timer, for stream velocity timing
A tape measure (at least 10–15 m) for measuring channel width and depth at multiple points
A wading rod or a long straight stick marked with depth increments, for measuring depth safely without stepping into deep or fast water
A floating object of consistent buoyancy (an orange, a tennis ball, or a purpose-bought hydrology float) for surface-velocity timing
A secchi disk (a black-and-white weighted disk on a marked cord) or a simple turbidity tube, for water clarity — an aquarium/pond-supply or science-education shop
pH test strips or a digital pH meter, and if available a basic freshwater aquarium dissolved-oxygen or nitrate test kit (sold for fish-keeping and perfectly usable for field water quality)
A topographic map (paper or a mapping app with contour lines) for sketching your catchment boundary
A notebook and pencil for logging measurements — pencil is preferred over pen because it still writes when wet

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Your Local Stream's Discharge and a Week of Rainfall
sections.body:
This is the exact float method that hydrologists used for a century before electronic flow meters became common, and it remains accurate enough for genuine field science, typically landing within 10 to 20 per cent of a properly instrumented gauging when the reach is well chosen.

Understanding why each part of the procedure exists makes the difference between a number and a measurement. The reach must be straight and uniform because a bend throws the fastest water to the outside of the curve and makes a single float path unrepresentative; obstructions create eddies where a float can stall or accelerate. Ten metres is a practical minimum because timing error is roughly constant, perhaps half a second of human reaction, and dividing that fixed error across a longer run reduces its proportional effect: half a second on a five-second run is a 10 per cent error, but on a twenty-second run it is only 2.5 per cent.

The 0.85 correction factor applied to surface velocity deserves explanation because it is the step most often taken on faith. Water in an open channel does not move at a single speed. Friction against the bed and banks slows the lower and outer water, producing a velocity profile that is roughly logarithmic with depth, fastest at or just below the surface and near zero at the bed. A float rides the fastest layer, so it systematically overstates the average. For a reasonably regular natural channel the depth-averaged velocity is about 0.85 of the surface value; for a very shallow, rough, cobble-bedded stream the true factor is nearer 0.8, and for a smooth deep channel nearer 0.9. Using 0.85 without qualification is honest as long as you record that you did, since it is the largest single uncertainty in the result.

Safety governs the whole exercise. Moving water exerts force proportional to the square of its velocity, so a stream that is merely brisk at ankle depth becomes genuinely dangerous at the knee, and water above mid-thigh moving at even one metre per second can take an adult off their feet. Face upstream when wading so the current presses you against your planted feet rather than buckling your knees, and abandon any measurement that requires entering water you would not comfortably stand in.
steps: Choose a straight, uniform stretch of stream at least 10 meters long with no major obstructions, and mark the start and end points on both banks.

Measure the width of the channel at three cross-sections along the stretch, and at each measure depth at several evenly spaced points with your wading rod, always facing upstream and never wading into water above knee height or with visibly fast current.
Calculate the average cross-sectional area at each section by approximating each strip between depth measurements as a small rectangle or trapezoid and summing them.
Drop your floating object at the upstream mark and time how long it takes to reach the downstream mark; repeat three times and average the results for a surface velocity.
Multiply that surface velocity by 0.85 (a standard correction, since surface water moves faster than the depth-averaged velocity due to bed friction) to estimate mean velocity.
Calculate discharge as Q = average cross-sectional area × corrected mean velocity, in cubic meters or feet per second.
Set up your rain gauge in an open location and record accumulated rainfall depth at the same time each day for one full week, resetting to zero after each reading.

At week's end, compare the timing of any rainfall against a change in the stream's discharge (repeat the discharge measurement after a rain event) — you should see a lag between rain and rise in flow, a direct measurement of your catchment's response time.

guides.title: Soil — How It Forms and Feeds Us
guides.summary: What soil actually is, the five factors and four processes that make it, how to read a soil profile and test texture by hand, the chemistry of pH and nutrients, and how to build and protect fertile ground.

sections.heading: What soil is: definition and composition
sections.body:
Soil is the unconsolidated mineral and organic material at Earth's surface that has been altered in place by climate and living organisms, and that serves as a medium for plant growth. It is not the same thing as dirt, which is simply soil that has been displaced and is no longer functioning in a profile, and it is not merely weathered rock — that loose broken material is called regolith, and it is the raw stock from which soil develops. The feature that distinguishes true soil from regolith is horizonation: the development of distinct, roughly horizontal layers with different colour, texture and chemistry, produced because water, roots and organisms move material downward and upward through the profile over long periods.
By volume, an ideal loam is close to 45 per cent mineral matter (the sand, silt and clay particles derived from rock), 25 per cent water held in pores, 25 per cent air in those same pores, and about 5 per cent organic matter — of which roughly four-fifths is humus, a tenth is living roots, and a tenth is the living organisms themselves. Two consequences follow immediately. First, half the volume of good soil is empty space, so soil is more nearly a foam than a solid. Second, the water and air fractions trade directly against each other: fill the pores with water and there is no air left, and the roots of most crops, which respire aerobically just as animals do, begin to suffocate within roughly 24 to 72 hours of waterlogging. That is why drainage, not just rainfall, decides whether a field is productive.
Organic matter is a small fraction by volume but carries a wildly disproportionate share of soil function, because humus holds water on its surfaces, carries negative electrical charge that retains nutrients, and glues mineral particles into stable crumbs. As a working figure, each additional one per cent of soil organic matter allows roughly 15,000 to 25,000 extra litres of water storage per hectare in the top 30 centimetres — the difference between a crop that survives a fortnight of drought and one that does not.
Soil is also alive in a way that is easy to underestimate. One teaspoon, about a gram, of healthy topsoil holds on the order of 100 million to a billion bacteria, several metres of fungal hyphae, thousands of protozoa and dozens of nematodes. A hectare of good soil supports one to two and a half tonnes of living biomass below ground, often more than stands above it, and earthworms alone may pass 10 to 40 tonnes of soil through their guts per hectare per year, leaving behind the macropores through which rain actually infiltrates.
Finally, soil is effectively non-renewable on human timescales. Natural formation runs at roughly 0.025 to 0.1 millimetres a year — 25 to 100 millimetres per thousand years, or about a tonne per hectare annually. Global cropland erosion averages 10 to 40 tonnes per hectare per year, meaning soil is being spent 10 to 40 times faster than it is made, and roughly a third of the world's soils are already measurably degraded.

sections.heading: The five soil-forming factors: CLORPT
sections.body:
In 1941 the soil scientist Hans Jenny formalised soil as a function of five independent state factors, written S = f(cl, o, r, p, t): climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. The value of the formulation is that it is predictive. Hold four factors roughly constant across a landscape and vary the fifth, and the resulting sequence of soils isolates that factor's effect — a technique still used to read soils in unfamiliar country.
Climate dominates at global scale, acting through temperature and water. Chemical reaction rates roughly double for every 10 degrees Celsius of warming, the rule of thumb chemists call Q10, and water is the transport medium that moves the products. Where precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration, leaching dominates: base cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium are washed downward and out of the profile, leaving acidic soils. Where evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation, capillary rise dominates, drawing dissolved salts and carbonates upward to accumulate near the surface as alkaline horizons and hardpans of caliche or calcrete. The great counterintuitive case is the humid tropics, where 10 to 30 metres of deeply weathered saprolite underlie rainforest yet the soil itself is poor, because virtually all nutrients are held in living biomass rather than in the mineral store.
Organisms set the organic input. Grassland roots die and decay throughout a deep rooting zone, building the thick, dark, base-rich surface horizons of the mollisols that underlie the world's grain belts, sometimes a metre and a half of black topsoil. Conifer forest instead drops acidic litter that leaches downward, bleaching a pale ash-grey horizon near the surface and producing a spodosol. Earthworms, ants, termites and burrowing mammals mix material vertically, a process called bioturbation; legumes carrying Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen at rates of roughly 50 to 300 kilograms per hectare per year.
Relief, meaning topography, controls how long water and material stay put. Steep slopes carry thin, young soils because erosion removes material as fast as it forms; footslopes and valley bottoms accumulate deep, dark, moist colluvium. Aspect matters strongly in the mid-latitudes: in the northern hemisphere, south-facing slopes are warmer, drier and thinner-soiled, while north-facing slopes stay cool and moist and build deeper organic layers. The pattern reverses south of the equator.
Parent material is the mineral starting stock, either residual — weathered in place from the bedrock beneath — or transported as river alluvium, gravity-moved colluvium, wind-blown loess, glacial till or volcanic ash. It sets initial texture, mineralogy and nutrient supply. Limestone weathers to clay-rich, calcium-rich, near-neutral soil; granite to sandy, acidic, quartz-dominated soil; basalt to fertile iron- and clay-rich soil, which is why volcanic districts such as Java and Campania are agricultural powerhouses; fresh volcanic ash gives andisols that fix phosphorus so strongly that fertiliser can vanish from plant availability within weeks.
Time is the slowest factor. A recognisable surface horizon needs perhaps 50 to 200 years, a distinct subsoil B horizon 1,000 to 10,000 years, and a fully differentiated mature profile 10,000 to more than 100,000 years. The most weathered tropical oxisols have been developing for millions.

sections.heading: The four processes and the soil profile
sections.body:
Four processes act simultaneously to build horizons: ADDITIONS (organic litter, dust, rainfall, fertiliser), LOSSES (leaching, erosion, gaseous loss, plant uptake and harvest removal), TRANSLOCATIONS (movement within the profile — ELUVIATION is removal from a horizon, ILLUVIATION is accumulation in one), and TRANSFORMATIONS (weathering, humification, mineral formation).
WEATHERING supplies the mineral raw material and comes in two kinds. PHYSICAL weathering breaks rock without changing its chemistry: frost wedging (water expands 9% on freezing, generating up to 200 MPa in a confined crack — the single most effective process in cold climates, most active where temperatures oscillate across 0 °C), salt crystallisation, thermal expansion, exfoliation from unloading, root wedging, and abrasion. CHEMICAL weathering changes mineral composition: HYDROLYSIS is the most important, where feldspar plus carbonic acid becomes clay — 2KAlSi₃O₈ + 2H₂CO₃ + 9H₂O → Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄ (kaolinite) + 4H₄SiO₄ + 2K⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻; OXIDATION rusts iron-bearing minerals (4FeO + O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃), giving soils their red and yellow colours; CARBONATION dissolves limestone (CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻), which is what makes caves; HYDRATION and biological chelation by root and lichen acids round it out. Physical weathering accelerates chemical weathering by multiplying surface area: splitting a 1 m cube into 1 cm cubes increases surface area 100-fold.
THE SOIL PROFILE, top to bottom:
• O HORIZON — organic litter, from fresh leaves (Oi) through partly decomposed (Oe) to fully humified (Oa). Absent in most cultivated and desert soils, thick in forests and peatlands.
• A HORIZON (topsoil) — mineral soil darkened by humus, the zone of maximum biological activity and root density. Typically 5–30 cm; up to 1 m in prairie mollisols. This is the horizon that erosion takes first and that agriculture depends on.
• E HORIZON — zone of maximum ELUVIATION, leached pale grey or white because clay, iron and aluminium have been stripped out. Prominent under conifers and in sandy, high-rainfall settings.
• B HORIZON (subsoil) — zone of ILLUVIATION, where the clay, iron oxides and carbonates removed from above accumulate. Denser, often more strongly coloured (red, brown, orange), and where you see structural development like blocky or prismatic peds.
• C HORIZON — weathered parent material, only slightly altered, still recognisably the original rock or sediment.
• R HORIZON — consolidated bedrock.
To examine a profile, dig a pit at least 1 m deep with one clean vertical face (or use a road cut or stream bank), face it away from the sun to see colour without glare, and describe each horizon's depth, colour (ideally with a Munsell chart — the notation is hue value/chroma, e.g. 10YR 3/2 for a dark greyish brown), texture, structure, consistence, root abundance, and boundary sharpness.

sections.heading: Texture, structure and water: the physical properties that decide everything
sections.body:
TEXTURE is the proportion by mass of the three mineral size fractions (USDA scale): SAND 2.0–0.05 mm (gritty, visible, low surface area), SILT 0.05–0.002 mm (smooth like flour when dry, slippery when wet), CLAY under 0.002 mm (sticky, plastic, enormous surface area — clay has 10,000 to 100,000 times the surface area per gram of sand, which is why it controls chemistry). LOAM is the balanced ideal, roughly 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay. Texture cannot be changed by management at any realistic scale — you must work with what you have.
THE HAND TEXTURE TEST (ribbon method), a reliable field procedure:
1. Take a walnut-sized ball of soil, remove stones and roots.
2. Add water a few drops at a time and knead until it is the consistency of putty — moist enough to be plastic, not wet enough to be sticky.
3. Squeeze the ball between thumb and forefinger, pushing upward to form a ribbon that hangs over your finger. If NO ribbon forms and the soil will not hold a ball → SAND. If it forms a ball but the ribbon breaks under 2.5 cm → LOAMY SAND or LOAM. Ribbon 2.5–5 cm → CLAY LOAM. Ribbon over 5 cm before breaking → CLAY.
4. Now wet a pinch excessively and rub between fingers: distinctly GRITTY → sandy (e.g. sandy clay loam); distinctly SMOOTH/silky → silty (silty clay loam); neither dominant → the plain version (clay loam).
THE JAR TEST for quantitative texture: fill a straight-sided jar one-third with soil, add water to nearly full plus a teaspoon of dish soap as a dispersant, shake vigorously for 2 minutes, then set down. Mark the settled level after 1 minute (sand), 2 hours (sand + silt), and 48 hours (total). Calculate each fraction as a percentage of total depth and plot on the USDA soil texture triangle.
STRUCTURE is how individual particles aggregate into PEDS, bound by fungal hyphae, root exudates, microbial glues (glomalin) and clay-humus complexes. Types: granular (best for agriculture — crumbly, porous, typical of a healthy A horizon), blocky, prismatic, columnar, platy (often a sign of compaction or crusting, and it impedes water and roots), and massive or single-grain (no structure). Unlike texture, structure CAN be improved: organic matter, root growth, cover cropping and reduced tillage all build it, while compaction, excessive tillage and working wet soil destroy it.
WATER RELATIONS. SATURATION is all pores full. FIELD CAPACITY is the water remaining after free drainage stops, about −33 kPa (−0.33 bar) matric potential, reached 1–3 days after a soaking. PERMANENT WILTING POINT is −1500 kPa (−15 bar), where roots can no longer extract water. PLANT-AVAILABLE WATER = field capacity − wilting point, and it varies enormously with texture: sand holds about 60–80 mm of available water per metre of depth, loam about 150–200 mm/m, clay about 150–180 mm/m (clay holds more total water but much of it is bound too tightly to release). WORKED EXAMPLE: a crop rooting 60 cm deep in a loam has 0.6 m × 175 mm/m ≈ 105 mm of available water. If evapotranspiration is 5 mm/day and you irrigate when 50% is depleted, you must irrigate every 105 × 0.5 / 5 ≈ 10 days, applying about 52 mm. The same crop on sand (70 mm/m → 42 mm available) needs irrigating every 4 days — which is precisely why sandy soils demand frequent, light watering and clay soils infrequent, deep watering.
BULK DENSITY = mass of oven-dry soil ÷ total volume including pores, in g/cm³. Healthy loam is 1.1–1.4 g/cm³; above about 1.6 g/cm³ in loam or 1.8 in sand, roots cannot penetrate. Porosity (%) = (1 − bulk density / particle density) × 100, taking particle density as 2.65 g/cm³. A soil at 1.3 g/cm³ has porosity = (1 − 1.3/2.65) × 100 = 51%.

sections.heading: Soil chemistry: pH, cation exchange and the nutrients
sections.body:
pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion activity: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is in mol/L. It is logarithmic, so pH 5 is TEN times more acidic than pH 6 and one hundred times more than pH 7. Most crops do best at pH 6.0–7.0 because that is where the widest range of nutrients is simultaneously available. Below pH 5.5, aluminium and manganese become soluble and toxic to roots, and phosphorus locks up with iron and aluminium. Above pH 7.5, phosphorus locks up with calcium, and iron, manganese, zinc and boron become unavailable — the classic cause of interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) in alkaline soils. Note that nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are all most available around pH 6.0–7.5, while iron and manganese peak in acid soil.
ADJUSTING pH: to RAISE pH, add agricultural lime (calcium carbonate). Rough rates to raise pH by 1.0 unit over the top 15 cm: sandy soil 1.0–1.5 kg per 10 m², loam 2.0–2.5 kg per 10 m², clay 3.0–4.0 kg per 10 m². Lime is slow — apply 3–6 months ahead, incorporate, and re-test; it takes a full season to act. Use dolomitic lime if magnesium is also low. Wood ash also raises pH (roughly half the strength of lime) and adds potassium, but is caustic and easy to overdo — cap it at about 1 kg per 10 m² per year. To LOWER pH, use elemental sulphur, which soil bacteria oxidise to sulphuric acid: roughly 0.5–1.0 kg per 10 m² lowers pH by about 1 unit in sand, 1.5–2.0 kg per 10 m² in clay, over 3–12 months. Never use anything stronger; do not attempt to acidify with household acids.
CATION EXCHANGE CAPACITY (CEC) is the soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrients on negatively charged clay and humus surfaces, measured in centimoles of charge per kilogram (cmol_c/kg, equivalently meq/100 g). Typical values: sand 1–5, loam 5–15, clay 25–50, organic/peat 50–100+. High CEC means the soil is a good nutrient bank that resists leaching; low CEC (sand) means nutrients wash straight through, so fertilise little and often. The exchangeable cations, in typical order of strength of adsorption, are Al³⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Mg²⁺ > K⁺ ≈ NH₄⁺ > Na⁺ > H⁺. A well-balanced soil has base saturation around 65–80% Ca, 10–15% Mg, 2–5% K.
THE ESSENTIAL NUTRIENTS. Plants need 17 elements. From air and water: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen (about 95% of dry plant mass). MACRONUTRIENTS from soil: nitrogen (N — the engine of leafy growth and all proteins; deficiency shows as uniform yellowing of the OLDEST leaves first, because N is mobile and the plant scavenges it from old tissue), phosphorus (P — roots, flowers, seeds, and all energy transfer via ATP; deficiency shows as stunting and purple leaf tinges), potassium (K — water regulation, stomatal control, disease resistance; deficiency shows as scorched, browning leaf MARGINS on older leaves). SECONDARY: calcium (cell walls; deficiency causes blossom-end rot in tomatoes — usually an uneven-watering transport problem rather than a genuine soil shortage), magnesium (the central atom of chlorophyll; deficiency gives interveinal yellowing on older leaves), sulphur (amino acids). MICRONUTRIENTS in trace amounts: iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, nickel. Note the diagnostic rule: MOBILE nutrients (N, P, K, Mg) show deficiency in OLD leaves first; IMMOBILE nutrients (Ca, Fe, B, S, Zn) show it in NEW growth first. Fertiliser N-P-K labelling gives percentage N, then P₂O₅, then K₂O by mass — so a 10 kg bag of 10-10-10 contains 1 kg N, 1 kg P₂O₅ (≈0.44 kg elemental P) and 1 kg K₂O (≈0.83 kg elemental K).

sections.heading: Building and keeping fertility: compost, cover crops and erosion control
sections.body:
COMPOSTING converts raw organic waste into stable humus, and the controlling variable is the CARBON-TO-NITROGEN RATIO. Target C:N of 25:1 to 30:1 in the starting mix. High-carbon "browns": dry leaves C:N ≈ 60:1, straw 80:1, sawdust 400:1, cardboard 350:1, wood chips 400:1. High-nitrogen "greens": fresh grass clippings 20:1, vegetable scraps 15:1, coffee grounds 20:1, manure 15–25:1, urine 0.8:1. A workable practical rule is 2–3 parts browns to 1 part greens BY VOLUME.
HOT COMPOST PROCEDURE:
1. Build a pile at least 1 m × 1 m × 1 m (1 m³) — smaller piles cannot retain heat.
2. Layer browns and greens in the 2–3:1 ratio, shredding material to 2–5 cm pieces to raise surface area.
3. Moisten to the "wrung-out sponge" test — squeeze a handful and one or two drops should appear, no more. Target 50–60% moisture.
4. The pile should reach 55–65 °C within 2–4 days. Sustaining 55 °C for 3 consecutive days kills most weed seeds and human pathogens; above 70 °C the beneficial microbes themselves die, so turn to cool it.
5. Turn every 3–7 days, moving the outside to the centre. Expect 5–8 turns.
6. Finished in 6–12 weeks (hot) or 6–12 months (cold, unturned). It is ready when it is dark, crumbly, smells of forest floor, and no original materials are recognisable.
TROUBLESHOOTING: ammonia smell = too much nitrogen, add browns. Rotten-egg smell = anaerobic, turn it and add bulky browns. Not heating = too dry, too small, or too little nitrogen. NEVER compost meat, dairy, oils, pet faeces from carnivores, or diseased plants in a home pile; and do not apply raw manure to soil within 90–120 days of harvesting food crops.
COVER CROPS AND GREEN MANURE: sow legumes (clover, vetch, field peas, beans) to fix 50–200 kg N/ha; sow grasses and cereals (rye, oats, barley) for biomass and deep rooting; sow brassicas (radish, mustard) to break compaction with taproots. Cut or roll before they set seed and incorporate or leave as mulch.
MULCH: a 5–10 cm layer of straw, leaves or wood chips reduces evaporation by 50–70%, suppresses weeds, moderates soil temperature by 5–10 °C, and feeds soil biology as it breaks down. Keep it a few centimetres clear of plant stems to avoid rot.
EROSION CONTROL — the single most important act of soil conservation. The Universal Soil Loss Equation, A = R·K·LS·C·P, states that annual soil loss A (t/ha/yr) depends on rainfall erosivity R, soil erodibility K, slope length and steepness LS, cover management C, and support practice P. You cannot change R or K, and LS only with earthworks — but C and P are entirely under your control, and C alone can vary by a factor of 100 between bare soil and full cover. Practical measures: (1) NEVER leave soil bare — bare soil can lose 100× more than covered soil; (2) contour ploughing across the slope rather than up and down, cutting loss by 50%; (3) terracing on slopes above about 10°; (4) strip cropping and grassed waterways; (5) windbreaks perpendicular to prevailing wind, effective for 10–20 times their height downwind; (6) no-till or reduced till, which preserves structure and the fungal network; (7) permanent vegetation on any slope above about 25%.
COMMON MISTAKES AND SAFETY. Working soil when it is wet destroys structure and creates a compacted layer that lasts years — test by squeezing a ball and dropping it from waist height: if it shatters, it is dry enough; if it stays a ball, wait. Over-tilling burns organic matter (each pass oxidises carbon) and pulverises aggregates. Over-fertilising with nitrogen leaches to groundwater as nitrate and runs off to cause algal blooms and hypoxic dead zones. Adding sand to clay in small amounts makes something close to concrete — add organic matter instead. Do not lime and add ammonium fertiliser at the same time (you lose nitrogen as ammonia gas). SAFETY: wear gloves and wash hands after handling soil, compost or manure — tetanus (ensure vaccination is current), and pathogens including E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria and Toxoplasma are real risks; avoid inhaling dry compost dust, which can carry Aspergillus and Legionella (dampen it first, work upwind, and consider a mask). Never grow food in soil that may be contaminated with lead (common near old painted buildings, old orchards and busy roads) — have it tested; if lead exceeds about 400 ppm, use raised beds with imported soil and a barrier. Do not use treated timber, railway sleepers or tyres as bed edging for food crops.

sections.heading: Soil Taxonomy: Reading a Soil's Name Like a Classification
sections.body:
Soil scientists classify soils formally, much as biologists classify species, and the classification is not decoration: a soil's name predicts its drainage, fertility, acidity and behaviour under the plough before anyone digs a hole. The two systems in wide use are USDA Soil Taxonomy, which sorts all soils into twelve orders, and the FAO's World Reference Base, the main international alternative. Both key on diagnostic horizons and measurable properties — base saturation, clay accumulation, organic carbon content, depth to carbonate — rather than on appearance, so two soils that look alike in a roadcut can land in different orders and behave differently.
Mollisols are the soils that feed the world. They form under grassland, where generations of fine roots die deep in the profile and decay in the presence of abundant calcium, building a thick, dark, crumb-structured surface horizon with organic carbon commonly between 3 and 7 per cent and base saturation above 50 per cent. They underlie the American Midwest, the Ukrainian and Russian steppe and the Argentine Pampas almost without exception. That is not agriculture following fertile ground by coincidence so much as several civilisations independently discovering the same physical fact.
Oxisols sit at the opposite pole. These are the deeply weathered soils of the humid tropics, red or yellow because decades of leaching have carried away silica and bases and left residual iron and aluminium oxides behind. They carry some of Earth's densest vegetation and are nonetheless chemically close to sterile, with cation exchange capacity often below 5 centimoles per kilogram and phosphorus locked to iron oxides. Nearly all the nutrient capital sits in the standing biomass, cycling through leaf fall and being reabsorbed by shallow roots and fungal partners within weeks. Clear the canopy and the loop breaks; a cleared oxisol can lose most of its usable fertility within two or three growing seasons, which is exactly why traditional slash-and-burn plots are abandoned on that schedule and left to regrow for fifteen or twenty years.
The remaining orders most likely to appear in an ordinary soil survey are aridisols, desert soils carrying subsurface accumulations of carbonate or gypsum and frequently at risk of salinisation under irrigation; alfisols, moderately weathered temperate forest soils with clay-enriched subsoils and reasonable fertility; ultisols, their more weathered and more acidic cousins; spodosols, the acidic sandy soils of conifer country with a bleached horizon over a rusty accumulation of iron and organic matter; vertisols, shrink-swell clays that crack open in drought and heave foundations; entisols and inceptisols, soils too young to have developed much; and histosols, the organic peats and mucks that subside irreversibly once drained. Reading a published soil survey for your own ground and looking up the order named there is the single fastest way to know what you are dealing with.

sections.heading: The Nitrogen, Phosphorus and Carbon Cycles Inside the Soil
sections.body:
Behind the pH numbers and nutrient totals reported on a soil test lies real biochemistry, and knowing it explains why fertilisers behave as they do. Atmospheric nitrogen gas is a triple-bonded molecule of exceptional stability; the bond energy is about 941 kilojoules per mole, which is why plants cannot touch it directly. Nitrogen must first be fixed. Biologically this is done by Rhizobium and related bacteria living in nodules on legume roots — beans, peas, clover, vetch — which is the reason a legume cover crop genuinely adds nitrogen rather than merely recycling it. Industrially it is done by the Haber-Bosch process, combining nitrogen and hydrogen at roughly 400 to 500 degrees Celsius and 150 to 300 atmospheres over an iron catalyst to make ammonia. It is arguably the single invention most responsible for twentieth-century population growth, and it consumes on the order of one to two per cent of world energy supply.
Once in the soil as ammonium, nitrogen is oxidised in two bacterial steps: Nitrosomonas and relatives convert ammonium to nitrite, then Nitrobacter and relatives convert nitrite to nitrate. The whole sequence is nitrification, it needs oxygen, and it runs fast in warm moist soil and nearly stops below about 5 degrees Celsius. Nitrate is the form roots take up most readily, but it carries a negative charge, and so do the clay and humus surfaces that hold the soil's exchangeable nutrients. Like charges repel, so nitrate is not retained; it travels with drainage water into groundwater and streams. That single electrostatic fact is the direct chemical link between an over-fertilised field and an algal bloom downstream, and it is also why splitting nitrogen applications across the season loses less than one heavy dose in spring.
Phosphorus behaves almost in the opposite way. It binds eagerly, precipitating with iron and aluminium in acid soils below about pH 5.5 and with calcium in alkaline soils above roughly pH 7.5, so plant availability peaks in a narrow window near pH 6.5. A soil can hold a large total phosphorus reserve and still starve a crop, because the problem is immobility rather than scarcity; phosphate ions diffuse only a millimetre or two through soil, which is why mycorrhizal fungi, whose hyphae reach centimetres further, matter so much to phosphorus nutrition.
Carbon completes the picture. Soil organic carbon comes from decomposing residues, and the speed of that decomposition is governed largely by the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the material. Residue near 24 to 1 roughly matches the body chemistry of the decomposer microbes themselves and breaks down efficiently. Straw runs about 80 to 1 and sawdust can exceed 400 to 1, forcing microbes to scavenge nitrogen from the surrounding soil to process it. That temporary immobilisation is nitrogen robbery, and it is why fresh wood chips tilled into a vegetable bed can visibly yellow and stunt the crop for a season while doing no harm at all when left on the surface as mulch.

sections.heading: The Dust Bowl and the Birth of Soil Conservation Science
sections.body:
The clearest historical demonstration that soil is a finite and losable resource came from the American and Canadian prairies in the 1930s. Native grassland had been broken for wheat across tens of millions of hectares during the high grain prices of the First World War and the 1920s, using mouldboard ploughs and disc harrows that pulverised the surface into a fine seedbed. The deep-rooted perennial grasses that had anchored fine silty prairie topsoil for millennia were gone, and the structure they maintained went with them. When a multi-year drought arrived in 1931 and the crops failed, there was nothing left holding the surface together.
What followed were the black blizzards. Dry aggregates broke down under wind, and once particles around 0.1 millimetres began bouncing along the surface — a process called saltation — each impact knocked more fine material into suspension, so the erosion accelerated itself. Storms stripped topsoil by the hundreds of millions of tonnes, buried fences to their top wire, cut visibility to a few metres and left farms scraped down to raw subsoil. Dust from the plains reached ships several hundred kilometres out in the Atlantic and settled on window ledges in Washington, D.C. The human cost was proportionate: dust pneumonia, roughly two and a half million people displaced from the plains states, and a farm economy that did not recover for a generation.
Hugh Hammond Bennett, a soil surveyor who had argued for more than a decade that American farming was causing severe and largely invisible erosion, used the crisis deliberately. Testifying before a Senate committee in 1935, he stalled his testimony until a dust cloud blown in from the plains darkened the sky over the capital, then gestured at the window. Congress created the Soil Conservation Service that year — the first national agency anywhere established specifically to fight soil erosion.
The practical toolkit that came out of it is still the standard. Contour ploughing runs furrows along the elevation contour rather than up and down the slope, so each furrow acts as a small dam and can cut runoff-driven soil loss by roughly half on moderate gradients. Terracing does the same at larger scale by shortening the effective slope length. Shelterbelts — rows of trees planted across the prevailing wind — reduce ground-level wind speed for a distance of about ten to twenty times their height downwind, and more than two hundred million were planted across the Great Plains. Strip cropping alternates bands of row crop and dense cover so an eroding strip is always caught by a protective one. Stubble mulching leaves residue standing rather than burying it. The later moves to no-till drilling and year-round cover cropping extend the same principle: keep something living or dead over the surface at all times. The lesson underneath all of it is arithmetic. Topsoil accumulates at a millimetre or so per decade and can be gone in one bad season, and no management practice can manufacture more of it on a schedule that matters to the person farming the field.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
A genuinely informative soil survey of your own garden, paddock or yard can be run with tools that mostly already exist in an ordinary kitchen and garage, and the results will tell you more about what will grow than any general advice can. The point of assembling the kit is that the three measurements worth having — texture, acidity and infiltration rate — each need a different sort of instrument, and none of them is expensive.
For sampling, what matters is getting soil from a consistent depth rather than scraping the surface. Most of the root activity and nearly all the organic matter of a garden soil sit in the top 20 to 30 centimetres, so that is the zone to sample; a purpose-made soil probe pulls a clean core, but a spade cutting one vertical face of a small pit works nearly as well and has the advantage of letting you see the horizons directly. Sample several spots and keep them separate at first, because soil varies enormously over a few metres — an old manure heap, a filled trench or a former path can shift pH by a full unit and texture by a whole class.
For texture, the jar method depends on particles settling at speeds proportional to the square of their diameter, so straight sides and a flat base matter far more than jar size; a curved-sided jar makes the layer boundaries impossible to measure honestly. For acidity, colour-change kits are adequate to about half a pH unit, which is enough for most decisions, while an inexpensive digital meter gives finer resolution but needs calibrating against buffer solutions and drifts badly if stored dry. Either beats guessing, because pH controls the availability of every major nutrient.
An open-ended cylinder driven into the ground turns a vague impression of drainage into a number in centimetres per hour. A soil thermometer is the least glamorous item and among the most useful, since germination is governed by soil temperature rather than air temperature, and a compost heap held above roughly 55 degrees Celsius for several days is the only reliable way to kill weed seed and pathogens. Basic hygiene is not optional: soil carries tetanus spores and, near manure, enteric bacteria, so gloves and thorough handwashing belong on the list rather than as an afterthought.
ingredients: A soil probe or a simple garden trowel/spade for extracting an intact vertical soil sample down to 20–30 cm
A clear straight-sided mason jar with a tight lid, for the soil texture settling test
A ruler for measuring settled sediment layers in the jar
A pH test kit — either simple color-change strips/capsules or an inexpensive digital soil pH meter — from a garden center or hardware store
A soil thermometer, useful for tracking when soil has warmed enough for spring planting or monitoring a compost pile's internal temperature
An empty tin can with both ends removed (or a section of PVC pipe), a rubber mallet, and a stopwatch, for a simple infiltration-rate test
Compost bin materials: a mix of 'browns' (dry leaves, straw, cardboard) and 'greens' (fresh grass clippings, vegetable scraps) plus a bin or simple wire enclosure
Work gloves, since handling soil, especially near a compost pile or manure, calls for basic hygiene precautions, and washing hands thoroughly afterward
A notebook for recording layer depths, colors (a soil color reference chart is a worthwhile inexpensive addition), and test results by location

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Run Your Own Soil Texture, pH and Infiltration Test
sections.body:
Three measurements — texture, acidity and infiltration rate — between them tell a gardener or small farmer almost everything that actually governs what a patch of ground will do, and each takes under an hour of active work. Texture is the permanent property, fixed by the mineral particles themselves and unchangeable by anything you can afford to add; it sets water-holding capacity, drainage and how the soil behaves when worked wet. Acidity is the adjustable master variable, because pH controls how much of each nutrient is chemically available regardless of how much is present. Infiltration rate is the diagnostic for structure and compaction: two soils of identical texture can differ tenfold in how fast they take water, and that difference is entirely the work of organic matter, roots and earthworms.
Two cautions decide whether the numbers mean anything. Sample when the soil is moist but not wet — working or probing saturated soil smears the structure you are trying to measure, and a bone-dry soil gives a falsely fast first infiltration reading because cracks swallow the water. And repeat each test in at least two or three separate spots several metres apart. Soil is patchy at garden scale, and a single reading tells you about one hole rather than about a field.
steps: Texture (jar test): fill a mason jar about one-third full with soil from 5–10 cm depth, add water until nearly full, add a small pinch of dish soap as a dispersant, seal tightly, and shake vigorously for 2–3 minutes to fully suspend the particles.

Set the jar level and undisturbed. Mark the sand layer that settles after exactly 1 minute, the silt layer after roughly 2 hours, and the final clay layer (still faintly cloudy) after it fully clears, which can take a day or several days — larger sand particles fall fastest under gravity while fine clay stays suspended far longer (Stokes' Law).

Measure the thickness of each layer with a ruler, calculate the percentage each represents of the total settled depth, and plot the three percentages on a standard soil texture triangle to get your texture class.

pH: follow your kit's instructions exactly, typically mixing soil with distilled water in a specified ratio and reading a color change or a digital probe; test two or three separate spots, since pH commonly varies over just a few meters.
Infiltration: drive the open tin can about 5 cm into the ground with the rubber mallet, keeping it level and not cracking the surrounding soil.
Pour a measured amount of water into the can (about 2.5 cm depth, roughly one inch) and start the stopwatch the instant you finish pouring.

Record the time for the water to fully infiltrate; repeat once more on the same spot to reduce the effect of initial dry-soil resistance, and calculate the infiltration rate in centimeters or inches per hour.

Compare your rate against reference values (well-structured loam typically infiltrates several centimeters per hour; compacted clay can be a tenth of that or less) to judge whether the soil's structure needs improvement, such as added organic matter or reduced foot/vehicle traffic.

guides.title: Reading the Landscape & Geology in the Field
guides.summary: How to interpret terrain like a geologist — the principles of relative dating, measuring strike and dip, recognising folds, faults and unconformities, decoding glacial, river, coastal and karst landforms, and using it all to find water, safe ground and useful materials.

sections.heading: The reasoning framework: how to date what you see with no instruments
sections.body:
Field geology rests on a handful of logical principles established between 1669 and 1830, and they let you order events in time using nothing but observation. Together they are called RELATIVE DATING — determining sequence, not calendar age.
• UNIFORMITARIANISM (Hutton, 1785) — "the present is the key to the past." Physical laws are constant, so the processes you can watch today (a river depositing sand, a wave rounding a pebble, a volcano erupting) explain identical features in ancient rock. This is the master principle; everything else follows.
• SUPERPOSITION (Steno, 1669) — in an undisturbed sequence of layered rocks, each bed is younger than the one below it and older than the one above. The bottom is the oldest.
• ORIGINAL HORIZONTALITY — sediment is deposited in near-horizontal layers under gravity. So tilted or folded beds have been deformed AFTER deposition, and the amount of tilt measures the deformation.
• LATERAL CONTINUITY — a bed extends in all directions until it thins to nothing or hits the edge of the basin. Matching beds on opposite sides of a valley means one continuous unit later cut by erosion.
• CROSS-CUTTING RELATIONSHIPS — any feature that cuts across another is younger than what it cuts. A fault that offsets a bed postdates the bed; a dyke that slices a granite postdates the granite; a fracture filled with quartz postdates the fracture.
• INCLUSIONS — fragments contained within a rock are older than the rock containing them. Granite pebbles inside a sandstone mean the granite existed first; sandstone fragments frozen into a granite mean the sandstone came first.
• BAKED AND CHILLED CONTACTS — an intrusion bakes the rock it invades (a metamorphic halo) and chills against it (fine-grained margins). Find a baked contact and you know the intrusion is younger. If instead the "intrusion" is overlain by an unbaked bed containing its fragments, it is a buried lava flow and is older.
• FAUNAL SUCCESSION (Smith, 1815) — fossil assemblages succeed one another in a definite, recognisable order worldwide, so distinctive short-lived, widespread fossils (INDEX FOSSILS such as trilobites for the Cambrian–Permian, ammonites for the Mesozoic, graptolites for the Ordovician–Silurian) date and correlate rocks between continents.
WORKED EXAMPLE — read this cliff. From the bottom: horizontal limestone; above it tilted sandstone; a granite body cutting both, with a baked halo; a basalt dyke cutting the granite; and a horizontal gravel capping everything, containing granite pebbles. Sequence: (1) limestone deposited; (2) sandstone deposited on it, then both tilted; (3) granite intruded (cross-cutting + baking); (4) dyke intruded (cuts granite); (5) uplift and erosion levelled the surface; (6) gravel deposited (superposition, and its granite pebbles confirm the granite was already exposed). Six events, no equipment, pure logic.

sections.heading: Structure: strike, dip, folds and faults
sections.body:
STRIKE and DIP describe the orientation of any planar feature — a bedding plane, a fault, a joint, a foliation. STRIKE is the compass bearing of the horizontal line formed where the plane intersects a horizontal surface. DIP is the angle, measured in the vertical plane perpendicular to strike, between the plane and horizontal, from 0° (flat) to 90° (vertical). Dip direction is always 90° from strike; you must also record which way it dips (e.g. "strike 045°, dip 30° SE").
MEASURING WITHOUT A GEOLOGICAL COMPASS: (1) For strike, place a water bottle on the bed surface, or trickle water on it and mark the horizontal line where the water does NOT run (water runs directly down dip, so the line perpendicular to its flow, in the plane, is strike). Sight along that line with any compass. (2) For dip, hold a smartphone flat against the bed perpendicular to strike and read its inclinometer, or make a simple clinometer: a protractor with a weighted string hanging from its centre, held with one straight edge against the rock — the string reads the complement of the angle. Always take three or more readings on different parts of a bed and average them; a single reading on a lumpy surface can be 10° out.
FOLDS form under compression, in ductile conditions (deeper, warmer, slower strain). An ANTICLINE arches upward with the OLDEST rocks in the core; a SYNCLINE troughs downward with the YOUNGEST rocks in the core. This age criterion, not the surface shape, is the definition, because erosion can leave an anticline as a valley and a syncline as a ridge (INVERTED RELIEF). Parts of a fold: the AXIAL PLANE divides it symmetrically; the HINGE is the line of maximum curvature; the LIMBS are the flanks. A fold is symmetric, asymmetric, overturned (one limb rotated past vertical) or recumbent (axial plane near-horizontal) — and increasing asymmetry indicates increasing strain and tells you the direction the compression came from, because folds "lean away" from the push. A MONOCLINE is a single step-like bend. In map view, eroded plunging folds make distinctive V or hairpin outcrop patterns: an eroded plunging anticline's beds V in the direction of plunge; a syncline's V opposite.
FAULTS form under brittle conditions (shallow, cooler, faster strain). The HANGING WALL lies above an inclined fault plane; the FOOTWALL below (the old miner's terms: you hang your lamp on one and stand on the other).
• NORMAL fault — hanging wall moves DOWN. Caused by EXTENSION (tension). Produces horsts (upthrown blocks) and grabens (downdropped blocks), rift valleys, and Basin-and-Range topography. The crust is stretched and lengthened.
• REVERSE fault — hanging wall moves UP. Caused by COMPRESSION. A THRUST fault is a reverse fault with a dip under 30°, which can push older rock over younger for tens of kilometres — the single most common way superposition appears violated.
• STRIKE-SLIP fault — horizontal motion, no vertical component. Described as right-lateral (dextral) or left-lateral (sinistral) by which way the far side appears to move as you face the fault. The San Andreas is right-lateral.
FIELD EVIDENCE OF FAULTING even when displacement is not visible: SLICKENSIDES (polished, grooved fault surfaces — the grooves give the slip direction), fault BRECCIA and GOUGE (crushed and powdered rock in the fault zone), abrupt truncation of beds, repeated or missing stratigraphy in a section, springs aligned in a straight line, an abnormally straight valley or scarp, and offset streams or ridges.
JOINTS are fractures with NO displacement, and they matter practically far more than their subtlety suggests: they control where water enters rock, where weathering attacks, where cliffs fail, and how quarried blocks split. Columnar jointing (the hexagonal columns of the Giant's Causeway) forms by contraction as thick lava cools; sheeting joints form parallel to the surface as overburden is removed and granite expands, producing the domes of Yosemite.

sections.heading: Unconformities and reading a landscape's missing time
sections.body:
An unconformity is a buried surface of erosion or non-deposition — a gap in the rock record standing for time during which no rock was preserved at that spot. Recognising unconformities is arguably the single most powerful skill in reconstructing a region's history, because each one records an entire cycle: rock formed, the region was lifted above sea level, the top of the pile was stripped away by weather and rivers, and then the surface subsided again and fresh sediment buried the erosional scar. The missing interval is often longer than everything preserved above it.
