By mass, oxygen is the most abundant element in the crust, making up roughly 46 percent, and silicon is second at about 28 percent; together they account for nearly three-quarters of the crust. Given such an overwhelming supply of oxygen and silicon, and their strong chemical affinity for one another, it is unsurprising that minerals combining the two make up the great bulk of crustal rock. Silicate minerals constitute well over 90 percent of the Earth's crust and mantle, so that the solid Earth beneath us is, chemically, largely a body of silicates.

The importance of silicates extends beyond mere abundance. Because they form under a wide range of temperatures and pressures, silicate minerals record the conditions of their formation, and geologists read them to reconstruct the histories of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary environments. The order in which silicate minerals crystallise from a cooling magma, described by Bowen's reaction series, governs how igneous rocks differentiate and why the crust and mantle differ in composition. The breakdown of silicates by weathering releases the nutrients that soils and life depend upon and consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide over geological time. Silicates are thus central not only to what the Earth is made of but to how it works.

Silicates also underpin much of human material culture. Quartz becomes glass and the substrate of electronics; feldspars and clays are the raw materials of ceramics; micas insulate; zeolites purify and catalyse; and many prized gemstones, from emerald to garnet to topaz, are silicates. At the same time, certain silicates pose serious hazards, notably the dust of crystalline silica and the fibres of asbestos minerals, which cause grave lung disease. To study silicate minerals is therefore to study a class of materials that build the planet, drive its chemical cycles, supply industry, and demand respect for the dangers a few of them carry, all of which flow from a single, elegant structural building block examined in the next section.

sections.heading: The Silicon-Oxygen Tetrahedron: The Fundamental Unit
sections.body:
Every silicate mineral is built from a single structural motif, the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron. At its centre sits one small, highly charged silicon ion, and around it, at the four corners of a regular tetrahedron, sit four oxygen ions. Written chemically the unit is SiO4, and because silicon carries a charge of plus four while each of the four oxygens carries minus two, the isolated group has a net charge of minus four, so it is often written as the silicate anion. This tetrahedron is the indivisible brick from which the entire, immensely varied class of silicate minerals is assembled.

The geometry follows from the sizes and charges of the ions. Silicon is a small cation, and oxygen is a comparatively large anion; the ratio of their radii is such that exactly four oxygens can pack closely around one silicon, touching it and forming the four-cornered tetrahedral shape rather than, say, a six-cornered octahedron. This is an instance of the general rules of ionic packing worked out by Linus Pauling, which predict coordination number from radius ratio. The silicon-oxygen bond itself is short, strong, and intermediate between purely ionic and purely covalent in character, sharing about half its bonding electrons; this strength gives silicates their hardness and durability.

The crucial property of the tetrahedron is that its corner oxygens can be shared. Because each oxygen has one unused unit of negative charge after bonding to its silicon, an oxygen at a corner can bond to a second silicon in an adjacent tetrahedron, becoming a bridge between the two. When two tetrahedra share a corner oxygen, they are said to be polymerised. The extent to which tetrahedra share corners, from no sharing at all up to every corner shared, is the master variable that defines the different silicate structures, and it is the basis of the entire classification scheme.

The charge balance of a silicate is bookkeeping on those shared and unshared oxygens. Every oxygen that is not shared between two silicons retains negative charge that must be neutralised by other cations, chiefly metal ions such as magnesium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium, and aluminium, which occupy the spaces between the tetrahedra. The more the tetrahedra share oxygens with each other, the fewer such spare charges remain and the fewer additional cations the structure needs; the less they share, the more metal cations must be present to balance the charge. This simple relationship between the degree of tetrahedral linkage and the amount and kind of other cations present controls the composition, density, melting behaviour, and even the colour of silicate minerals, all of which trace back to how the humble SiO4 unit is connected to its neighbours.

sections.heading: Polymerization: How Tetrahedra Link
sections.body:
The single most useful idea in silicate mineralogy is polymerization, the sharing of corner oxygens between tetrahedra, because the degree of polymerization determines almost everything else about a silicate. A tetrahedron has four corners, and each may either stand alone, its oxygen bonded only to its own silicon and to surrounding metal cations, or be shared, its oxygen bridging to a second silicon. By counting how many corners are shared, ranging from zero to four, mineralogists sort all silicates into a small number of structural families, and this framework is the backbone of the classification presented in the following sections.

The relationship between polymerization and composition is captured by the ratio of silicon to oxygen. When no corners are shared, each silicon has four oxygens to itself and the ratio is one to four. As corners are shared, oxygens are used by two silicons at once and the ratio of silicon to oxygen rises. Sharing two corners gives chains with a ratio of one to three; sharing three corners gives sheets with a ratio of two to five; sharing all four corners gives a three-dimensional framework with a ratio of one to two, the composition of pure silica. This progression, from one to four up to one to two, is a compact summary of the whole silicate class and can be recited as a ladder of increasing linkage.

Polymerization also governs physical and chemical behaviour in a systematic way. Because the silicon-oxygen bond is the strongest bond in these structures, the more extensively the tetrahedra are linked, the more the mineral's strength derives from this robust framework and the less it depends on the weaker bonds to intervening metal cations. Highly polymerised silicates, such as framework structures, therefore tend to be hard, resistant to weathering, and rich in silicon, and their melts are viscous. Weakly polymerised silicates, rich in metal cations, tend to be denser, to melt at higher temperatures, and to weather more readily at the Earth's surface.

This structural logic even orders the way igneous rocks form, through Bowen's reaction series. In a cooling magma the least polymerised silicates, such as the isolated-tetrahedron mineral olivine, crystallise first at the highest temperatures, followed by chain and then sheet silicates, with the fully polymerised framework silicates like quartz crystallising last from the coolest, most silica-rich residual liquid. The same sequence, read in reverse, describes the order in which silicates break down during weathering: the last to crystallise, quartz, is the most stable at the surface and survives, while the first to crystallise, olivine, decomposes most quickly. Thus a single organising principle, the degree to which silicon-oxygen tetrahedra share their corners, threads through structure, composition, melting, crystallisation, and weathering alike.

sections.heading: Nesosilicates and Sorosilicates: Isolated and Paired Tetrahedra
sections.body:
The least polymerised silicates are the nesosilicates, also called island or ortho-silicates, in which the tetrahedra share no corner oxygens at all. Each SiO4 group stands alone, bonded only to surrounding metal cations, giving a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of one to four. Because the structure relies heavily on the metal-oxygen bonds between the isolated tetrahedra, nesosilicates tend to be dense and hard, and they often crystallise at high temperatures. Their properties are relatively isotropic, that is, similar in all directions, since there are no chains or sheets to impose a preferred grain, so they usually lack strong cleavage and break with a conchoidal or uneven fracture instead.

The most important nesosilicate is olivine, a solid solution between a magnesium end-member and an iron end-member, with the general formula in which magnesium and iron together balance the isolated silicate groups. Olivine is a principal mineral of the Earth's mantle and of dark igneous rocks such as basalt and peridotite, and its high-temperature, high-pressure forms make up much of the deep interior. Other significant nesosilicates include the garnets, a family of hard silicates used both as gemstones and as abrasives; zircon, a durable mineral whose trapped uranium makes it invaluable for radiometric dating of the oldest crustal rocks; and the aluminium silicates kyanite, andalusite, and sillimanite, whose appearance signals particular metamorphic pressures and temperatures. Topaz, prized as a gem, also belongs here.

Sorosilicates are only slightly more linked, containing pairs of tetrahedra that share a single corner oxygen between them, forming a double unit with a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of two to seven. This paired grouping is less common than the other structural types, and sorosilicates are correspondingly a smaller family. The best known is the epidote group, minerals that form during low-grade metamorphism and hydrothermal alteration and that give many altered rocks a distinctive pistachio-green colour. Hemimorphite, a zinc-bearing sorosilicate, is a minor ore of zinc. Some minerals, notably certain members of the epidote group, contain both isolated and paired tetrahedra, blurring the boundary between the two categories.

Together the nesosilicates and sorosilicates represent the low-polymerization end of the silicate spectrum, the structures richest in metal cations and generally densest, hardest to weather in some cases yet, in the case of olivine, among the first minerals to break down at the surface. Their significance is out of proportion to the small number of species, because olivine dominates the mantle, garnet and the aluminium silicates are key indicators of metamorphic conditions, and zircon anchors the geological time scale. Studying these minerals shows how, even with no linkage between tetrahedra, the identity and arrangement of the balancing cations produce a rich diversity of minerals with widely different roles in the Earth, from the deep interior to the dating of its most ancient rocks.

sections.heading: Cyclosilicates: The Ring Silicates
sections.body:
Cyclosilicates occupy a distinctive niche in the classification, in which tetrahedra share two corners each but arrange themselves into closed rings rather than open chains. Each tetrahedron bridges to its two neighbours, and the ring closes back on itself, giving a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of one to three, the same ratio as the single-chain silicates because both share exactly two corners per tetrahedron. Rings of three, four, or six tetrahedra are known, but the six-membered ring is by far the most important, and it defines the two great cyclosilicate minerals, beryl and tourmaline. The rings stack above one another to form channels running through the crystal.

Beryl is a beryllium aluminium cyclosilicate whose six-membered rings create prominent open channels along the crystal's length. Pure beryl is colourless, but trace impurities occupying or bordering these channels produce the mineral's famous gem varieties: chromium or vanadium yields the deep green of emerald, iron the pale blue-green of aquamarine, manganese the pink of morganite, and other elements give golden and colourless forms. The channels can also hold water molecules and alkali ions. Beryl is the principal ore of beryllium, a light, stiff metal valued in aerospace and specialised alloys, so the mineral is economically important as well as ornamental.

Tourmaline is a chemically complex boron-bearing cyclosilicate, so variable in composition that it is best described as a group rather than a single species. Its structure combines six-membered silicate rings with additional sites holding a wide array of cations, and this compositional flexibility produces an extraordinary range of colours, sometimes several within a single crystal, as in the pink-and-green watermelon variety. Tourmaline is also notable for its physical peculiarities: it is both pyroelectric and piezoelectric, developing an electric charge when heated or squeezed, a property it shares with quartz and one that reflects the polar, non-symmetric arrangement of its structure.

Other cyclosilicates include cordierite, an iron and magnesium aluminium silicate that forms in metamorphosed rocks rich in aluminium and serves as an indicator of certain temperature and pressure conditions, and it has industrial use in heat-resistant ceramics because of its very low thermal expansion. As a group, the cyclosilicates illustrate a general theme of silicate mineralogy: that the same degree of polymerization, here two shared corners per tetrahedron, can be realised in more than one geometry, rings as opposed to chains, and that the resulting channels and cavities in ring structures give these minerals distinctive abilities to host trace elements and water. Those hosted impurities, in turn, are responsible for the vivid colours that have made beryl and tourmaline among the most sought-after of all gem minerals, tying atomic structure directly to the appearance and value of the stones.

sections.heading: Inosilicates: The Chain Silicates
sections.body:
Inosilicates are the chain silicates, in which tetrahedra link into long strands, and they divide into two great families according to whether the chains are single or double. In a single chain each tetrahedron shares two of its corners, one with the tetrahedron ahead and one with the one behind, producing an endless strand with a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of one to three. These single chains define the pyroxenes, one of the most important rock-forming mineral groups. The chains run parallel through the crystal, bound side by side by metal cations, and this internal architecture governs the minerals' cleavage, which is a diagnostic feature.

The pyroxenes are magnesium, iron, and calcium silicates that crystallise in basalts, gabbros, and many metamorphic rocks, and they are, with olivine and feldspar, among the chief constituents of the Earth's crust and upper mantle. Common examples include augite, the dark pyroxene of basalt; enstatite, the magnesium end-member; and diopside, a calcium-magnesium pyroxene. Because the bonds holding one chain to the next are weaker than the strong bonds within a chain, pyroxenes cleave between the chains, and their two cleavage planes meet at angles close to ninety degrees, near eighty-seven and ninety-three degrees, a feature that helps distinguish them from the superficially similar amphiboles.

Double-chain inosilicates, the amphiboles, are formed when two single chains join along their length, so that alternate tetrahedra share a third corner, giving a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of four to eleven. The most important structural difference from pyroxenes, beyond the doubled chain, is that amphiboles contain hydroxyl groups, meaning water is built into their structure; this makes them minerals of somewhat wetter, lower-temperature conditions than the anhydrous pyroxenes. Hornblende, a dark, complex amphibole, is widespread in intermediate igneous and metamorphic rocks. The wider spacing of the double chains gives amphiboles a characteristically different cleavage, with the two planes meeting at angles near fifty-six and one hundred twenty-four degrees rather than close to right angles.

That difference in cleavage angle, roughly sixty and one hundred twenty degrees for amphiboles against about ninety degrees for pyroxenes, is one of the most reliable field tests in silicate identification, because the two groups are otherwise similar in colour and hardness. The chain silicates also include a hazardous subgroup: some amphiboles crystallise in a fibrous habit and constitute several of the asbestos minerals, whose thin, durable fibres cause serious lung disease when inhaled. The inosilicates thus span from ordinary dark rock-forming minerals, essential to understanding basalt and gabbro, to industrially valued and dangerous fibrous forms, all arising from the simple architectural choice between single and double chains of tetrahedra and the way those chains are bound together by intervening cations.

sections.heading: Phyllosilicates: The Sheet Silicates
sections.body:
When tetrahedra share three of their four corners, they link not into chains but into continuous two-dimensional sheets, and the minerals built this way are the phyllosilicates, from the Greek word for leaf. The shared corners lie in a plane and connect each tetrahedron to three neighbours, giving a silicon-to-oxygen ratio of two to five, while the fourth, unshared corner of every tetrahedron points the same way out of the sheet, its spare charge available to bond to a layer of metal cations. This combination of a tetrahedral sheet bonded to an adjacent layer of cations, often with hydroxyl groups, is the defining feature of the group and the source of its most characteristic properties.

The dominant physical trait of sheet silicates is a single, exceptionally perfect cleavage parallel to the sheets. Because the bonds within each sheet are strong silicon-oxygen bonds while the bonds holding one sheet-and-cation layer to the next are much weaker, the minerals split easily into thin, flexible plates or flakes. This is most familiar in the micas, muscovite and biotite, which peel into transparent elastic sheets and have been used as furnace windows and electrical insulators precisely because they cleave into thin, heat-resistant, non-conducting laminae. Talc, the softest mineral on the Mohs scale, is a phyllosilicate whose weakly bonded sheets slide over one another so readily that it feels greasy and serves as a lubricant and the basis of talcum powder.

The clay minerals form the most abundant and, in many ways, most consequential branch of the phyllosilicates. Kaolinite, illite, and the smectite group are fine-grained sheet silicates produced chiefly by the weathering of other silicates, especially feldspars, at the Earth's surface. Their tiny particle size, enormous surface area, and layered, charge-bearing structure give clays the ability to hold water and to adsorb and exchange ions, which makes them central to soil fertility, to the plasticity of muds, and to the behaviour of sediments. Some clays, the swelling smectites, take water between their sheets and expand, causing the shrink-swell soils that crack in drought and damage foundations.

The phyllosilicates also include serpentine and chlorite, and here the group meets both economic and health significance. Chlorite is a common product of low-grade metamorphism, giving many rocks a green colour. Serpentine forms from the alteration of olivine-rich rocks and, in one fibrous variety, chrysotile, is the most widely used form of asbestos, whose sheets roll into thin tubes that separate into inhalable fibres. Thus the same structural theme, tetrahedra sharing three corners into sheets, yields minerals as diverse as gem-like transparent mica, soft slippery talc, the humble but vital clays of every soil, and a dangerous asbestos, all unified by the easy parting between weakly bonded layers that a sheet structure inevitably produces.

sections.heading: Tectosilicates: The Framework Silicates
sections.body:
At the fully polymerised end of the spectrum lie the tectosilicates, or framework silicates, in which every tetrahedron shares all four of its corner oxygens with neighbouring tetrahedra, building a continuous three-dimensional network. With all oxygens shared between two silicons apiece, the silicon-to-oxygen ratio falls to one to two, the composition of pure silica. Because the structure is held together entirely by strong silicon-oxygen bonds extending in all directions, framework silicates tend to be hard, chemically durable, and relatively low in density and in metal-cation content. This group is the most abundant of all, since its two great members, quartz and the feldspars, together make up the majority of the continental crust.

Quartz is the simplest tectosilicate, essentially pure silica, a rigid framework of tetrahedra with no additional cations required, because every charge is satisfied within the network. This structural completeness gives quartz its great hardness, ranking seven on the Mohs scale, its resistance to chemical attack, and its lack of cleavage; instead it breaks with a smooth conchoidal fracture. Quartz is extraordinarily stable at the Earth's surface, so it survives weathering when other minerals decay and accumulates as the dominant grain of sand and sandstone. Its non-symmetric structure makes it piezoelectric, generating a voltage under stress, a property exploited in the quartz oscillators that keep time in watches and electronics.

The feldspars are the most abundant minerals in the crust, and they show how a framework can accommodate additional elements. Substituting some aluminium for silicon in the tetrahedra creates a charge deficit, because aluminium carries one less positive charge than silicon, and this deficit is balanced by admitting large cations, sodium, potassium, or calcium, into cavities in the framework. The result is two main series: the alkali feldspars, ranging between sodium-rich and potassium-rich compositions such as orthoclase, and the plagioclase feldspars, forming a continuous solid solution between sodium-rich albite and calcium-rich anorthite. Feldspars have two good cleavages meeting at nearly ninety degrees, and plagioclase often shows fine parallel striations from twinning.

Related framework silicates extend the group's range. The feldspathoids, such as nepheline and leucite, resemble feldspars but form in magmas poor in silica, where there is not enough silica to make feldspar. The zeolites are framework silicates with unusually open structures riddled with channels and cavities large enough to admit water and exchangeable cations, and they can lose and regain water without collapsing; these properties make natural and synthetic zeolites valuable as molecular sieves, water softeners, and industrial catalysts, notably in petroleum refining. From the pure, timekeeping rigidity of quartz to the porous, chemically active zeolites, the tectosilicates demonstrate how a single fully linked framework, modified by aluminium substitution and the cations it invites, produces the most abundant and among the most useful of all silicate minerals.

sections.heading: Crystal Chemistry: Substitution and Solid Solution
sections.body:
Silicate compositions are rarely fixed and pure; instead most silicate minerals are solid solutions, structures in which different ions can occupy the same crystallographic site in varying proportions, giving a range of compositions between end-members. The governing principle, worked out by Victor Goldschmidt and others, is that one ion can substitute for another in a crystal site if the two are similar enough in size and, ideally, in charge. Ionic radius is the primary control: ions whose radii differ by less than about fifteen percent substitute freely, while larger differences restrict substitution. This is why magnesium and iron, close in size, interchange so readily throughout the silicates.

The clearest example is olivine, where magnesium and ferrous iron substitute for one another without limit, producing a complete solid solution from the pure magnesium end-member to the pure iron end-member. Any intermediate composition is possible and stable, and a given olivine crystal simply reports how much of each metal was available when it grew. Similar magnesium-iron substitution runs through the pyroxenes, amphiboles, micas, and garnets, so that the dark, iron-and-magnesium-bearing silicates form interlocking families whose members shade into one another. Because iron and magnesium behave so similarly, chemical formulas for these minerals are usually written with both elements bracketed together.

When the substituting ions differ in charge, the balance must be maintained by a second, coupled substitution elsewhere in the structure, an elegant piece of natural bookkeeping. The plagioclase feldspars are the textbook case. Sodium and calcium can both occupy the large cavity in the feldspar framework, but sodium carries one positive charge and calcium two, so simply swapping one for the other would unbalance the crystal. The structure compensates by simultaneously exchanging one silicon for one aluminium in the tetrahedral framework, since silicon carries four positive charges and aluminium three. Thus a sodium-plus-silicon pair is replaced by a calcium-plus-aluminium pair, keeping the total charge constant, and this coupled substitution allows the continuous plagioclase series from albite to anorthite.

Substitution has consequences that geologists exploit and industry must reckon with. The composition of a solid-solution mineral records the temperature, pressure, and chemistry of its formation, so measuring, for instance, the magnesium-to-iron ratio of a pyroxene or the sodium-to-calcium ratio of a plagioclase serves as a geothermometer or geobarometer, a way to read past conditions from present crystals. Trace substitutions produce the colours of gems and provide the radioactive parent elements, such as uranium substituting into zircon, that make radiometric dating possible. At the same time, unwanted substitutions introduce impurities that degrade the performance of quartz in electronics or of feldspar and clay in ceramics. The chemistry of substitution and solid solution therefore turns each silicate species from a fixed compound into a continuously variable recorder of Earth's conditions, and understanding it is essential to reading rocks and to using their minerals.

sections.heading: Identifying Silicate Minerals: Physical Properties
sections.body:
Identifying silicate minerals in hand specimen relies on a small set of physical properties that can be tested with simple tools, and each property connects back to the atomic structure discussed earlier. The most fundamental is crystal structure expressed as external form and, more usefully in broken samples, as cleavage and fracture. Cleavage is the tendency to split along planes of weak bonding, and its presence, number, and angles are highly diagnostic: nesosilicates like olivine and garnet lack cleavage and fracture unevenly, chain silicates cleave in two directions whose angle distinguishes pyroxene from amphibole, sheet silicates show one perfect cleavage into flakes, and framework feldspars show two cleavages near ninety degrees while quartz shows none.

Hardness, the resistance to scratching, is measured against the Mohs scale, a sequence of ten reference minerals from talc at one to diamond at ten. Silicates span much of this range, and several serve as scale standards: talc defines one, feldspar six, quartz seven, and topaz eight. In practice a geologist tests hardness with common objects of known value, a fingernail, a copper coin, a steel knife, and a glass plate, to bracket a mineral's hardness quickly. Because hardness reflects bond strength and structure, the highly polymerised, strongly bonded silicates such as quartz and topaz are among the hardest common minerals, while the weakly interlayer-bonded talc is the softest of all.

Colour, though the first thing one notices, is often the least reliable property, because trace impurities and substitutions can colour a mineral almost any hue, as the many varieties of beryl and tourmaline show. More dependable is streak, the colour of the mineral's powder rubbed on unglazed porcelain, and lustre, the way the surface reflects light, described as vitreous or glassy for most silicates, pearly for micas, or greasy for talc and some serpentine. Diaphaneity, whether a mineral is transparent, translucent, or opaque, and specific gravity, its density relative to water felt as heft in the hand, add further clues; the dense, iron-magnesium silicates feel notably heavier than framework minerals like quartz and feldspar.

For rigorous identification, especially of fine-grained rocks, geologists turn to the polarising microscope and to instrumental methods. A thin slice of rock ground to about thirty micrometres becomes transparent, and under polarised light each silicate displays characteristic optical properties, colour, relief, birefringence, and extinction behaviour, that identify it and reveal its texture and relationships to neighbouring grains. Beyond optics, X-ray diffraction determines the crystal structure directly by the way a mineral scatters X-rays, and electron microprobe analysis measures its precise chemical composition point by point. These laboratory techniques resolve ambiguities that hand-specimen tests cannot, but the field properties of cleavage, hardness, lustre, and heft remain the practised geologist's first and often sufficient means of telling one silicate from another.
ingredients: A hardness kit: fingernail (about 2.5), copper coin (about 3.5), steel knife or nail (about 5.5), glass plate (about 5.5), and a quartz sample (7)
A streak plate (a piece of unglazed white porcelain tile)
A hand lens, typically 10x magnification
A small magnet (to detect iron-rich minerals)
Dilute hydrochloric acid, used mainly to distinguish carbonates from silicates (silicates do not fizz)
steps: Examine the fresh, unweathered surface in good light and note the lustre (glassy, pearly, greasy, metallic) and colour, treating colour as a weak clue only.
Look for cleavage: turn the sample so light glints off flat surfaces, and count the directions of flat cleavage planes and estimate the angles between them.
Test hardness by attempting to scratch the mineral with each tool in turn, from softest to hardest, to bracket its Mohs value.
Rub the mineral across the streak plate and note the colour of the resulting powder.
Judge the specific gravity by heft, comparing the sample with a similarly sized piece of quartz.
Combine the observations: for example, two cleavages near 90 degrees with hardness about 6 suggests feldspar, whereas no cleavage with hardness 7 and conchoidal fracture suggests quartz.
If hand tests are inconclusive, submit a thin section for polarising-microscope study or the sample for X-ray diffraction.

sections.heading: Silicates in Rocks and the Rock Cycle
sections.body:
Silicate minerals are the principal actors in the rock cycle, the endless transformation of rock among igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms, and each rock type expresses the silicates appropriate to its conditions. Igneous rocks crystallise from molten magma, and the silicates that grow depend on the magma's composition and cooling. In accordance with Bowen's reaction series, silica-poor magmas crystallise the high-temperature, weakly polymerised silicates first, olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase, yielding dark, dense rocks like basalt and gabbro, while silica-rich magmas end with the low-temperature framework silicates, quartz and potassium feldspar, producing pale rocks like granite and rhyolite.

The classification of igneous rocks is essentially a classification by silicate mineralogy. A rock dominated by quartz, alkali feldspar, and sodium-rich plagioclase, with subordinate mica or amphibole, is granitic and characteristic of the continental crust; a rock dominated by calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene, with olivine, is basaltic and characteristic of the oceanic crust and much of the mantle. The relative proportions of light framework silicates and dark iron-magnesium silicates thus define the whole spectrum of igneous rocks and reflect deep differences in where and how the magmas formed. Grain size, a separate variable, records how fast the magma cooled, coarse for slow plutonic cooling and fine for rapid volcanic quenching.

Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to heat and pressure that recrystallise their minerals without melting, and silicates are exquisitely sensitive recorders of these conditions. As pressure and temperature rise, silicate assemblages change in a predictable sequence: clays give way to micas, then to garnet, staurolite, kyanite, and sillimanite in aluminous rocks, each mineral or combination marking a metamorphic grade. Geologists map these index minerals across the landscape to reconstruct ancient episodes of mountain building and burial. The alignment of platy micas and elongate amphiboles under directed pressure produces the foliation, the layering and schistosity, that gives many metamorphic rocks their characteristic texture.

Sedimentary rocks close the cycle, and here silicates appear in two roles. First, the durable survivors of weathering, above all quartz, accumulate as sand and are cemented into sandstone, while the new clay minerals produced by weathering settle as mud and lithify into shale, the most abundant sedimentary rock. Second, silicates dissolved and reprecipitated, and the ions released to rivers and seas, feed both these clastic sediments and the chemistry of the oceans. Weathering, transport, deposition, burial, and eventual metamorphism or melting return the material to the start of the cycle. Because silicates make up the overwhelming bulk of crustal rock, the rock cycle is, in chemical terms, largely a cycle of silicate minerals being repeatedly rearranged, and reading any rock means reading the silicates it contains and the conditions they record.

sections.heading: Weathering, Soils, and Economic Importance
sections.body:
At the Earth's surface, silicate minerals meet water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and life, and they slowly break down through chemical weathering, a process of profound geological and biological importance. The dominant reaction is hydrolysis, in which mildly acidic rainwater attacks the mineral, stripping away soluble cations such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium and leaving behind new, more stable minerals, chiefly clays. The archetypal reaction converts feldspar into kaolinite clay while releasing dissolved ions and consuming carbon dioxide. The order of susceptibility mirrors Bowen's series in reverse: olivine and calcium plagioclase weather fastest, quartz slowest, which is why beach sand is so rich in quartz.

This weathering has two consequences that reach far beyond the outcrop. First, it builds soil. The clays produced by silicate weathering, mixed with organic matter, form the mineral skeleton of soils, and their layered, charged structure gives soils the capacity to hold water and to store and release the nutrient cations, potassium, calcium, magnesium, that plants require. The steady breakdown of silicate minerals thus continuously resupplies the nutrients that terrestrial life draws down, and the fertility of a region often traces back to the silicates in its parent rock, with soils on fresh volcanic silicates among the most productive on Earth.

Second, silicate weathering regulates the long-term climate by consuming carbon dioxide. When rainwater made acidic by atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves silicate minerals, the carbon is carried to the sea as bicarbonate and eventually buried as carbonate rock, removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over hundreds of thousands of years. This silicate-weathering feedback speeds up when the climate is warm and wet and slows when it is cold and dry, acting as a planetary thermostat that has helped keep Earth's surface habitable across geological time. The humble decay of feldspar and olivine on hillsides is therefore linked to the greenhouse balance of the whole planet.

The economic importance of silicates is vast and touches daily life at every turn. Quartz supplies glass, foundry sand, abrasives, and the ultrapure silicon of semiconductors and solar cells, and its piezoelectric crystals regulate electronic clocks. Feldspars and clays are the raw materials of the entire ceramics and pottery industry, from bricks and tiles to fine porcelain, and clays are essential to paper, drilling muds, and cement. Micas insulate electrical equipment and add sheen to paints and cosmetics; talc fills and lubricates countless products; and zeolites soften water, purify gases, and catalyse the refining of petroleum. Many gemstones, emerald and aquamarine from beryl, the garnets, topaz, tourmaline, peridot from olivine, and zircon, are silicates. From the soil that feeds agriculture to the glass, ceramics, and electronics of modern technology, silicate minerals are among the most economically indispensable of all natural materials.

sections.heading: Health, Hazards, and Responsible Handling
sections.body:
While silicate minerals are abundant, useful, and mostly harmless in bulk, a few present serious dangers when they enter the lungs as fine particles or fibres, and understanding these hazards is a necessary part of studying the group. The two principal threats are crystalline silica dust and asbestos, both of which cause severe and often fatal disease, and both of which arise precisely from the durability and structure that make silicates valuable. The danger lies not in touching or being near these minerals in solid form but in inhaling airborne particles small enough to reach the deepest parts of the lung.

Crystalline silica, chiefly finely divided quartz, is released whenever silica-bearing rock, sand, concrete, stone, or engineered quartz worktops are cut, drilled, ground, or crushed, generating respirable dust. Inhaled over time, these sharp particles scar the lungs, producing silicosis, an incurable, progressive fibrosis that stiffens the lungs and impairs breathing, and prolonged exposure also raises the risk of lung cancer, tuberculosis, and other diseases. Silicosis is one of the oldest known occupational diseases, historically afflicting miners, quarry workers, and stone masons, and it has re-emerged among workers fabricating artificial stone countertops. Because the disease develops silently over years, prevention through dust control is the only effective defence.

Asbestos is a collective term for several silicate minerals that crystallise in a fibrous habit, including the serpentine mineral chrysotile and the amphiboles crocidolite and amosite. Their thin, strong, heat-resistant fibres made them widely used in insulation, fireproofing, and building materials through much of the twentieth century, but when the material is disturbed the fibres become airborne and, once inhaled, lodge permanently in lung tissue. There they cause asbestosis, a scarring disease, and, decades later, lung cancer and mesothelioma, a rare and almost invariably fatal cancer of the lining of the lungs and abdomen. The amphibole forms are the most dangerous, and there is no known safe level of exposure, which is why asbestos has been banned or strictly regulated in many countries.

Responsible handling follows directly from how these hazards arise, namely from airborne particles. The core principle is to prevent dust and fibres from becoming airborne and, where that is impossible, to prevent their inhalation. Cutting or grinding silica-bearing materials should be done with water suppression or local exhaust ventilation to capture dust at the source, together with properly fitted respirators rated for fine particulates; dry sweeping, which throws dust back into the air, should be avoided in favour of wet methods or vacuuming with high-efficiency filters. Suspected asbestos should never be disturbed by untrained persons; its identification, removal, and disposal are tasks for licensed specialists using sealed containment. With these precautions the genuine dangers of a small number of silicate minerals can be managed, allowing the enormous benefits of the class as a whole to be enjoyed safely.

guides.title: Carbonate, Oxide and Sulfide Minerals
guides.summary: The structure, chemistry, occurrence and identification of the three great non-silicate mineral classes — carbonates, oxides and sulfides — and the roles they play in the carbon cycle, in the iron and metal ores, and in the weathering of the Earth's crust.

sections.heading: Three Classes That Run the Planet's Chemistry
sections.body:
Silicate minerals make up something over 90 percent of the Earth's crust by volume, and a mineralogy course quite reasonably spends most of its time on them. Yet three much smaller classes carry a disproportionate share of the planet's chemical work, and almost all of its industrial value. Carbonates hold the great reservoir of carbon locked out of the atmosphere. Oxides supply nearly all the world's iron, titanium, chromium, tin, manganese and aluminium, and they carry the magnetic record from which plate tectonics was reconstructed. Sulfides are the source of essentially all copper, lead, zinc, nickel, molybdenum and much of the silver and gold, and their breakdown at the surface produces both spectacular secondary minerals and one of the most persistent forms of industrial pollution.

They are grouped this way because mineral classification is organised by anion — the negatively charged unit that gives the structure its skeleton — rather than by the metal cation. This convention, established by James Dwight Dana in his System of Mineralogy from 1837 onwards and refined in the twentieth century into the Nickel-Strunz scheme still in general use, works because the anion determines the structural architecture far more strongly than the cation does. Every carbonate is built around the flat triangular carbonate group. Every simple oxide is built around a close-packed array of oxygen atoms with metals tucked into the gaps. Sulfides are built on the very different bonding chemistry of sulfur, which is larger, more polarisable and far less electronegative than oxygen.

The three classes therefore behave in three coherent, predictable ways. Carbonates are soft, soluble in acid, usually light-coloured and transparent, and dissolve and reprecipitate freely at surface conditions. Oxides tend to be hard, dense, chemically stubborn and stable across an enormous range of temperature and pressure, which is why they survive weathering and concentrate in placer deposits. Sulfides are heavy, opaque, metallic in appearance, mostly soft, and profoundly unstable in the presence of oxygen and water — which is why they form deep and rot fast.

Understanding them together rather than separately is worthwhile because they are chemically linked. The oxidation of a sulfide generates acid; that acid attacks carbonate; the neutralisation of that acid precipitates oxides and hydroxides. A gossan — the rusty, leached cap over a buried ore body — is a single outcrop in which all three classes are visibly reacting with one another. The same three-way relationship governs the chemistry of mine drainage, of soil formation on mineralised ground, and of the long-term regulation of atmospheric carbon dioxide by silicate weathering and carbonate burial.

Their relative abundances are worth holding in mind. Carbonates make up something like 10 to 15 percent of all sedimentary rock and perhaps 3 to 4 percent of the crust as a whole. Oxides account for another 3 to 4 percent, most of it iron and titanium phases dispersed as accessory grains. Sulfides make up well under 0.1 percent of the crust, and yet that fraction contains most of the metal that industrial civilisation is built from. Rarity and importance are not the same thing, and in mineralogy they are frequently opposites.

sections.heading: What a Mineral Is, and Why Anions Organise the System
sections.body:
A mineral, in the strict definition used by the International Mineralogical Association, is a naturally occurring, generally inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition, expressible by a formula, and an ordered internal atomic arrangement — a crystal structure. Each of those clauses does work. Naturally occurring excludes laboratory products; the IMA maintains a separate register for synthetic analogues. Generally inorganic admits a small number of organic-compound minerals such as whewellite, calcium oxalate, while excluding coal and petroleum. Definite composition allows for solid solution, in which one element substitutes for another across a range, provided the structure is unchanged. Ordered atomic arrangement excludes glass, opal and other amorphous materials, which are formally mineraloids.

Roughly 6,000 mineral species are currently recognised, with sixty to a hundred new ones approved each year, and yet fewer than a hundred are common enough that a geologist will meet them regularly. Of those, perhaps a dozen carbonates, a dozen oxides and two dozen sulfides account for nearly all practical encounters.

The reason classification proceeds by anion is structural rather than merely conventional. In an ionic or partly ionic solid, the anions are usually the larger species — oxygen has an ionic radius of about 1.40 ångströms, sulfur about 1.84, while iron in the ferrous state is 0.78 and aluminium only 0.535 — so the anions form the framework and the smaller cations occupy the interstices between them. Change the cation and you change the colour, density and often the symmetry; change the anion and you change the entire architecture.

The governing principle is Linus Pauling's set of rules, published in 1929, of which the first two carry most of the weight. The radius ratio of cation to anion determines the coordination number: a ratio between 0.414 and 0.732 gives six-fold octahedral coordination, between 0.225 and 0.414 gives four-fold tetrahedral, and above 0.732 gives eight-fold cubic or higher. The second rule, electrostatic valence, requires that the charge on each anion be balanced by the sum of bond strengths reaching it from surrounding cations. Together these predict, with surprising accuracy, which structures are possible.

Bond character matters as much as size, and this is the deep reason sulfides behave so differently from oxides. Electronegativity on the Pauling scale runs 3.44 for oxygen and only 2.58 for sulfur, against 1.83 for iron and 1.90 for copper. An iron-oxygen bond is therefore substantially ionic; an iron-sulfur bond is largely covalent with significant metallic character. That covalent-metallic bonding gives sulfides their metallic lustre, their opacity, their electrical conductivity and their generally low hardness, and it is why they are described with the language of alloys and semiconductors as much as that of ionic crystals.

sections.heading: The Carbonate Ion: A Flat Triangle That Shapes a Whole Class
sections.body:
Every carbonate mineral is built around a single, remarkably rigid molecular unit: the carbonate ion, one carbon atom bonded to three oxygens. The carbon sits at the centre of an equilateral triangle of oxygens, exactly coplanar with them, with carbon-oxygen distances of about 1.28 ångströms and oxygen-carbon-oxygen angles of precisely 120 degrees. The carbon is sp2 hybridised, using three hybrid orbitals for the sigma bonds while its remaining p orbital forms a delocalised pi system spread over all three oxygens. The group carries a charge of minus two and has point symmetry D3h.

Two features of this unit dictate everything about carbonate minerals. First, it is strongly bonded internally and behaves as a rigid body, so carbonate structures can be understood as arrangements of triangles and metal cations rather than as networks of individual atoms. Second, and crucially, it is flat. A tetrahedral group such as the silicate unit can polymerise in three dimensions by sharing corners, which is why silicates build chains, sheets and frameworks of enormous variety. The flat triangle cannot polymerise in the same way, so carbonates are all essentially isolated triangles held together by cations. The class is consequently small and structurally simple: roughly 200 species against several thousand silicates, and only a handful of distinct structure types.

The pronounced anisotropy of the flat group also produces the class's most distinctive optical property. In calcite the triangles all lie in parallel planes perpendicular to the c axis, so light polarised in the plane of the triangles interacts far more strongly with the delocalised pi electrons than light polarised along the axis. The result is an extraordinary birefringence: the ordinary refractive index is 1.658 and the extraordinary index only 1.486, a difference of 0.172 that is among the largest of any common mineral. A clear rhomb of calcite laid over a printed line shows two distinct images. Erasmus Bartholin described exactly this in Icelandic spar in 1669, and the phenomenon underpinned the development of polarised-light optics through Huygens, Malus and Nicol.

The other defining behaviour is the reaction with acid. Carbonate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so adding a stronger acid protonates it to bicarbonate and then to carbonic acid, which decomposes to water and carbon dioxide gas. Placing a drop of cold dilute hydrochloric acid on calcite produces immediate vigorous effervescence, and this remains the single most useful field test in sedimentary geology.

Not all carbonates fizz equally. Dolomite reacts only weakly unless powdered or the acid is warmed, siderite and magnesite still more sluggishly, and the difference is a genuine diagnostic — a function of how tightly the smaller, more highly charged cations bind their oxygens and slow the proton exchange at the crystal surface.

sections.heading: Calcite and Aragonite: One Formula, Two Minerals
sections.body:
Calcium carbonate, CaCO3, crystallises in two common forms and one rare one, and the difference between them is one of the most instructive cases of polymorphism in all of mineralogy — the same composition adopting different structures under different conditions.

Calcite is trigonal, space group R-3c, and its structure is a distorted version of rock salt: replace the sodium with calcium, replace each chlorine with a flat carbonate triangle, and squash the cube along one body diagonal to accommodate the triangles, which all lie parallel in planes perpendicular to the threefold axis. Calcium sits in six-fold octahedral coordination with oxygen. The consequence of this layered arrangement is perfect cleavage in three directions, none at right angles, which splits any fragment into rhombohedra with angles of about 75 and 105 degrees. Hardness is 3 on the Mohs scale — the reference mineral for that value — and specific gravity is 2.71.

Aragonite is orthorhombic, space group Pmcn, and packs the same components more tightly. Calcium sits in nine-fold coordination, and the carbonate triangles lie in two slightly offset orientations. The denser packing gives a specific gravity of 2.95, about nine percent higher, and hardness 3.5 to 4. Cleavage is poor, and aragonite typically appears as fibrous, columnar or radiating aggregates, or as pseudohexagonal twins that mimic a sixfold symmetry the mineral does not possess.

Because aragonite is the denser structure, thermodynamics favours it at high pressure and calcite at low. At Earth-surface conditions aragonite is metastable: it should convert to calcite, and it does, but so slowly in dry conditions that shells and cave deposits survive as aragonite for millions of years. In the presence of water the conversion accelerates markedly, and aragonite is essentially absent from limestones older than about the Carboniferous, having recrystallised to calcite and in the process destroyed much of the original shell microstructure that palaeontologists would like to read.

What actually decides which form precipitates from seawater is largely the magnesium content. Magnesium ions adsorb onto growing calcite surfaces and poison them, while leaving aragonite growth relatively unimpeded. When the molar magnesium to calcium ratio of seawater exceeds roughly 2, aragonite and high-magnesium calcite dominate; below that, low-magnesium calcite does. That ratio has oscillated through the Phanerozoic in response to changing rates of seafloor spreading and hydrothermal exchange, producing alternating aragonite seas and calcite seas — a pattern first argued in detail by Philip Sandberg in 1983 and now supported by fluid inclusion measurements. Organisms building shells tracked those changes: reef-building shifted between aragonitic and calcitic taxa in step with the seawater chemistry.

A third polymorph, vaterite, is hexagonal, still less stable, and appears mainly as a fleeting precursor phase, in some gallstones and in the repair tissue of damaged mollusc shells. Its rarity is a good illustration of Ostwald's step rule, the tendency of a crystallising system to pass through less stable phases on the way to the stable one.

sections.heading: Dolomite and a Problem That Is Still Not Fully Solved
sections.body:
Dolomite, CaMg(CO3)2, is one of the most abundant minerals in the sedimentary record and one of the most awkward. Structurally it resembles calcite with every alternate cation layer replaced by magnesium, producing a stack of calcium layers, carbonate layers, magnesium layers and carbonate layers repeating along the c axis. That ordering lowers the symmetry from calcite's R-3c to R-3, removing the glide plane. Hardness is 3.5 to 4, specific gravity 2.85, and the cleavage is again rhombohedral in three directions. Crystals commonly show curved, saddle-shaped faces — an unusual habit produced by slight lattice mismatches accumulating during growth, and a reliable field clue.

The mineral is named for the French naturalist Déodat Guy de Dolomieu, who in 1791 noticed that certain Alpine limestones did not effervesce properly in acid; Nicolas de Saussure analysed them and named the rock in his honour in 1792. That same weak reaction remains the standard field discrimination: a drop of cold dilute hydrochloric acid produces vigorous fizzing on calcite and almost none on a solid dolomite surface, though scratching the surface to powder it, or warming the acid, will produce a slow reaction.

The dolomite problem is the persistent failure to reconcile the mineral's abundance in ancient rocks with the near-impossibility of growing it in the laboratory at surface temperatures. Vast Palaeozoic and Precambrian carbonate platforms are dolomite; modern environments producing it are rare, restricted and small. Attempts to precipitate ordered dolomite from seawater-like solutions at 25 degrees Celsius have essentially failed for well over a century, even when the solution is strongly supersaturated.

The obstacle is kinetic rather than thermodynamic. Dolomite is thermodynamically stable in ordinary seawater; it simply will not nucleate. The magnesium ion holds its shell of water molecules very tightly — its hydration energy is roughly 1,920 kilojoules per mole against about 1,505 for calcium — and stripping that shell to incorporate magnesium into a growing crystal face is slow. Worse, the alternating cation ordering demands that magnesium and calcium attach in strict sequence, which compounds the difficulty.

Several partial resolutions are argued and none commands full agreement. Elevated temperature helps, and much dolomite is demonstrably a burial replacement formed at 50 to 100 degrees over long timescales. High salinity and high magnesium-to-calcium ratios help, which explains dolomite forming in sabkha environments such as the Persian Gulf coast. Sulfate reduction by microbes removes sulfate ions that otherwise inhibit nucleation, and laboratory cultures of sulfate-reducing bacteria have produced disordered protodolomite. A 2023 study reported that cyclic fluctuations in saturation, dissolving poorly ordered surface layers between growth episodes, can grow ordered dolomite at low temperature — a promising result whose general applicability to ancient platforms is still being tested. The honest position is that dolomite formation is better understood than it was, but not solved.

sections.heading: The Rest of the Carbonate Family
sections.body:
Beyond calcium carbonate and dolomite, the carbonate class divides neatly by which cation sits between the triangles, and cation size determines which of two structure types is adopted.

Cations small enough for six-fold coordination take the calcite structure and form a continuous group: magnesite MgCO3, siderite FeCO3, rhodochrosite MnCO3, smithsonite ZnCO3 and the rarer sphaerocobaltite CoCO3. All share rhombohedral cleavage and hardness near 3.5 to 4.5, and all show extensive solid solution with one another and partially with calcite. Siderite is a common iron ore mineral, buff to brown, with specific gravity 3.9, and it weathers readily to iron oxides, so surface exposures are typically rust-stained. Rhodochrosite is unmistakable when good — a translucent rose pink, often banded in stalactitic masses, and a minor manganese ore. Smithsonite, named for James Smithson whose bequest founded the Smithsonian Institution, forms botryoidal crusts in the oxidised zone over zinc deposits and was the historic ore of zinc before sphalerite mining.

Cations too large for six-fold coordination take the aragonite structure, with nine-fold coordination: strontianite SrCO3, witherite BaCO3 and cerussite PbCO3. Cerussite is the important one, a lead carbonate with a striking specific gravity of 6.55, adamantine lustre and frequent lattice-like twinning, forming abundantly where galena weathers.

The copper carbonates deserve separate mention because they are hydroxyl-bearing and unusually conspicuous. Malachite, Cu2(CO3)(OH)2, is the intense green mineral of botryoidal crusts and banded ornamental stone; azurite, Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2, is a deep azure blue. Both form in the oxidised upper zones of copper deposits, and azurite is metastable relative to malachite in humid air, which is why medieval and Renaissance paintings using azurite blue have in places turned green over centuries. Their vivid colours come from crystal field transitions in the copper two ion.

Several carbonates matter economically or environmentally out of proportion to their abundance. Nahcolite, sodium bicarbonate, and trona, a hydrated sodium carbonate-bicarbonate, are evaporite minerals mined at Green River in Wyoming for soda ash. Bastnäsite, a fluorocarbonate of the light rare earth elements, is the principal ore of cerium, lanthanum and neodymium, and the Bayan Obo deposit in Inner Mongolia and Mountain Pass in California between them have supplied most of the world's rare earth supply.

Carbonatites — igneous rocks composed of more than fifty percent carbonate minerals — are the strangest occurrence of all. Fewer than six hundred are known, they are strongly associated with continental rift zones, and Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania erupts natrocarbonatite lava at only about 500 to 590 degrees Celsius, so fluid it flows like water and so unstable that the black lava turns white within hours of exposure to atmospheric moisture.

Finally, the industrial weight of the class is easy to underestimate. Limestone burned at about 900 degrees Celsius decomposes to quicklime and carbon dioxide, and that calcination reaction is the basis of mortar, plaster and Portland cement. Cement manufacture accounts for roughly 7 to 8 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and about 60 percent of that comes not from the fuel but from the decomposition of the carbonate itself — a chemical consequence of the mineralogy, not an inefficiency better furnaces could remove.

sections.heading: Carbonates in the Earth System: Limestone, Karst and the Carbon Cycle
sections.body:
Carbonate minerals are the largest reservoir of carbon on the planet by an enormous margin. Sedimentary carbonate rocks hold something on the order of 60 to 100 million gigatonnes of carbon, against roughly 900 gigatonnes in the atmosphere and about 38,000 in the ocean. Essentially all of that limestone was once atmospheric carbon dioxide, and the slow transfer of carbon into carbonate rock is the mechanism that has kept Earth's climate within habitable bounds over geological time.

The controlling reaction pair is deceptively simple. Silicate weathering consumes carbon dioxide: rainwater carrying dissolved CO2 attacks calcium silicate minerals, releasing calcium and bicarbonate ions that rivers carry to the sea. Marine organisms and inorganic precipitation then convert those ions to calcium carbonate, burying the carbon. Subduction and metamorphism eventually return some of it as volcanic CO2. This is the Urey cycle, and because the weathering rate rises with temperature and rainfall, it acts as a negative feedback on climate — a thermostat operating on timescales of hundreds of thousands to millions of years, far too slow to counteract present-day emissions but decisive over the history of the planet.

Most limestone is biological in origin. Foraminifera, coccolithophores, corals, molluscs, brachiopods and calcareous algae all build carbonate skeletons, and the accumulation of their remains forms the great chalk and limestone sequences. The White Cliffs of Dover are almost entirely coccolith debris deposited in the Late Cretaceous. Below the carbonate compensation depth in the ocean — currently around 4,200 to 4,500 metres in the Pacific and somewhat deeper in the Atlantic — the pressure and cold make seawater undersaturated and falling carbonate dissolves before it can accumulate, which is why deep ocean floors are red clay and siliceous ooze rather than limestone.

At the surface, the solubility of calcite in carbonic acid produces karst. Rainwater equilibrated with soil CO2 dissolves limestone along joints and bedding planes, enlarging them into conduits and caves. Roughly 15 percent of the ice-free land surface is karst, and about a quarter of the world's population depends on karst aquifers for water — aquifers that are unusually vulnerable to contamination because water travels through open conduits rather than filtering slowly through pores. When groundwater degasses CO2 on entering a cave, the reaction reverses and calcite precipitates as stalactites, stalagmites and flowstone, typically at rates of 0.01 to 1 millimetre a year.

The same chemistry is now running backwards in the ocean. Since 1750 the surface ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of anthropogenic carbon dioxide, and its pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 — a 30 percent increase in hydrogen ion concentration. Lower pH reduces carbonate ion availability and shoals the aragonite saturation horizon, and because aragonite is the more soluble polymorph, pteropods, many corals and larval molluscs are affected first. This is ocean acidification, and it is a direct, well-constrained consequence of carbonate mineral equilibria.

sections.heading: Oxides: Close-Packed Oxygen and the Metals in Its Gaps
sections.body:
Oxide minerals are compounds of oxygen with one or more metals, excluding by convention the silicates, in which the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron gets its own class. Quartz, SiO2, is chemically an oxide but is classified as a framework silicate for structural reasons — an inconsistency universally acknowledged and universally retained. The oxide class as usually counted holds roughly 500 species, of which perhaps twenty matter.

The structural principle is straightforward. Oxygen ions, at 1.40 ångströms, are large; metal cations are small. The oxygens therefore adopt one of the two efficient close packings — cubic close packing, equivalent to a face-centred cubic array, or hexagonal close packing — and the metals occupy the interstitial holes. In any close-packed array there are two hole types: tetrahedral sites, twice as numerous as the anions and suitable for small cations, and octahedral sites, equal in number to the anions and suitable for medium ones. Which holes are filled, and in what pattern, generates the whole family of oxide structures.

Three archetypes recur constantly. The corundum structure has hexagonal close-packed oxygen with two-thirds of the octahedral sites filled by trivalent cations, and is adopted by corundum Al2O3, hematite Fe2O3 and, in an ordered variant with alternating cations, ilmenite FeTiO3. The spinel structure has cubic close-packed oxygen with one-eighth of the tetrahedral and one-half of the octahedral sites filled, giving the general formula AB2O4; spinel MgAl2O4, magnetite Fe3O4 and chromite FeCr2O4 all belong here. The rutile structure is a tetragonal arrangement of edge-sharing octahedra adopted by rutile TiO2, cassiterite SnO2 and pyrolusite MnO2 — and it is worth noting that these three, despite very different chemistry, look confusingly similar in hand specimen for precisely this reason.

Because oxygen-metal bonds are strong and substantially ionic, oxide minerals are typically hard, refractory and chemically resistant. Corundum is hardness 9, the definition point on the Mohs scale, and second only to diamond among natural materials in ordinary abrasion resistance. Hematite is 5 to 6, magnetite 5.5 to 6.5, cassiterite 6 to 7. That durability has an important geological consequence: oxides survive chemical weathering and mechanical transport that destroys most other minerals, so they accumulate in residual soils and in placer deposits. Most of the world's titanium, zirconium, tin and much of its gold has been mined from such concentrations rather than from primary rock.

Hydroxides and oxyhydroxides are usually treated with the oxides, and they are the weathering products. Goethite, alpha-FeO(OH), is the ubiquitous yellow-brown of rusty rock and soil; gibbsite Al(OH)3, boehmite and diaspore together make bauxite, the only economic aluminium ore. Limonite is not a mineral species but a useful field term for fine-grained mixed iron oxyhydroxides.

Oxides also serve as geological thermometers and barometers. Because the iron-titanium oxides magnetite and ilmenite exchange elements with one another in a temperature- and oxygen-dependent way, the composition of a coexisting pair records both the temperature of crystallisation and the oxygen fugacity of the magma. This oxide geothermometry, developed by Buddington and Lindsley in 1964, remains a standard method for reconstructing the conditions inside a volcano before an eruption.

sections.heading: The Iron Oxides: Ore, Colour and the Magnetic Record
sections.body:
Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the crust and the most abundant by mass in the Earth as a whole, and its oxides are simultaneously the world's most important ore, the pigment of most coloured rock and soil, and the recording medium for the planet's magnetic history.

Hematite, Fe2O3, takes the corundum structure with iron in the trivalent state. Its hardness is 5 to 6 and specific gravity 5.26. Its most reliable diagnostic is its streak — the colour of its powder rubbed on unglazed porcelain — which is always a distinctive brick to cherry red regardless of whether the specimen is a dull earthy ochre, a silvery micaceous plate or a black botryoidal kidney ore. That red powder is the pigment of red beds, terra rossa soils, Palaeolithic cave art and the surface of Mars.

Magnetite, Fe3O4, is an inverse spinel: the formula is better written Fe3+(Fe2+Fe3+)O4, with half the ferric iron in tetrahedral sites and the other half sharing octahedral sites with the ferrous iron. That arrangement produces ferrimagnetism — the tetrahedral and octahedral sublattices are antiferromagnetically coupled but unequal, leaving a net moment. Magnetite is strongly attracted to a magnet and pieces are sometimes naturally magnetised as lodestone. Its Curie temperature is 580 degrees Celsius, above which the ordering is lost. Hardness is 5.5 to 6.5, specific gravity 5.2, streak black, and crystals are typically octahedra.

That Curie temperature is what makes magnetite the workhorse of palaeomagnetism. As a lava cools through 580 degrees, magnetite grains lock in the direction of the ambient field. Reading those directions from successively erupted basalts revealed both the wandering of continents and the repeated reversals of the geomagnetic field, and the symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of mid-ocean ridges, mapped through the 1950s and interpreted by Vine, Matthews and Morley in 1963, provided the decisive evidence for seafloor spreading.

The great iron ores are the banded iron formations, laid down chiefly between about 2.6 and 1.8 billion years ago as alternating iron oxide and chert layers, and holding the majority of world iron reserves in Western Australia, Brazil, South Africa and the Lake Superior region. Their formation is tied to the Great Oxidation Event: dissolved ferrous iron in anoxic Archaean oceans was oxidised to insoluble ferric oxide as photosynthetic oxygen accumulated, and precipitated out. Whether the banding reflects seasonal cycles, episodic upwelling or microbial blooms is still argued.

Other iron oxides matter in specific settings. Maghemite, a cation-deficient ferrimagnetic form of Fe2O3, forms by low-temperature oxidation of magnetite and complicates palaeomagnetic interpretation. Wüstite, FeO, is unstable at surface conditions but important in the lower mantle. Ilmenite, FeTiO3, is the world's principal titanium ore and a common accessory in mafic igneous rocks.

sections.heading: Spinels, Corundum and the Colour of Gemstones
sections.body:
The spinel group takes its name from magnesium aluminate, MgAl2O4, and its cubic structure accommodates an unusually wide range of substitutions, which is why the group spans ordinary rock-forming accessories and several critical ore minerals. The general formula AB2O4 has divalent A cations — magnesium, iron, zinc, manganese — and trivalent B cations — aluminium, iron, chromium. In a normal spinel the A cations occupy tetrahedral sites and B the octahedral; in an inverse spinel half the B cations swap into the tetrahedral sites, which is what magnetite does and what gives it its magnetism.

Chromite, FeCr2O4, is the only ore of chromium and occurs in two settings: stratiform layers in large layered mafic intrusions, of which the Bushveld Complex in South Africa is overwhelmingly the largest and holds the majority of world reserves, and podiform bodies in the mantle sections of ophiolites. Gahnite is the zinc member, franklinite the manganese-zinc one from the extraordinary Franklin deposit in New Jersey. Spinel proper, when transparent and red from chromium substitution, is a gemstone that was for centuries mistaken for ruby; several famous crown jewels, including the Black Prince's Ruby in the British Imperial State Crown, are in fact spinels, a confusion only resolved in the nineteenth century.

Corundum, Al2O3, deserves attention because it demonstrates how trace chemistry generates colour. Pure corundum is colourless, since aluminium three and oxygen have no partly filled d orbitals and therefore no electronic transitions in the visible range. Substituting roughly 0.1 to 1 percent of chromium three for aluminium introduces a partly filled d shell whose crystal field splitting absorbs yellow-green and violet light, transmitting the deep red of ruby. Substituting iron and titanium together produces a different mechanism: an electron transfers between an adjacent ferrous iron and a titanium four ion, a process called intervalence charge transfer, which absorbs strongly in the yellow to red and leaves the blue of sapphire. Iron alone gives yellow and green sapphires; the pink-orange padparadscha involves chromium plus a colour centre.

The same principles explain colour across the oxides. Hematite's red comes from ligand-to-metal charge transfer between oxygen and ferric iron. Rutile's remarkable refractive indices, from 2.61 to 2.90, are among the highest of any transparent mineral and arise from the high polarisability of the titanium-oxygen bonds; needles of rutile included in quartz produce the golden shimmer of rutilated quartz and, when oriented along three directions, the star of asterism.

Several other simple oxides carry economic weight. Cassiterite, SnO2, with a specific gravity of 6.9 to 7.1 and an adamantine to submetallic lustre, is essentially the world's only tin ore and concentrates readily in placers. Uraninite, UO2, is the principal uranium mineral. Pyrolusite and romanechite supply manganese. Ice, H2O, is formally an oxide mineral and by mass one of the most abundant minerals at the Earth's surface, a fact more often noted as a curiosity than pursued.

sections.heading: Sulfides: Metallic Bonding, Opacity and Density
sections.body:
The sulfide class contains roughly 600 species and behaves so distinctively that a specimen can usually be assigned to it across a room. Sulfides are opaque, metallic or submetallic in lustre, dense, and mostly soft. The reason lies in bonding. Sulfur's electronegativity of 2.58 is far closer to that of the metals it combines with than oxygen's 3.44, so metal-sulfur bonds are largely covalent, and in many sulfides the metal d orbitals overlap sufficiently to produce delocalised, metal-like electronic bands.

Those bands are what make sulfides opaque and lustrous: incident light is absorbed and re-emitted by free or nearly free electrons rather than transmitted. Many sulfides are semiconductors or, like pyrite and molybdenite, useful ones — the crystal radio sets of the early twentieth century used a galena crystal and a fine wire "cat's whisker" as the first practical point-contact diode. Because covalent bonds are directional and generally weaker than the strong ionic bonds of oxides, sulfides tend to be soft: galena is 2.5, sphalerite 3.5 to 4, chalcopyrite 3.5 to 4, molybdenite only 1 to 1.5. The exceptions, pyrite at 6 to 6.5 and arsenopyrite at 5.5 to 6, owe their hardness to strong sulfur-sulfur covalent pairs within the structure.

Density is high because the metals involved are heavy and the packing efficient. Galena, PbS, has a specific gravity of 7.6, cinnabar 8.1, and even the comparatively light sphalerite reaches 4.0. In practice a small piece of sulfide feels startlingly heavy for its size, and hefting is a genuine field test.

Three structure types dominate. The halite type has the metal and sulfur alternating on a face-centred cubic lattice, giving galena its perfect cubic cleavage in three directions at right angles and its habit of breaking into little grey cubes. The sphalerite or zincblende type is the diamond structure with zinc and sulfur alternating, tetrahedrally coordinated, producing six directions of perfect dodecahedral cleavage — a distinctive property once recognised. The pyrite type is a halite derivative in which each chlorine is replaced by a covalently bonded sulfur pair, an S2 dumbbell, with the dumbbells oriented along different body diagonals; this lowers the symmetry from the full cubic group and produces pyrite's characteristic striated cube faces and the twelve-faced pyritohedron.

Sulfosalts form a related subclass in which a semimetal — antimony, arsenic or bismuth — occupies a structural role akin to a cation rather than substituting for sulfur. Tetrahedrite and tennantite, forming a solid solution series, are the commonest, are often significant silver carriers, and are a nuisance in smelting because their arsenic and antimony are penalty elements.

One further property explains much of the class's geological behaviour: sulfides are almost insoluble in water at ordinary conditions but readily soluble in hot chloride brines, where metals travel as chloride and bisulfide complexes. A fluid at 300 degrees Celsius can carry hundreds of parts per million of copper or lead and drop nearly all of it within a few metres when it cools, boils or mixes. That sensitivity is why sulfide ore bodies are so sharply bounded, and why barren and rich rock can lie centimetres apart.

sections.heading: The Sulfides You Will Actually Meet
sections.body:
Pyrite, FeS2, is the most abundant sulfide by a wide margin. It is pale brass yellow with a distinctly metallic lustre, hardness 6 to 6.5, specific gravity 5.0, and gives a greenish-black to brownish-black streak that immediately separates it from gold, which is far softer, malleable, deeper yellow and leaves a yellow streak. Cubes with striations running perpendicular on adjacent faces are diagnostic, as are pyritohedra and octahedra. It forms in almost every environment: magmatic, hydrothermal, metamorphic and sedimentary, where it precipitates in anoxic muds through bacterial sulfate reduction and preserves fossils in golden replicas. Marcasite is the orthorhombic polymorph, paler and more brittle, formed at low pH and low temperature, and it decomposes on museum shelves — the phenomenon misleadingly called pyrite disease, which is more often marcasite.

Chalcopyrite, CuFeS2, is the world's principal copper ore mineral. It is a deeper, more golden brass than pyrite, softer at 3.5 to 4 so a steel needle scratches it, and characteristically develops an iridescent purple-blue tarnish. Bornite, Cu5FeS4, tarnishes even more spectacularly and is known as peacock ore. Chalcocite, Cu2S, is dark grey, soft and the highest-grade copper sulfide, and it forms the enriched blanket beneath weathered porphyry deposits.

Galena, PbS, is unmistakable: lead grey, bright metallic when fresh, cleaving into perfect cubes, hardness 2.5, and extraordinarily heavy. It commonly carries silver in solid solution or as inclusions, and for most of history it was the principal source of both lead and silver.

Sphalerite, ZnS, is the sole important zinc ore and the most variable in appearance. Pure it is colourless and transparent; increasing iron substitution darkens it through honey yellow and red-brown to black. Lustre is resinous to adamantine, streak pale yellow to brown, and the six directions of cleavage combined with a hardness of 3.5 to 4 identify it.

Pyrrhotite, Fe(1-x)S, is bronze, tarnishing brown, and weakly to moderately magnetic because of ordered iron vacancies — a useful and easily tested property. Molybdenite, MoS2, is layered like graphite, greasy to the touch, hardness 1 to 1.5, and leaves a bluish-grey mark on paper. Cinnabar, HgS, is a striking vermilion red with a scarlet streak and specific gravity 8.1. Stibnite, Sb2S3, forms spectacular steel-grey bladed crystals. Arsenopyrite, FeAsS, is silvery-white and gives a garlic odour when struck. Realgar and orpiment, the red and yellow arsenic sulfides, are visually gorgeous and chemically dangerous; realgar breaks down to yellow powdery pararealgar on prolonged exposure to light, so museum specimens are kept in the dark.

Covellite, CuS, is an indigo blue with an iridescent sheen and unmistakable once seen. Native gold causes endless confusion with pyrite: gold is malleable, has a specific gravity of 19.3 and deforms under a knife point, whereas pyrite is brittle and shatters.
