Among the yellow metallic minerals hardness separates them cleanly — gold below 3, chalcopyrite 3.5 to 4, pyrite 6 to 6.5. Among the grey ones cleavage does the work: galena cleaves into cubes, molybdenite into flexible sheets, stibnite into bladed splinters, arsenopyrite not at all.

sections.heading: How These Minerals Become Ore Deposits
sections.body:
An ore deposit is a place where a geological process has concentrated a metal far above its crustal average — copper from about 60 parts per million to 4,000 or more, gold from 4 parts per billion to several parts per million. Nearly all such processes involve either a hot aqueous fluid or a segregating magma, and the great majority precipitate sulfides or oxides.

Magmatic sulfide deposits form when a mafic magma becomes saturated in sulfur and an immiscible sulfide liquid separates, like oil from water. Nickel, copper and the platinum-group elements partition strongly into that liquid — partition coefficients in the hundreds to tens of thousands — so a small volume scavenges the metal from a large one, then settles to the base of the chamber. Sudbury in Ontario, whose formation was triggered by a meteorite impact 1.85 billion years ago, and Noril'sk in Siberia, associated with the Siberian Traps, are the classic examples. Layered intrusions such as the Bushveld produce chromite and platinum-bearing seams by a related process of crystal settling.

Porphyry deposits form above a cooling intrusion at two to five kilometres depth, where magmatic fluids exsolve, fracture the surrounding rock into a dense stockwork of veinlets, and deposit chalcopyrite, bornite and molybdenite over volumes of cubic kilometres. Grades are low, typically 0.3 to 1 percent copper, but tonnages are enormous, and porphyries supply roughly three-quarters of world copper and most of its molybdenum. The Andes of Chile and Peru host the largest.

Volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits form on the seafloor where hydrothermal circulation through hot oceanic crust leaches metals and discharges them into cold seawater. The abrupt drop from around 350 degrees to 2 degrees precipitates sulfides instantly, building the chimneys of black smokers. Ancient equivalents include the Iberian Pyrite Belt and Kidd Creek in Ontario. SEDEX deposits form similarly but in sediment-filled rift basins from lower-temperature brines, producing the great stratiform lead-zinc bodies of Broken Hill and Red Dog.

Mississippi Valley Type deposits are the low-temperature end member: basinal brines at 75 to 200 degrees migrate through carbonate platforms and precipitate galena and sphalerite in karst voids and dolomitised breccias. They are metal-rich, sulfur-poor and structurally simple, and they illustrate the class interaction directly, since the host rock is carbonate.

Oxide ores form by different routes. Banded iron formations are chemical sediments. Bauxite is a residual soil produced by intense tropical weathering that leaches everything but aluminium and iron. Placer deposits concentrate dense, durable oxides — cassiterite, rutile, ilmenite, zircon — by fluvial and beach sorting; the tin fields of Malaysia and Indonesia and the mineral sands of eastern Australia are of this type. Laterites weathered from ultramafic rock supply a growing share of world nickel as oxides and hydrous silicates rather than sulfides.

sections.heading: Weathering, Gossans and Acid Mine Drainage
sections.body:
Sulfide minerals are stable only where oxygen is absent. Bring them to the surface and they oxidise, and the chemistry that follows is the origin of both the classic prospector's clue and one of the most stubborn environmental problems in mining.

The controlling reaction for pyrite proceeds in stages. Oxygen and water attack the sulfide to give ferrous iron, sulfate and acid: one mole of pyrite yields two moles of sulfuric acid equivalent. Dissolved ferrous iron then oxidises to ferric, which above pH 3 hydrolyses and precipitates as ferric hydroxide, releasing further acid. Crucially, ferric iron in solution is itself a powerful oxidant of pyrite, and that pathway is far faster than direct oxidation by dissolved oxygen. The rate-limiting step is therefore the oxidation of ferrous to ferric, which is slow abiotically at low pH but is accelerated by up to a million times by the bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans. The system is thus autocatalytic and microbially driven, and once running it sustains itself.

The environmental consequence is acid mine drainage: waters at pH 2 to 4 loaded with iron, aluminium, and whatever heavy metals the ore contained, staining streambeds with orange ferric hydroxide precipitate known as yellow boy. It affects thousands of kilometres of watercourse worldwide, persists for centuries after mining ceases, and is expensive to treat — usually by adding limestone or lime to neutralise the acid and precipitate the metals, which is another direct interaction between the three classes. Where the host rock is naturally carbonate-rich, the acid is buffered and the problem is far smaller; where it is quartz or shale, it is severe.

The prospecting side of the same chemistry is the gossan. Above a weathering sulfide body the sulfides dissolve away and iron precipitates in place, leaving a porous, rusty, boxwork-textured cap of goethite, hematite and jarosite. The boxwork — a honeycomb of iron oxide fins outlining the vanished sulfide crystals — often preserves the shape of the original mineral closely enough to identify it, and reading gossan textures was a standard prospecting skill long before geochemistry. Gossans have led to many major discoveries, including Broken Hill in 1883.

Beneath the gossan, the metals leached from above descend and re-precipitate where they meet reducing conditions at the water table, a process called supergene enrichment. Copper is the classic case: chalcopyrite at roughly 34 percent copper is replaced by chalcocite at 80 percent, producing a blanket of much higher grade that has been the economic making of many porphyry mines. Above that blanket sits the oxidised zone with its malachite, azurite, cuprite and native copper, and it is these brightly coloured secondary minerals — green and blue stains on outcrop — that first draw attention.

sections.heading: Identifying Them in the Field
sections.body:
Hand-specimen identification rests on a small set of physical properties, applied in a deliberate order. The properties are not independent of structure and chemistry; each one is a direct readout of something about the atomic arrangement. Hardness reflects bond strength, cleavage reflects planes of weak bonding, density reflects atomic mass and packing efficiency, streak reflects intrinsic rather than surface colour, and lustre reflects the electronic structure at the surface.

Colour alone is the least reliable property and the one beginners over-weight. Sphalerite ranges from colourless to black; fluorite spans the spectrum; quartz likewise. Streak, by contrast, is dependably constant for a given species because grinding removes tarnish and surface films and reduces the effect of grain size.

The kit required is modest and has barely changed in two centuries: a hand lens of ten or twenty times magnification, a streak plate of unglazed white porcelain, a small steel knife or nail, a copper coin, a magnet, a dropper bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid, and a geological hammer with safety glasses. Everything below can be done with those.
steps: Assess lustre first, because it splits the field immediately. A metallic lustre with an opaque body points to the sulfide class or to a few oxides such as magnetite and hematite. A non-metallic, glassy or earthy lustre points to carbonates, most oxides and everything else.

Take the streak on unglazed porcelain. Hematite gives brick red however it looks, magnetite black, pyrite greenish-black, galena grey-black, sphalerite pale yellow to brown, cinnabar scarlet. Most carbonates give white regardless of body colour.

Test hardness against known references: a fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin 3.5, a steel knife or nail 5.5, and window glass about 5.5. Carbonates scratch with a coin; pyrite scratches glass; galena and molybdenite yield to a fingernail.
Heft the specimen. Anything that feels notably heavier than an equal-sized piece of quartz is likely a sulfide or a dense oxide. Galena, cinnabar and cassiterite are unmistakable by weight alone.

Apply a drop of cold dilute hydrochloric acid, about 10 percent. Vigorous immediate fizzing indicates calcite or aragonite. Weak or absent fizzing on a solid surface that becomes a slow reaction when the surface is scratched to powder indicates dolomite. Very sluggish reaction suggests siderite or magnesite.
Bring a magnet close. Strong attraction indicates magnetite or, occasionally, pyrrhotite, which is weaker and more variable. This single test settles most black opaque specimens.

Examine cleavage in good light by rotating the specimen and counting the directions of reflecting flat surfaces. Three directions at right angles suggests galena; three not at right angles suggests a carbonate; six directions suggests sphalerite; none, with a conchoidal fracture, suggests pyrite or quartz.

Check habit and any twinning. Striated cubes indicate pyrite; curved saddle-shaped rhombs indicate dolomite; octahedra suggest magnetite or spinel; radiating fibrous masses suggest aragonite or malachite.

sections.heading: Limits, Hazards and Honest Uncertainty
sections.body:
Field identification has real boundaries, and knowing them prevents confident error. Fine-grained material defeats almost every test: an earthy red mass may be hematite, or a mixture of goethite and clay stained by it, and no hand lens will resolve the difference. Solid solution means many specimens are not one species but a composition somewhere along a series — a carbonate rhomb may be anywhere between calcite and magnesite, and only chemical analysis will place it. Weathering rinds mask everything, which is why a fresh broken surface is essential. Where identity actually matters, the tools are X-ray diffraction, which reads the structure directly, electron microprobe analysis for composition, and reflected-light microscopy for opaque sulfides.

Some genuinely contested questions remain in these classes. The dolomite problem is unresolved in the sense that no single mechanism explains all ancient dolomite. The precise cause of banded iron formation layering is debated. The relative roles of magmatic and meteoric fluids in several deposit types are argued vigorously in the literature. Presenting any of these as settled would misrepresent the state of knowledge.

The hazards are more concrete and deserve care. Sulfide minerals frequently contain toxic elements in high concentration. Cinnabar is mercury sulfide, roughly 86 percent mercury by mass; it is poorly absorbed when swallowed as an intact crystal but genuinely dangerous if ground, heated or handled repeatedly, and heating it liberates mercury vapour. Realgar and orpiment are arsenic sulfides, and arsenopyrite releases arsenic on weathering and gives off arsenic-bearing fumes if struck hard or heated. Galena is lead sulfide, and its dust is a straightforward lead exposure, particularly hazardous to children. Any of these should be handled with dry hands, kept out of the mouth and away from food, and never cut, ground or heated outside a fume hood.

Dust is the general hazard. Cutting, grinding or hammering any of these minerals generates respirable particles, and the crystalline silica in the surrounding rock is a well-established cause of silicosis. Eye protection when hammering is not optional; rock fragments travel fast and hardness 6 minerals are effectively small chisels.

Two further cautions apply. Acid used for carbonate testing should be dilute, carried in a purpose-made dropper bottle, and kept away from eyes and clothing; a 10 percent solution is entirely adequate and a stronger one gains nothing. And storage matters: marcasite and pyrrhotite specimens can decompose in humid air, generating sulfuric acid that damages labels, containers and neighbouring specimens, so they are best kept dry and inspected periodically.

A legal and physical caution catches collectors out. Most protected areas prohibit collecting, and entering a working or abandoned mine is usually trespass and often lethal — old workings accumulate oxygen-deficient and hydrogen-sulfide-bearing air, and timbering fails without warning.

The broader lesson is that a mineral's properties follow from its structure with unusual directness. A flat rigid anion gives soft, acid-soluble, strongly birefringent minerals; a close-packed oxygen framework gives hard, dense, durable ones; covalent metal-sulfur bonding gives heavy, opaque, chemically fragile ones. Once that link is internalised, identification becomes reasoning rather than memorisation.

guides.safetyNote: Many sulfide minerals carry toxic elements in concentrated form: cinnabar is mercury sulfide, realgar and orpiment are arsenic sulfides, arsenopyrite releases arsenic on weathering, and galena is lead sulfide. Handle specimens with dry hands, keep them away from food and out of reach of children, wash afterwards, and never grind, cut or heat them without proper ventilation and protection. Wear eye protection when hammering rock, and avoid breathing the dust, which carries a silicosis risk. Use only dilute (about 10 percent) hydrochloric acid for carbonate testing, in a sealed dropper bottle, away from eyes and skin.

guides.title: The Feldspar Group
guides.summary: A full account of the feldspars — the aluminosilicate minerals that make up around sixty per cent of Earth's crust — covering their structure and chemistry, the plagioclase and alkali series, ordering, exsolution and twinning, how to identify them, their role in rock classification and weathering, and their occurrence from lunar highlands to ceramics.

sections.heading: The Most Abundant Minerals on Earth
sections.body:
Feldspar is not a single mineral but a family of closely related ones, and together they make up
roughly sixty per cent by volume of the Earth's crust — more than every other mineral group combined.
Pick up almost any rock from a continent and you are holding feldspar. The pale blocky grains in
granite are feldspar. The grey lath-shaped crystals threading through basalt are feldspar. The white
sand of a river bar is quartz and feldspar. The bright white highlands of the Moon, visible to the
naked eye as the lighter regions of the lunar face, are a rock composed almost entirely of one
feldspar species. If you wanted to understand the solid Earth by learning about a single group of
minerals, feldspar would be the correct choice.

The name comes from the German Feldspat, from Feld meaning field and Spat, an old miners' term for a
pale, cleavable, non-metallic mineral — the mineral that turns up in ploughed fields. It entered
English in the eighteenth century, and the alternative spelling felspar, once common in Britain,
arose from a mistaken assumption that the first element was Fels, meaning rock. The correct spelling
is feldspar.

Chemically, feldspars are aluminosilicates of potassium, sodium and calcium, with the general formula
written as X Al(1 to 2) Si(3 to 2) O8, where X is potassium, sodium, calcium, or occasionally barium.
The three dominant end members are potassium feldspar or orthoclase, KAlSi3O8; albite, NaAlSi3O8; and
anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8. Almost every naturally occurring feldspar is a mixture of two of those three,
and the way those mixtures behave as magma cools is one of the most information-rich records available
to a geologist.

That is the reason feldspar repays study out of proportion to its familiarity. A feldspar crystal
carries, encoded in its composition, its internal atomic ordering, its exsolution textures and its
zoning, a detailed account of the temperature, pressure, water content and cooling rate of the magma
that made it. Reading a feldspar is close to reading a thermometer, a barometer and a clock at once.
Beyond geology, feldspar sits at the centre of the global carbon cycle through chemical weathering, it
is the raw material of virtually all ceramics and much glass, it produces several well-known
gemstones including moonstone and labradorite, and it provides the mineral used to date archaeological
sediments by luminescence.

A note on scope is useful before going further. Mineralogists divide the group into two series that
overlap only partly: the alkali feldspars, running from potassium-rich to sodium-rich compositions,
and the plagioclase feldspars, running from sodium-rich to calcium-rich. Names within each series
refer sometimes to composition and sometimes to internal atomic arrangement, which is a genuine source
of confusion for newcomers and is worth holding lightly at first. Orthoclase, microcline and sanidine
may share one formula. Albite belongs to both series at once, sitting at the corner where they meet.
The apparent untidiness is not arbitrary; it reflects the fact that a feldspar is defined by two
independent variables, what it is made of and how its atoms are arranged, and both carry geological
meaning.

sections.heading: Crystal Structure: A Framework of Linked Tetrahedra
sections.body:
All feldspars are tectosilicates, or framework silicates, which is the most polymerised of the silicate
structural classes. The building block is the silica tetrahedron: one small silicon atom at the centre
surrounded by four oxygen atoms at the corners of a triangular pyramid. In a framework silicate every
one of those four oxygens is shared with a neighbouring tetrahedron, so the tetrahedra link into a
continuous three-dimensional scaffold extending through the whole crystal. Quartz is the simplest such framework, pure SiO2.

Feldspar arises when some of the silicon in that framework is replaced by aluminium. Aluminium sits in
the same tetrahedral site and is a similar size, so the substitution is geometrically easy — but
silicon carries a charge of plus four and aluminium only plus three, so each substitution leaves the
framework one positive charge short. That deficit is balanced by admitting a large cation into the
irregular cavities that run through the structure. Substituting one aluminium for one silicon in four
requires one singly charged ion, giving KAlSi3O8 or NaAlSi3O8. Substituting two in four requires a
doubly charged ion, giving CaAl2Si2O8. This is the coupled substitution that defines the entire group,
usually written as the exchange of one sodium plus one silicon for one calcium plus one aluminium.

The framework itself has a characteristic architecture: rings of four tetrahedra linked into
double-crankshaft chains running parallel to one crystallographic axis and cross-linked into a
three-dimensional net. The cavities between those chains are the sites the large cations occupy, and
cation size matters enormously. Potassium has an ionic radius around 1.51 ångströms in eight-fold
coordination; sodium is much smaller at about 1.18; calcium is 1.12. Potassium is therefore a poor fit
alongside sodium and calcium, and that mismatch is the physical reason the feldspars divide into two
series that mix freely within themselves and only reluctantly across.

Two consequences follow directly. The chains are bound together more weakly in two directions than
along their length, so the crystal parts along two planes, indexed (001) and (010), meeting at or very
near a right angle; every feldspar therefore breaks into blocky fragments with flat rectangular faces,
the group's most reliable field signature. And because the framework is open, feldspars are among the
least dense common rock-forming silicates, from about 2.55 grams per cubic centimetre for potassium
feldspar to 2.76 for anorthite, against 3.2 to 4.4 for olivine. That buoyancy contrast is why
plagioclase floats in a basaltic melt, and it is the mechanism behind the entire crust of the Moon.

Symmetry follows from how the aluminium is distributed among the tetrahedral sites. If aluminium is
scattered randomly, the structure is statistically monoclinic — one twofold axis, one mirror plane.
If aluminium concentrates preferentially into particular sites, the symmetry drops to triclinic, with
no symmetry beyond a centre of inversion, and the crystal axes become slightly oblique. Because the
degree of ordering depends on temperature and on how slowly the crystal cooled, feldspar symmetry is
not a fixed property of a chemical composition but a record of thermal history, which is a genuinely
unusual and very useful thing for a mineral to be.

sections.heading: The Ternary System: Reading the Feldspar Triangle
sections.body:
Because nearly all feldspars are mixtures of three end members, mineralogists plot them on a triangular
composition diagram with orthoclase (Or, the potassium end member) at the top apex, albite (Ab, sodium)
at the lower left and anorthite (An, calcium) at the lower right. Any feldspar can be described by
three numbers summing to one hundred, for example Or5 Ab70 An25, and that single notation captures
almost everything a petrologist first needs to know.

The striking feature of the diagram is that natural feldspars do not fill it. They cluster along two
edges. The bottom edge, from albite to anorthite, is the plagioclase series, and compositions along it
form a complete solid solution at high temperature: sodium and calcium substitute for one another in
any proportion. The left edge, from albite to orthoclase, is the alkali feldspar series, in which
sodium and potassium substitute for one another. The interior of the triangle and the right-hand edge
from orthoclase to anorthite are almost empty in nature, because potassium and calcium differ too much
in both size and charge to coexist in the same site in significant amounts.

The reason for the two-series structure is the coupled substitution. Along the plagioclase edge, the
exchange of sodium plus silicon for calcium plus aluminium changes the framework composition as well as
the cavity occupant, and both ions are similar in size, so the series is continuous. Along the alkali
edge, sodium and potassium swap directly with no change to the aluminium-to-silicon ratio, but they
differ by nearly thirty per cent in radius, so at low temperature they cannot stay mixed and the series
unmixes.

That unmixing is captured by a curve on the diagram called the solvus, a dome-shaped boundary below
which a single homogeneous alkali feldspar is unstable and separates into a sodium-rich phase and a
potassium-rich phase. Above the crest of the solvus, at roughly 650 to 700 degrees Celsius for dry
compositions, any mixture is stable. Below it, the gap widens as temperature falls, so that at surface
temperature almost no intermediate alkali feldspar composition can exist as a single homogeneous
crystal.

The solvus position is not fixed. Dissolved water lowers it substantially, so a wet granitic magma may
crystallise a single alkali feldspar that would have unmixed immediately in a dry system. Pressure
raises it modestly. This means the presence of one homogeneous alkali feldspar versus two separate
feldspars in a rock is itself diagnostic information: granites that crystallised a single alkali
feldspar which later exsolved are called hypersolvus, and those that crystallised two separate
feldspars from the start are subsolvus, a distinction that maps directly onto how much water the magma
carried.

The plagioclase series has its own, subtler complications: a series of low-temperature miscibility gaps
known as the peristerite, Bøggild and Huttenlocher intergrowths, each occurring over a narrow
compositional range and producing extremely fine-scale lamellae. These are invisible to the eye but
they diffract light, and they are precisely what makes labradorite flash blue and gold. A cosmetic
property of a gemstone turns out to be a direct optical readout of thermodynamics.

sections.heading: The Plagioclase Series: From Albite to Anorthite
sections.body:
The plagioclase feldspars form the single most important continuous solid solution in petrology. At
one end sits albite, NaAlSi3O8, which melts at about 1,118 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure. At
the other sits anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8, melting at about 1,553 degrees. Between them, every intermediate
composition is stable at magmatic temperatures, and the series is conventionally divided into six named
ranges by the percentage of the anorthite component: albite from An0 to An10, oligoclase An10 to An30,
andesine An30 to An50, labradorite An50 to An70, bytownite An70 to An90 and anorthite An90 to An100.
These divisions are a convenience of nomenclature rather than a reflection of any structural break, and
modern practice increasingly quotes the An number directly.

All plagioclase is triclinic. The name comes from the Greek for oblique fracture, referring to the fact
that its two cleavages meet at 86 degrees rather than the near-90 of the monoclinic alkali feldspars,
though in hand specimen the difference is barely perceptible.

The behaviour that matters most is how plagioclase crystallises from a melt. Because the solid that
forms is always richer in calcium than the liquid it grows from, a cooling magma produces
calcium-rich cores which are progressively mantled by more sodium-rich rims as the melt evolves. If
cooling is slow and diffusion in the crystal keeps up, the whole crystal re-equilibrates and ends
uniform. In practice diffusion in plagioclase is extremely sluggish — the coupled substitution
requires framework aluminium and silicon to move, not just cavity cations — so re-equilibration almost
never completes and the crystal preserves compositional zoning.

That zoning is visible under a petrographic microscope as concentric bands of differing extinction
position, and it is a remarkably detailed record. Simple normal zoning, calcium-rich core to
sodium-rich rim, records straightforward cooling. Reverse zoning records injection of hotter, more
primitive magma. Oscillatory zoning, in which composition swings back and forth across dozens of fine
bands, records repeated changes in the magma chamber, whether from recharge events, pressure
fluctuations, or local depletion and replenishment at the crystal surface. Volcanologists now use
oscillatory-zoned plagioclase, together with diffusion modelling of the smoothing of sharp
compositional steps, to estimate how long before an eruption a magma chamber was recharged — timescales
of days to decades, obtained by measuring how far elements have blurred across a boundary.

Plagioclase also carries a pressure signal. At higher pressures the plagioclase stability field shrinks,
because the mineral is comparatively low in density; in the deep crust and upper mantle, calcium and
aluminium are taken up instead by garnet and by clinopyroxene. The disappearance of plagioclase at
roughly 25 to 30 kilometres depth marks the transition from plagioclase peridotite to spinel
peridotite, one of the fundamental divisions in the structure of the upper mantle.

sections.heading: The Alkali Feldspars: Sanidine, Orthoclase, Microcline and Anorthoclase
sections.body:
The alkali feldspars run from potassium-rich KAlSi3O8 to sodium-rich NaAlSi3O8, and unlike plagioclase
they are named principally by structural state rather than by composition. This is initially confusing
and is worth stating plainly: sanidine, orthoclase and microcline can all have essentially the same
chemical formula. What differs is how the aluminium is distributed among the tetrahedral sites, and
that in turn depends on the temperature at which they crystallised and how fast they cooled.

Sanidine is the high-temperature form, monoclinic, with aluminium distributed almost randomly among
the four tetrahedral sites. It forms in volcanic rocks, especially rhyolites and trachytes, where
crystals grew fast in hot lava and were then quenched before ordering could occur. Sanidine is
typically glassy, colourless to pale, and often occurs as clear tabular phenocrysts.

Orthoclase is the intermediate form, still monoclinic but partially ordered, with aluminium
preferentially occupying two of the four sites. It is characteristic of medium-grade metamorphic rocks
and of plutonic rocks that cooled at moderate rates, and it is the familiar pink or white blocky
feldspar of many granites.

Microcline is the fully ordered, low-temperature form, triclinic, with aluminium concentrated almost
entirely into a single site. It forms in slowly cooled plutonic rocks and in pegmatites, and it is
diagnostic under the microscope because the ordering process, occurring after the crystal had already
grown with monoclinic symmetry, generates a fine cross-hatched twinning pattern found in no other
mineral. Microcline is also the host of amazonite, the vivid blue-green gem variety whose colour
derives from trace lead together with structural water and radiation damage, an origin that was
debated for a century and is still not entirely settled.

Anorthoclase occupies the sodium-rich end of the high-temperature series, roughly Or10 to Or36, and is
triclinic. It is characteristic of sodium-rich volcanic rocks and is well known from Mount Erebus in
Antarctica, where spectacular centimetre-scale anorthoclase crystals are thrown out in volcanic bombs.

Adularia is a term still encountered: a low-temperature potassium feldspar of variable structural
state, forming in Alpine-type hydrothermal fissures and named after the Adula massif in Switzerland.
It is not a distinct modern species, but the name survives because adularia is the classic host of
moonstone and adularescence takes its name from it.

Composition within the series carries its own signal. Potassium feldspar in a granite is rarely pure,
usually holding five to thirty per cent albite component — exactly the material that later exsolves.
Barium substitutes readily for potassium and has been used as a tracer of magma source, and rubidium
substitutes too, which made feldspar a standard rubidium-strontium geochronometer for decades.

The high-temperature sodium end member is monalbite, which inverts on cooling through about 980
degrees Celsius to high albite and, with continued ordering, to low albite. The full sequence — random
aluminium at high temperature, ordered aluminium at low temperature, and a symmetry change along the
way — is the same story told at both ends of the series, and it is the single most important idea in
alkali feldspar mineralogy.

sections.heading: Aluminium-Silicon Ordering and Feldspar as a Thermometer
sections.body:
The ordering of aluminium among tetrahedral sites deserves separate treatment because it is the
mechanism behind most of what makes feldspars informative, and it is not intuitive.

In the feldspar framework there are four crystallographically distinct tetrahedral sites, labelled T1o,
T1m, T2o and T2m. At high temperature, thermal energy overwhelms the small energetic preference
aluminium has for particular sites, and the aluminium is essentially randomly distributed, one atom in
four everywhere. This disordered arrangement is statistically symmetric and the crystal is monoclinic.
As temperature falls, the energetic preference begins to dominate. Aluminium migrates preferentially
into the T1o site, and once its occupancy there differs appreciably from T1m, the mirror symmetry
relating those sites is broken and the crystal becomes triclinic.

The rate of this process is the crucial point. Moving aluminium and silicon between framework sites
requires breaking strong aluminium-oxygen and silicon-oxygen bonds, so diffusion is extremely slow —
orders of magnitude slower than the diffusion of cavity cations like potassium and sodium. At 500
degrees Celsius the ordering of a feldspar crystal may take millions of years. This sluggishness is
what preserves the record: a volcanic sanidine quenched from 900 degrees stays disordered indefinitely
at surface conditions, and a pegmatite microcline that spent ten million years cooling through 400
degrees is fully ordered. The structural state is therefore frozen evidence of cooling history rather
than of present conditions.

The degree of order can be measured. X-ray powder diffraction gives the unit cell parameters, and the
difference between the b and c cell dimensions varies systematically with ordering, allowing a
quantitative order parameter to be extracted from the positions of a few diffraction peaks — a method
developed principally by W. S. MacKenzie and by Julian Goldsmith and Fritz Laves in the 1950s and
refined since. Infrared and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy give complementary measures.

There is a useful contrast with the plagioclase series here. In plagioclase, ordering and composition
are coupled, because the coupled substitution changes the framework aluminium content itself; low
albite is fully ordered while anorthite has an ordering scheme imposed by its one-to-one
aluminium-silicon ratio, and intermediate compositions show incommensurate structures with satellite
diffraction spots that puzzled crystallographers for decades. In the alkali series the composition is
fixed at one aluminium in four and only the arrangement changes, which is why structural state and
chemistry can be treated as independent variables there and not in plagioclase.

Combined with composition, this becomes two-feldspar thermometry, one of the standard tools of
metamorphic petrology. If a rock contains both an alkali feldspar and a plagioclase that equilibrated
together, their compositions must lie on opposite limbs of the solvus at the temperature of
equilibration. Measure both compositions with an electron microprobe, find the temperature at which the
solvus passes through both, and you have an estimate of the temperature of last equilibration, usually
good to within about fifty degrees. The method's honest weakness is that the two feldspars often
continue to exchange after peak conditions, so the recorded temperature may be a partly reset
closure temperature rather than the peak of metamorphism.

sections.heading: Exsolution: Perthite and the Record of Cooling Rate
sections.body:
When a homogeneous alkali feldspar crystallised at high temperature cools below the solvus, it becomes
thermodynamically unstable as a single phase and separates into two: a potassium-rich phase and a
sodium-rich phase. Because the crystal is solid, this separation cannot happen by the two phases
physically parting company. Instead they unmix in place, forming intergrown lamellae that share the
same framework and are crystallographically continuous with one another. This process is called
exsolution, and the resulting texture is perthite.

The terminology depends on which phase dominates. Perthite proper is a potassium-rich host containing
lamellae or films of sodium-rich albite. Antiperthite is the reverse: a sodium-rich host with
potassium-rich lamellae. Mesoperthite has roughly equal amounts of each and is characteristic of
high-grade metamorphic rocks such as granulites, where the original feldspar crystallised at very high
temperature well above the solvus crest and therefore had an intermediate bulk composition.

Scale is where the information lives. The coarseness of exsolution lamellae depends directly on how
slowly the crystal cooled, because coarsening requires diffusion and diffusion requires time at
temperature. Rapidly cooled volcanic feldspars show no exsolution at all — they are quenched
homogeneous, and this is why sanidine phenocrysts are optically clear. Feldspars from shallow
intrusions show cryptoperthite, lamellae so fine, on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometres, that
they are invisible even under the highest optical magnification and are detectable only by X-ray
diffraction or transmission electron microscopy. Deeper plutonic feldspars show microperthite,
resolvable under a petrographic microscope. Slowly cooled pegmatites and deep granulites show
macroperthite, coarse enough to see with the unaided eye as fine white streaks threading a pink
crystal, and in extreme cases the two phases separate into patch perthite with domains a millimetre
or more across.

The practical consequence is that a hand lens plus a microscope can distinguish a lava, a shallow
sill, a batholith and a lower-crustal granulite from feldspar texture alone. Comparing observed
lamellar spacing with experimentally calibrated coarsening rates even yields quantitative cooling
rates, though with wide error bars.

Exsolution has a mechanical consequence too. The two phases have slightly different unit cell
dimensions, so the intergrowth is elastically strained, and that stored energy makes perthitic
feldspar more susceptible to fracture and to fluid attack along the lamellar boundaries. Deuteric
alteration — reaction with the magma's own late-stage water as it cools — exploits those boundaries,
converting strained cryptoperthite into coarser, strain-free patch perthite. A coarsely exsolved
feldspar may therefore record a fluid event rather than slow cooling.

Cryptoperthitic exsolution also produces optical effects. Where the lamellae are spaced at a fraction
of the wavelength of visible light, they scatter and interfere with incident illumination, producing
the soft blue-white internal glow known as adularescence, which is precisely what makes moonstone. The
finest moonstones are cryptoperthitic intergrowths of orthoclase and albite, and the intensity of the
sheen scales with how uniformly the lamellae are spaced. The gem is thus a direct visual expression of
a phase diagram.

sections.heading: Twinning: Carlsbad, Albite, Pericline and the Tartan Pattern
sections.body:
Twinning is the intergrowth of two or more crystals of the same mineral in a specific, symmetry-related
orientation, and feldspars twin more variously and more usefully than almost any other mineral group.
Recognising the common twin laws is one of the most reliable ways to identify a feldspar and to
distinguish its species.

Carlsbad twinning, named for the Bohemian locality now called Karlovy Vary, is a growth twin in which
two individuals are related by a 180-degree rotation about the c axis, meeting on a near-vertical
composition plane. It is very common in alkali feldspars and produces a hand-specimen crystal that
appears divided down its long axis into two halves which extinguish at different rotations under
crossed polarisers. A pale blocky crystal in granite showing two flashing halves is almost certainly
orthoclase with a Carlsbad twin.

Albite twinning is the diagnostic feature of plagioclase. It is a polysynthetic twin, meaning many
individuals repeat in parallel, related by reflection across the (010) plane. In thin section under
crossed polarisers this produces the unmistakable pattern of fine parallel black and white stripes
that alternately extinguish as the stage is rotated. In hand specimen the same twinning shows on a
cleavage surface as very fine parallel striations, visible with a hand lens and detectable as a subtle
striping of reflected light when the specimen is tilted. This is the single most useful field
discriminator between plagioclase and potassium feldspar: plagioclase is striated, potassium feldspar
is not.

Pericline twinning is another polysynthetic law in plagioclase, with a composition plane roughly
perpendicular to albite twinning. On its own it is inconspicuous, but combined with albite twinning it
produces the cross-hatched or tartan pattern that is absolutely diagnostic of microcline. That tartan
texture arises because the crystal originally grew as monoclinic sanidine or orthoclase, and when it
later ordered and dropped to triclinic symmetry it could do so in two equivalent orientations. Domains
of each orientation nucleated throughout the crystal and interlocked, producing the characteristic
irregular, slightly wavy grid. Tartan twinning is therefore not a growth feature at all but a
transformation twin, a fossil of a symmetry change.

Two further growth laws produce striking specimens. Baveno twinning, from the Italian locality on Lake
Maggiore, gives a near-square cross-section; Manebach twinning gives a crystal that appears folded
across the basal plane. Both occur most often in cavity or pegmatite crystals.

Twins are grouped by mechanism, and the distinction carries real information. Growth twins, including
Carlsbad, Baveno and Manebach, form as the crystal grows, when a new layer nucleates in a
symmetrically equivalent but rotated orientation, and they record growth conditions. Transformation
twins, of which microcline's tartan is the classic example, form after growth when the crystal changes
symmetry, and they record cooling history. Deformation twins, produced by stress, occur in plagioclase
in strongly deformed rocks and are recognisable because the lamellae taper, bend or terminate within
the grain rather than running cleanly across it, making them useful strain indicators in mylonites.

One practical caution: albite twinning is diagnostic of plagioclase, but its absence is diagnostic of
nothing, since unfavourably cut sections show no lamellae at all.

sections.heading: Identifying Feldspar in Hand Specimen
sections.body:
Feldspar identification in the field rests on a short, reliable checklist, and the properties are
consistent enough across the group that a beginner can become competent quickly.

Hardness is 6 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale. This means feldspar will not be scratched by a steel knife
blade or a nail, which sit around 5 to 5.5, but will be scratched by quartz at 7. That single test
separates feldspar from calcite, mica, gypsum, and most of the softer minerals it might be confused
with, though it does not separate it from quartz, which requires other criteria.

Cleavage is the strongest diagnostic. Feldspars have two excellent cleavages meeting at or very near a
right angle — precisely 90 degrees in the monoclinic alkali feldspars, and 86 degrees in triclinic
plagioclase, a difference too small to judge by eye. Broken feldspar therefore shows flat, mirror-like
rectangular faces that catch the light in flashes as the specimen is turned. Quartz, by contrast, has
no cleavage at all and breaks with a curved conchoidal fracture and a greasy lustre. Distinguishing
quartz from feldspar in a granite comes down almost entirely to this: flat flashing faces are feldspar,
glassy curved surfaces are quartz.

Colour is suggestive but never conclusive. Potassium feldspar is commonly white, cream, salmon pink or
brick red, the reddish tints coming from micro-inclusions of iron oxide, and it can also be the green
of amazonite. Plagioclase is more often white, grey or bluish grey. But a white potassium feldspar and
a white plagioclase are indistinguishable by colour alone.

Specific gravity ranges from 2.55 for potassium feldspar to 2.76 for anorthite, so feldspar feels
noticeably lighter in the hand than any of the ferromagnesian minerals it accompanies. Lustre is
vitreous to slightly pearly on cleavage faces. Feldspar is not magnetic, does not react with dilute
acid, and leaves a white streak.

A methodical field routine, which works with nothing more than a knife, a hand lens and a good light:
steps: Scratch the grain with a steel knife. If it scratches easily it is not feldspar; feldspar at Mohs 6 to 6.5 resists a knife.
Turn the specimen slowly under a strong light and look for flat faces that flash on and off together. Two such sets meeting at about a right angle confirm feldspar cleavage.

With a hand lens, examine a cleavage face for very fine parallel striations. Present means plagioclase; absent means alkali feldspar, though a fresh look at several grains is wise since striations can be faint.
Look for a single straight division splitting a blocky crystal into two halves that reflect light differently. That is a Carlsbad twin, common in orthoclase and microcline.
Note the colour. Salmon pink, brick red or green points to alkali feldspar; white to bluish grey with striations points to plagioclase.
Check the associated minerals. Quartz plus abundant pink feldspar suggests granite; grey striated feldspar plus dark pyroxene and no quartz suggests basalt, gabbro or dolerite.
If a definite answer matters, take the sample for a thin section. Optical determination of composition and twinning is decisive where hand specimen work is only probable.

sections.heading: Feldspar Under the Microscope: Optical Determination
sections.body:
A thin section is a slice of rock ground to thirty micrometres, thin enough that light passes through
and mineral grains show their optical properties. Feldspar in thin section is colourless with low
relief and unremarkable first-order grey to white interference colours, which sounds unpromising, but
its twinning and its refractive indices make it one of the most precisely determinable minerals
available.

Relief is the first clue. Relief describes how strongly a grain stands out against the mounting
medium, and it depends on the difference in refractive index. Canada balsam and modern epoxy mounts
have a refractive index near 1.537. Potassium feldspar has indices from about 1.518 to 1.526, so it
has slightly negative relief and appears very faintly sunken. Albite is close to 1.529 to 1.539,
essentially matching the mount, so it almost vanishes. Anorthite reaches 1.575 to 1.590, giving
distinctly positive relief. This means the relief of a plagioclase grain tracks its anorthite content,
and the direction of the Becke line — the bright halo that migrates toward the higher-index material
as the focus is raised — gives a quick semi-quantitative composition estimate against quartz or against
the mount.

The classical quantitative method is the Michel-Lévy technique, in which the maximum extinction angle
is measured on grains cut perpendicular to the (010) plane, identified by the symmetry of the albite
twin lamellae. The measured angle is then read against a calibration curve to give the anorthite
content, generally to within about five per cent An. The method is a century old, was refined by
Auguste Michel-Lévy in the 1890s, and remains genuinely useful, though it is fiddly and requires
finding correctly oriented grains. A universal stage, which allows the section to be tilted about
several axes, gives better precision. The modern approach is simply to point an electron microprobe at
the grain and read the composition directly, but microscopy remains the fast, cheap, non-destructive
first pass.

Distinguishing the species under the microscope follows the twinning. Polysynthetic albite twinning
means plagioclase. Cross-hatched tartan twinning means microcline. Carlsbad twinning without
polysynthetic lamellae, on a grain with slightly negative relief, means orthoclase or sanidine, and
the two are separated by optic axial angle: sanidine has a small 2V, often under 30 degrees and
sometimes near zero, whereas orthoclase has a larger 2V of 35 to 75 degrees.

Alteration provides another clue. Potassium feldspar characteristically alters to a cloudy dusting of
fine sericite, giving grains a dirty grey appearance, while plagioclase alters to sericite plus
saussurite, a fine mixture of epidote, zoisite and albite that gives a mottled speckled texture. In
practice a dirty, cloudy feldspar in an otherwise fresh rock is usually a good sign that you are
looking at plagioclase or altered potassium feldspar rather than at quartz, which almost never clouds.

sections.heading: Crystallisation: Bowen's Reaction Series and the Feldspar Path
sections.body:
In 1922 the Canadian petrologist Norman Levi Bowen published the experimental results that became
Bowen's reaction series, still the standard framework for understanding the order in which minerals
crystallise from a cooling silicate melt. The series has two branches, and feldspar occupies one of
them entirely.

The discontinuous branch describes the ferromagnesian minerals: olivine crystallises first at the
highest temperatures, then reacts with the remaining melt to form pyroxene, which reacts to form
amphibole, which reacts to form biotite. Each step is a distinct mineral with a distinct structure, so
the series is discontinuous.

The continuous branch is plagioclase. Calcium-rich anorthite crystallises at high temperature, and as
the melt cools the already-formed crystals continuously react with the liquid, exchanging calcium and
aluminium for sodium and silicon, so that the composition evolves smoothly toward albite without ever
changing mineral. The two branches converge at low temperature, where potassium feldspar, muscovite
and finally quartz crystallise from the residual, silica-rich, alkali-rich melt.

This ordering explains a great deal about rocks. A basalt, formed from a melt that crystallised at high
temperature and was erupted before differentiation went far, contains calcium-rich plagioclase near
An60 to An80 together with pyroxene and olivine. A granite, formed from the residual product of long
differentiation or from melting of continental crust, contains sodium-rich plagioclase near An10 to
An30 together with abundant potassium feldspar and quartz. Andesite and diorite sit in between with
intermediate plagioclase, which is exactly why the name andesine was given to the plagioclase of that
range.

Bowen's series also explains why plagioclase zoning is normal rather than reversed in most rocks: the
reaction relationship means the crystal is always trying to become more sodium-rich than its core, and
sluggish diffusion preserves the failure to fully re-equilibrate.

Buoyancy adds a physical mechanism to the chemical one. In a basaltic melt of density around 2.7 to
2.8 grams per cubic centimetre, plagioclase at 2.7 is nearly neutrally buoyant and can float where
olivine at 3.3 sinks. In large slowly cooling intrusions this separates crystals from melt and
produces layered complexes: the Bushveld Complex in South Africa, the Stillwater Complex in Montana
and the Skaergaard intrusion in east Greenland all show rhythmic layers where plagioclase-rich bands
alternate with pyroxene- and olivine-rich ones. Reading plagioclase composition upward through such a
sequence traces the magma chamber's chemical evolution directly. Anorthosite, more than ninety per
cent plagioclase, is the extreme case; why terrestrial massif anorthosites cluster so strikingly in
the interval 1.8 to 1.0 billion years ago remains an open problem.

The framework has real limits and it is important not to over-apply it. Bowen worked in a dry system
at one atmosphere. Adding water lowers melting temperatures dramatically, by several hundred degrees
for a granitic composition, and shifts the sequence. Increasing pressure suppresses plagioclase in
favour of denser aluminous phases. Magma mixing, crustal assimilation and the physical removal of
crystals from a melt all complicate the simple picture of a closed system cooling slowly. Bowen
himself was clear that the series was an idealisation. It remains the right first model and the wrong
last word.

sections.heading: Feldspar in Rock Classification: The QAPF Diagram
sections.body:
Because feldspar is so abundant and its composition varies so systematically, the international
classification of igneous rocks is built directly on it. The scheme, adopted by the International Union
of Geological Sciences Subcommission on the Systematics of Igneous Rocks and codified principally by
Albert Streckeisen in the 1970s, uses a double-triangle diagram known as QAPF.

The four corners are Q for quartz, A for alkali feldspar including albite up to An5, P for plagioclase
from An5 to An100, and F for feldspathoids. Quartz and feldspathoids can never coexist in equilibrium,
because a feldspathoid is by definition a mineral that forms when there is too little silica to make
feldspar; if free silica were present it would react with the feldspathoid to make feldspar. So the
diagram is drawn as two triangles sharing the A-P edge, with Q above and F below, and a rock plots in
one or the other but never both.

The proportions are recalculated to one hundred per cent using only these four groups, ignoring the
dark minerals, and the resulting point names the rock. A coarse-grained rock with 20 to 60 per cent
quartz and roughly equal alkali feldspar and plagioclase is a granite. Shift the feldspar strongly
toward plagioclase and it becomes a granodiorite, then a tonalite. Remove the quartz and it becomes a
syenite, a monzonite or a diorite depending on the feldspar ratio. Rocks with more than 90 per cent
plagioclase are anorthosite. Below the A-P line, replacing quartz with nepheline gives nepheline
syenite, and so on.

Fine-grained volcanic rocks use the same diagram with a parallel set of names: rhyolite for granite,
dacite for granodiorite, andesite and basalt for diorite and gabbro, trachyte for syenite, phonolite
for nepheline syenite. The distinction between andesite and basalt in the field is conventionally made
on silica content and on the anorthite content of the plagioclase, with basalt carrying calcium-rich
plagioclase above roughly An50.

Feldspar organises sedimentary classification too, because feldspar breaks down during transport while
quartz survives. A sandstone with more than twenty-five per cent feldspar is an arkose, implying rapid
erosion of a granitic source, short transport and often an arid or cold climate where chemical
weathering is suppressed; the Torridonian sandstones of north-west Scotland and the Fountain Formation
beneath the Colorado Flatirons are classic examples. A quartz arenite with almost no feldspar implies
long transport, repeated recycling or intense tropical weathering. The provenance diagrams of
Dickinson and Suczek, published in 1979, plot quartz against feldspar against lithic fragments to
distinguish sediment shed from a stable craton, a magmatic arc or a recycled orogen.

For the volcanic rocks, whose crystals are often too small to count, a chemical classification is used
instead. The total alkali versus silica diagram, or TAS, plots the weight percentage of sodium oxide
plus potassium oxide against silica, and was formalised by the same IUGS subcommission in 1986. Its
fields were drawn to match the QAPF names as closely as possible, and the reason it works at all is
that the alkali content of a rock is very largely a statement about its feldspar.

sections.heading: Weathering: How Feldspar Becomes Clay and Regulates Climate
sections.body:
Feldspar forms at high temperature and is thermodynamically out of equilibrium at the Earth's surface,
where it reacts with water and dissolved carbon dioxide. That reaction, chemical weathering by
hydrolysis, is the source of most of the world's clay, most of the dissolved sodium, potassium and
calcium in rivers and oceans, and — over geological time — the principal thermostat regulating Earth's
climate.

The archetypal reaction converts potassium feldspar to kaolinite: two units of KAlSi3O8 plus two
hydrogen ions plus nine water molecules yield one unit of kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, plus four silicic
acid molecules and two potassium ions in solution. The hydrogen ions come from carbonic acid formed
when atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in rainwater and soil water, the latter typically far more
acidic because of root and microbial respiration. The essential chemistry is that hydrogen ions attack
the framework, prise out the large cations, and break enough of the aluminium-oxygen and
silicon-oxygen bonds to collapse the three-dimensional framework into a two-dimensional sheet
structure.

Which clay mineral results depends on climate and drainage. In a hot, wet, well-drained tropical
setting, leaching is intense, silica and all the cations are flushed away, and the product is kaolinite
or, in extreme cases, the aluminium hydroxide gibbsite that forms bauxite. In a temperate climate with
less leaching, some potassium is retained and illite forms. In a poorly drained setting with
restricted leaching and abundant magnesium and calcium, smectite forms, the swelling clay responsible
for expansive soils that crack building foundations. Feldspar weathering is therefore the origin of
soil clay mineralogy, which in turn controls soil fertility, water retention and engineering behaviour.

The rates matter and are surprisingly slow. Laboratory dissolution rates for feldspar at pH 5 and 25
degrees Celsius, extrapolated to a one-millimetre grain, imply a lifetime of the order of hundreds of
thousands of years, and field rates measured on dated surfaces are typically slower still than the
laboratory by one to three orders of magnitude — a long-standing and genuinely unresolved discrepancy
usually attributed to surface armouring by secondary precipitates, to approaching chemical
equilibrium in stagnant pore water, and to a shrinking reactive surface area.

The climatic significance rests on the fate of the calcium. Weathering of calcium-bearing plagioclase
consumes carbon dioxide, releases calcium and bicarbonate to rivers, and those ions are eventually
precipitated as calcium carbonate in the ocean, locking the carbon into limestone. The net effect,
sometimes summarised as the Urey reaction after Harold Urey's 1952 formulation, is a slow removal of
carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Because weathering rates rise with temperature and with rainfall,
the process is a negative feedback: a warmer world weathers faster, draws down more carbon dioxide and
cools. This silicate weathering thermostat, developed quantitatively by Walker, Hays and Kasting in
1981, is the leading explanation for why Earth's surface has remained habitable for billions of years
despite a sun that has brightened by roughly thirty per cent. Its response time is hundreds of
thousands of years, which is why it offers no help with anthropogenic warming.

sections.heading: Feldspathoids, Barium Feldspars and the Silica-Poor Branch
sections.body:
Feldspar requires enough silica to build a fully polymerised framework. When a magma is
silica-undersaturated — poor in silica relative to its alkali content — the framework cannot be
completed and a related group of minerals forms instead: the feldspathoids. Understanding them
clarifies what feldspar is by showing what happens when the recipe runs short.

Nepheline, ideally NaAlSiO4 though usually containing potassium as (Na,K)AlSiO4, has an
aluminium-to-silicon ratio of one to one rather than feldspar's one to three or one to one for
anorthite in a different structural context. Its framework is a stuffed derivative of tridymite, a
silica polymorph, with cavities occupied by sodium and potassium. Leucite, KAlSi2O6, is intermediate
in silica content and is famous for its distinctive trapezohedral crystals in the lavas of Vesuvius.
Sodalite, nosean, haüyne and cancrinite complete the common list, and their frameworks accommodate
additional anions such as chloride, sulphate and carbonate in cage-like cavities.

The fundamental rule is that feldspathoids and quartz are mutually exclusive in an equilibrium
assemblage. Free silica reacts with a feldspathoid to make feldspar: nepheline plus silica gives
albite, and leucite plus silica gives orthoclase. Finding both in one rock therefore indicates
disequilibrium — usually magma mixing or rapid quenching. This is precisely why the QAPF classification
splits into two triangles that share the feldspar edge.

Silica-undersaturated rocks are volumetrically minor but geologically important. They occur in
continental rift settings, in ocean island volcanism and in carbonatite complexes, and they are
enriched in incompatible elements including the rare earths, zirconium and niobium, which makes
nepheline syenite complexes such as Ilímaussaq in Greenland and Lovozero in Russia significant
strategic mineral deposits.

At the opposite corner of feldspar chemistry sits the barium series. Celsian, BaAl2Si2O8, is the barium
analogue of anorthite, with barium substituting for calcium in the cavity and the same coupled
aluminium substitution. Hyalophane is the intermediate between celsian and potassium feldspar. Both are
rare, occurring mainly in manganese-rich metamorphic rocks and in some barium-rich hydrothermal
deposits, but they demonstrate that the feldspar framework will accept any sufficiently large cation
whose charge can be balanced by adjusting the aluminium content.

Leucite carries a diagnostic subtlety. It is cubic above about 605 degrees Celsius and tetragonal
below, developing a fine polysynthetic twinning on cooling through the inversion. Because leucite is
unstable at high pressure it occurs only in lavas and very shallow intrusions, so a leucite-bearing
rock is unambiguously near-surface in origin.

Nepheline is also the raw material of a substantial industry. Nepheline syenite, quarried notably at
Blue Mountain in Ontario and in Norway, substitutes for feldspar in glass and ceramics: it supplies
more alumina and alkali per tonne, melts lower, and contains almost no free quartz, an advantage where
crystalline silica dust is a regulated hazard.

Two further relatives are worth naming. Reedmergnerite is the boron analogue, NaBSi3O8, with boron
replacing aluminium. Buddingtonite is an ammonium feldspar, NH4AlSi3O8, found in hydrothermally altered
rocks and identified spectroscopically in remote sensing, where the ammonium ion gives distinctive
absorption features used to map alteration zones from the air.

sections.heading: Industrial Uses and Gem Varieties
sections.body:
Feldspar is mined at a scale of roughly thirty million tonnes a year worldwide, principally in Turkey,
Italy, China, India and the United States, and almost all of it goes into two industries: ceramics and
glass.

In ceramics feldspar serves as a flux, a material that lowers the melting temperature of the mixture.
A traditional porcelain body is roughly fifty per cent kaolin clay, twenty-five per cent quartz and
twenty-five per cent feldspar. During firing at 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius the feldspar melts to a
viscous glass that flows between the clay and quartz particles, bonding them and filling the pore
space to produce a dense, translucent, vitrified body. Without a flux, the clay would need to be fired
to temperatures far beyond the reach of a practical kiln. Potassium feldspar is preferred for
porcelain because its melt is more viscous over a wider temperature range, giving a broader firing
window and less risk of the ware slumping; sodium feldspar melts at a lower temperature with lower
viscosity and is used where a sharper, cheaper vitrification is acceptable. Feldspar is also a primary
constituent of glazes and of sanitaryware, tile and tableware bodies.

In glassmaking feldspar supplies alumina, which improves chemical durability and mechanical strength
and reduces the tendency to devitrify, while simultaneously supplying alkalis that would otherwise
have to be added as more expensive soda ash. Container glass, flat glass and fibreglass all use
feldspar or the related rock nepheline syenite for this purpose. Minor uses include functional filler in paints,
plastics and rubber, mild abrasive in scouring powders, and welding electrode coatings.

Specification for industrial use turns almost entirely on iron. A few tenths of a per cent of iron
oxide colours a ceramic body or glass batch, so feldspar is graded on Fe2O3, with the best ceramic
grades below about 0.1 per cent. Producers achieve this by froth flotation — first floating off mica
and iron minerals, then separating feldspar from quartz in a second stage — backed by magnetic
separation. Pegmatites, yielding coarse and very pure feldspar, were historically the main source, but
most modern production comes from large granite and feldspathic sand deposits worked by flotation.

The gem varieties are disproportionately famous relative to their economic weight. Moonstone is
orthoclase-albite cryptoperthite whose lamellar intergrowth scatters light into a soft blue-white
sheen called adularescence, with the finest material historically from Sri Lanka and southern India.
Labradorite, from An50 to An70 plagioclase, shows labradorescence: intense flashes of blue, green,
gold and occasionally violet produced by interference at the Bøggild exsolution lamellae, with the
finest material from Labrador in Canada and from Finland, where the highly iridescent variety is
marketed as spectrolite. Amazonite is blue-green microcline, from Colorado, Russia and Madagascar.
Sunstone is plagioclase or occasionally alkali feldspar containing oriented platelets of hematite or
native copper, which produce a glittering aventurescence; the copper-bearing Oregon sunstone can be
red or green and is faceted as a genuine gemstone rather than a curiosity.

sections.heading: Feldspar Beyond Earth, and Reading Time with It
sections.body:
Feldspar is not merely an Earth mineral. It is abundant throughout the inner solar system, and its
behaviour has been used to reconstruct the earliest history of the Moon and to date human occupation
of archaeological sites.

The lunar highlands, the bright areas that make up about eighty per cent of the Moon's surface, are
composed of ferroan anorthosite: rock consisting of more than ninety per cent calcium-rich
plagioclase, generally An94 to An97. The Apollo missions returned samples, and the sample known as
15415, collected by David Scott and James Irwin in 1971 and nicknamed the Genesis Rock, is nearly pure
anorthite. Its significance is that plagioclase is less dense than a magnesium-iron silicate melt.
The standard interpretation, developed rapidly after Apollo 11 and refined since, is that the early
Moon was covered by a global magma ocean hundreds of kilometres deep; as it crystallised, dense olivine
and pyroxene sank while buoyant plagioclase floated to the top and accumulated as a crust. The lunar
highlands are therefore a plagioclase flotation cumulate, and their existence is the primary evidence
for the magma ocean model, which has since been extended to Earth, Mars and the larger asteroids.

Plagioclase is likewise abundant in Martian basalts, in the basaltic achondrite meteorites believed to
come from the asteroid Vesta, and in many chondrites. Its detection by orbital infrared spectroscopy
is one of the standard means of mapping crustal composition on rocky bodies. Shocked plagioclase
carries additional information: a sufficiently strong impact converts it to maskelynite, a dense
diaplectic glass that retains the original crystal shape but has lost its crystalline order. Finding
maskelynite in a meteorite establishes that the parent rock experienced shock pressures of roughly 25
to 45 gigapascals, and it was the presence of maskelynite in the shergottite meteorites, together with
trapped gases matching the Martian atmosphere measured by the Viking landers, that established their
Martian origin.

On Earth, feldspar has become a workhorse of Quaternary dating through luminescence. Ionising
radiation from trace uranium, thorium and potassium in surrounding sediment knocks electrons in the
feldspar lattice into metastable trap states, where they accumulate at a rate proportional to the dose
received. Exposure to sunlight empties the traps. So a grain of feldspar buried in sediment begins
accumulating trapped charge from the moment it was last exposed to daylight, and measuring the light
emitted when the traps are emptied in the laboratory — by heating for thermoluminescence, or by
stimulating with infrared light for infrared stimulated luminescence — gives the accumulated dose and
hence the burial age. Feldspar saturates at higher doses than quartz, extending the datable range to
several hundred thousand years, at the cost of a complication called anomalous fading, in which some
trapped charge leaks away by quantum tunnelling and must be corrected for. The technique has dated
sand dunes, river terraces, loess sequences and the sediments enclosing early human artefacts, and it
rests on the same slow, stubborn atomic-scale behaviour of the feldspar framework that makes the
mineral such a patient recorder of everything else.

sections.heading: Pitfalls, Limits and Unresolved Questions
sections.body:
Working with feldspar goes wrong in a small number of recurring ways, and knowing them in advance
saves a great deal of misinterpretation.

The commonest identification error is confusing feldspar with quartz in a coarse igneous rock. The
resolution is always cleavage: feldspar has two good cleavages producing flat reflective faces, quartz
has none. A second frequent error is calling every pink mineral potassium feldspar. Pink plagioclase
exists, particularly in anorthosites and some altered rocks, and colourless potassium feldspar is
ordinary in sanidine-bearing lavas. Striations, not colour, are the discriminator. A third is mistaking
heavily altered feldspar for a different mineral entirely; a feldspar that has partly become sericite
or kaolinite is soft, dull and earthy and may be scratched with a fingernail, which invites the
conclusion that it was never feldspar at all.

The interpretive limits are more consequential. Two-feldspar thermometry assumes the two phases
equilibrated with each other and then stopped exchanging, which is often not true; continued exchange
during slow cooling resets the recorded temperature downward, so the number obtained may be a closure
temperature rather than a peak. The plagioclase composition in a volcanic rock may not represent the
magma it sits in, because crystals are commonly inherited from an earlier magma or scavenged from
chamber walls; a rock can contain populations of plagioclase with entirely different histories, and
treating them as one population produces nonsense. Exsolution coarseness as a cooling-rate indicator
is calibrated with substantial uncertainty and is strongly affected by water, which is rarely
independently constrained.

Several genuine open questions remain. The persistent discrepancy of one to three orders of magnitude
between laboratory and field feldspar dissolution rates is not fully explained, and it matters because
global weathering models — including estimates of how quickly enhanced rock weathering might sequester
carbon dioxide — depend on which rate is used. The origin of amazonite's blue-green colour, most often
attributed to lead in combination with structural water and radiation-induced defects, is still argued
over. The precise thermodynamics of the low-temperature plagioclase miscibility gaps are difficult to
determine experimentally because equilibrium is unattainably slow at the relevant temperatures, so much
of what is known comes from inference from natural samples rather than from experiment. And anomalous
fading in feldspar luminescence dating, though empirically correctable, still rests on a tunnelling
model whose long-term extrapolation is not fully verified.

The general lesson is worth stating plainly. Feldspar is an exceptionally rich recorder precisely
because its internal processes are slow, but the same sluggishness means the information it preserves
is often partial, out of date, or a mixture of several histories superimposed. The mineral almost
never lies; it simply answers a slightly different question from the one being asked, and careful work
consists largely in establishing which question a particular crystal is actually answering.

guides.title: Quartz and the Silica Minerals
guides.summary: A comprehensive account of silica in the Earth: the atomic structure of quartz, its polymorphs and cryptocrystalline forms, how and where it grows, how to identify it, what it is used for, and the serious dust hazard of working it.

sections.heading: Silica: The Commonest Substance in the Earth's Crust
sections.body: Silicon dioxide, written SiO2 and called silica, is the single most abundant chemical compound in the outer part of the planet. Oxygen makes up about 46 percent of the continental crust by mass and silicon about 28 percent, and the two are bound together so persistently that almost every common rock-forming mineral is built from silicon-oxygen units. Of these minerals, quartz is the purest expression: a mineral of pure SiO2 with no other essential ingredient. Quartz alone accounts for something like twelve percent of the continental crust by volume, and it dominates whole classes of rock. Granite is typically twenty to forty percent quartz. Ordinary beach and desert sand is usually quartz. Sandstone, quartzite, chert, flint, agate and opal are all silica or nearly so. If you pick up a random handful of loose grains from a riverbank almost anywhere on a continent, most of what you are holding is silicon dioxide. The reason for this dominance is chemistry plus durability. Silicon sits in group 14 of the periodic table with four bonding electrons, and in the oxidising, oxygen-rich conditions of the crust it almost invariably ends up surrounded by four oxygen atoms. The bond between silicon and oxygen is unusually strong, roughly half covalent and half ionic in character, with a bond energy near 450 kilojoules per mole. That strength makes silica chemically stubborn: it dissolves only sluggishly in ordinary surface waters, resists most acids apart from hydrofluoric acid, and survives repeated cycles of erosion, transport, burial and re-exposure that destroy softer or more reactive minerals. Feldspar, which is more abundant than quartz in fresh igneous rock, breaks down into clay when it weathers. Quartz simply gets smaller and rounder. Over hundreds of millions of years this differential survival concentrates quartz in sediments, which is why the world's great sand seas are made of it. Silica also matters far beyond geology. It is the raw material of glass, of the crucibles in which semiconductor silicon is grown, of the optical fibres carrying most of the world's data, of foundry moulds, abrasives, and the hydraulic fracturing sand used in oil and gas wells. It was the stone of choice for the first deliberately manufactured tools, because flint and chert break with a predictable conchoidal fracture that produces edges sharper than surgical steel. Understanding silica therefore means understanding a large fraction of the solid Earth, a large fraction of industrial materials, and the oldest technology our species possesses. It also means understanding a genuine occupational hazard, because the same fine crystalline dust that makes silica useful causes an incurable lung disease when it is breathed. One point of orientation is worth making early. The word quartz names a specific crystalline mineral, but silica takes many structural forms, from ordered lattices to the fibre bundles of chalcedony and the sphere-stacked glass of opal. All share the same formula and differ only in how their atoms are arranged. That difference in arrangement, not in composition, decides whether a lump of SiO2 is a gemstone, a razor-sharp tool, an optical fibre or evidence of a meteorite impact.

sections.heading: The Silicon-Oxygen Tetrahedron and the Quartz Framework
sections.body: Every silica mineral is built from one repeating unit: a silicon atom at the centre of four oxygen atoms arranged at the corners of a tetrahedron. The silicon-oxygen distance is close to 1.61 angstroms, an angstrom being a ten-billionth of a metre, and the oxygen-silicon-oxygen angles are near the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5 degrees. This unit, written SiO4, is the single most important building block in mineralogy. What distinguishes one silicate family from another is how the tetrahedra connect. In olivine they stand alone, isolated and bridged by magnesium and iron. In pyroxenes they link into single chains, in amphiboles into double chains, in micas and clays into sheets. In the silica minerals they achieve the maximum possible linkage: every one of the four corner oxygens is shared with a neighbouring tetrahedron. That complete sharing is what produces the formula SiO2 rather than SiO4. Each oxygen belongs half to one silicon and half to another, so the ratio of silicon to oxygen becomes one to two. Because every bond is satisfied internally, the structure needs no other cations to balance its charge, which is why quartz is a pure compound while nearly every other abundant mineral carries sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium or iron. Mineralogists call such a fully linked arrangement a framework or tectosilicate structure. Feldspars are also frameworks, but there some silicon is replaced by aluminium, which carries one less positive charge and so demands an extra cation to compensate. In quartz specifically, the tetrahedra spiral. Follow a chain of linked tetrahedra along the crystal's principal axis, conventionally called the c-axis, and it turns through a helix that repeats after three tetrahedra. The result is a trigonal structure with open channels running parallel to the c-axis, roughly 2 angstroms across at their narrowest. These channels are not empty in nature: they host trace hydrogen, lithium, sodium and aluminium, and they let small ions diffuse along the axis far faster than across it. The silicon-oxygen-silicon bridging angle is about 144 degrees, notably bent rather than straight, and this flexibility in the bridge rather than in the rigid tetrahedron is what allows silica to adopt so many different structures. The density that follows from this packing is 2.65 grams per cubic centimetre for quartz, a figure worth memorising because it underlies practical geology. It is the density assumed in settling calculations for sand, in the standard specific gravity of soil solids used by engineers, and in gold panning, where the fifteen-to-one density contrast between gold and quartz sand is the entire basis of the technique. The unit cell of alpha quartz, the smallest repeating box of atoms, contains three formula units of SiO2 and measures about 4.91 by 4.91 by 5.41 angstroms. Those numbers were determined by William Bragg and colleagues in the years after 1912, when X-ray diffraction first made it possible to see inside a crystal. The geometry explains an important asymmetry: because the spiral channels run along the c-axis, quartz grows fastest in that direction, which is why its crystals are elongate prisms rather than equant blocks.

sections.heading: Purity, Trace Elements, and the Colours of Quartz
sections.body: Chemically analysed, natural quartz is startlingly pure. A typical vein or pegmatite crystal is more than 99.5 percent SiO2, and the impurities that remain are measured in parts per million rather than percent. The framework structure is the reason: there is simply no room and no charge-balancing requirement for foreign ions. Aluminium is the commonest substitute, replacing silicon at levels of perhaps 10 to 300 parts per million, with a paired alkali ion such as lithium, sodium or hydrogen tucked into a structural channel to make up the missing charge. Iron, titanium, germanium and phosphorus appear in smaller quantities. Yet these vanishingly small impurities produce the entire spectacular colour range of gem quartz, because colour in minerals is often a trace-level phenomenon. Amethyst, the purple variety, owes its colour to iron. An Fe3+ ion substituting for silicon is hit by natural gamma radiation from potassium-40, uranium or thorium in the surrounding rock, loses an electron and becomes an Fe4+ colour centre that absorbs yellow-green light. Heat the crystal to between 400 and 550 degrees Celsius and the defect anneals away, the purple vanishes and the stone turns yellow or orange. Almost all commercial citrine is heat-treated amethyst, a fact the trade rarely advertises.
