Smoky quartz is the same story with aluminium instead of iron: an Al3+ substitution plus radiation produces a hole centre absorbing broadly across the visible spectrum, giving everything from pale brown to the near-black variety called morion. Smoky quartz is a natural radiation dosimeter, and its intensity in granite roughly tracks the radioactivity of the host rock. Rose quartz is different again and was long misunderstood. The common massive rose quartz of pegmatites gets its pink from microscopic fibrous inclusions of a mineral in the dumortierite group, only a few nanometres thick, which is why it is almost always cloudy and almost never found as clear crystals. The rare transparent pink crystals are coloured instead by an aluminium-phosphorus centre and, unlike massive rose quartz, they fade in sunlight. Milky quartz, the commonest vein material of all, is not coloured by anything: it is white because it is packed with microscopic fluid inclusions, tiny sealed bubbles of water and carbon dioxide trapped during growth, which scatter light. Those inclusions are scientifically valuable. Heated on a microscope stage until the bubble disappears, they yield the temperature and pressure at which the crystal grew, a technique called fluid inclusion thermometry that underpins much of what is known about ore-forming systems. Several other varieties are worth naming. Rock crystal is colourless transparent quartz. Rutilated quartz contains golden needles of the titanium oxide rutile grown through it, and tourmalinated quartz contains black tourmaline needles; both are inclusions of a different mineral rather than a colour of quartz itself. Aventurine owes its glitter to platy inclusions of green fuchsite mica. Tiger's eye is quartz that has replaced fibrous crocidolite while preserving its fibre structure, so it shows a shifting silky band called chatoyancy. The general lesson is that in quartz almost every visual effect comes from something other than the SiO2 itself.

sections.heading: Alpha and Beta Quartz: The 573 Degree Inversion
sections.body: Quartz exists in two closely related forms that differ only in the tilt of their tetrahedra. Low quartz, or alpha quartz, is the form stable at ordinary temperatures and the form of essentially every quartz crystal you will ever handle. It has trigonal symmetry, space group P3121 or its mirror image P3221. High quartz, or beta quartz, is stable above about 573 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure and has higher, hexagonal symmetry, space group P6222 or P6422. The transition between them is displacive rather than reconstructive: no silicon-oxygen bond is broken. The tetrahedra merely rotate slightly, the bridging angle opens from about 144 to about 153 degrees, and the structure snaps between the two arrangements almost instantaneously. Because no bonds break, the change is fully reversible and cannot be quenched. There is no such thing as beta quartz sitting on a shelf at room temperature. This transition is one of the most practically consequential facts in all of silica science. It is accompanied by a volume increase of roughly 0.8 to 1.4 percent, concentrated over a narrow temperature interval of a few degrees. In a kiln, a foundry mould, a refractory brick or a fired ceramic body, that sudden expansion generates enormous internal stress. Potters know it as the quartz inversion, and it is the reason firing schedules slow dramatically as the kiln passes 550 to 600 degrees Celsius in both directions. Cool a silica-rich ceramic quickly through 573 degrees and it will crack, a defect called dunting. The same effect ruins concrete in fires: aggregate containing quartz expands at 573 degrees while the surrounding cement paste is shrinking, and the mismatch spalls the surface off structural members. Fire-resistant concrete for tunnels is therefore often made with limestone or basalt aggregate instead. The inversion also leaves a permanent record in crystals. A quartz crystal that grew above 573 degrees Celsius crystallised in the hexagonal beta form and inherited that outline, then converted internally to alpha quartz as it cooled while keeping its hexagonal external shape. Geologists call these beta quartz paramorphs, and their stubby, doubly terminated bipyramidal form with little or no prism face is a reliable signature of high-temperature growth. They are characteristic of volcanic rocks such as rhyolite and of quartz porphyry, and they contrast sharply with the long six-sided prisms capped by pyramids that grow at lower temperatures in veins. The transition temperature is also pressure-sensitive, rising by roughly 25 degrees Celsius per kilobar, so at ten kilometres depth in the crust the inversion happens nearer 640 degrees. Experimental petrologists use that dependence, and the presence or absence of paramorph shapes, as one more line of evidence about the conditions in which a rock formed. A related industrial trick exploits the same physics. Silica sand used for foundry moulds is sometimes replaced by chromite or olivine sand precisely to avoid the inversion, because a silica mould that expands abruptly as the poured metal heats it past 573 degrees will crack and spoil the casting, a defect founders call veining or scabbing.

sections.heading: The Silica Polymorphs: Tridymite, Cristobalite, Coesite, Stishovite
sections.body: Silicon dioxide is a champion of polymorphism, the ability of one composition to crystallise in several distinct structures. At least ten crystalline forms are known, and their stability fields map out temperature and pressure so cleanly that several are used as geological barometers. At atmospheric pressure and rising temperature the sequence is quartz, then tridymite above about 870 degrees Celsius, then cristobalite above about 1470 degrees, then molten silica above 1713 degrees. Unlike the alpha-beta quartz inversion, the changes between quartz, tridymite and cristobalite are reconstructive: bonds must be broken and the framework rebuilt. Reconstructive transitions are sluggish, so tridymite and cristobalite routinely persist metastably at room temperature in volcanic rocks and in fired refractory bricks. Cristobalite is common in high-fired silica products and in the dust generated by cutting them, where it is considerably more damaging to the lung than ordinary quartz. Push in the other direction, to high pressure, and silica becomes denser. Coesite forms above roughly 2 to 3 gigapascals, corresponding to depths of about 70 to 100 kilometres, and has a density of 2.91 grams per cubic centimetre. It was made in the laboratory by Loring Coes in 1953 and found in nature by Edward Chao in 1960 in the shocked sandstone of Meteor Crater, Arizona. Stishovite, named for Sergey Stishov who synthesised it in 1961, forms above about 8 to 10 gigapascals and is structurally radical: the silicon is surrounded not by four oxygens but by six, in the rutile arrangement, and the density jumps to 4.29 grams per cubic centimetre. Stishovite too was identified at Meteor Crater, again by Chao, in 1962. The practical importance of coesite and stishovite is that ordinary geological processes cannot make them at the Earth's surface, but a hypervelocity meteorite impact can. Their presence in a surface rock is therefore near-conclusive evidence of shock metamorphism, and their discovery settled long arguments about whether particular circular structures were volcanic or impact craters. Coesite is also found trapped inside diamonds and inside garnets from ultra-high-pressure terranes such as the Dora Maira massif in the Italian Alps, proving that continental crust has been subducted to a hundred kilometres and returned. Rarer polymorphs include moganite and seifertite. The reason polymorphism is so rich in silica comes back to the flexibility of the silicon-oxygen-silicon bridge. The tetrahedron itself is nearly rigid, but the angle at which two tetrahedra meet can vary from about 120 to 180 degrees at almost no energy cost. That gives the framework an enormous number of ways to fold, and small changes in conditions tip the balance from one folding to another. Open frameworks are favoured by high temperature, because a hot structure needs room to vibrate; dense ones are favoured by high pressure, in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle, because compression pushes the system toward whichever arrangement occupies less volume. Molten silica, correspondingly, is not a soup of separate SiO2 molecules but a continuous disordered network of linked tetrahedra, which is why it is roughly a million times more viscous than molten basalt.

sections.heading: Chalcedony, Agate, Flint and the Cryptocrystalline Silicas
sections.body: A large fraction of the silica at the Earth's surface is crystalline quartz, but at a scale too fine to see. Chalcedony is the general name for microcrystalline to cryptocrystalline quartz composed of fibres typically a fraction of a micrometre wide and a few tens of micrometres long, packed into radiating or banded aggregates. Because the crystallites are far smaller than the wavelength of light, chalcedony has no visible crystal faces, no glassy lustre and a waxy to dull appearance, and it is slightly less dense than macrocrystalline quartz, around 2.58 to 2.64 grams per cubic centimetre, because of submicroscopic porosity and trapped water. Detailed work since the 1990s has shown that most chalcedony is not pure quartz: it contains 5 to 20 percent moganite, a distinct monoclinic silica polymorph intimately intergrown with the quartz fibres, and the moganite content tends to decrease with the geological age of the deposit. The named varieties are mostly a matter of colour, banding and impurity. Agate is banded chalcedony, its layers formed by rhythmic deposition from silica-bearing solutions in cavities, typically the gas vesicles of basalt lava flows. The banding can be concentric, following the cavity wall, or horizontal, in which case it records gravity and works as a fossil spirit level showing which way was up when the rock formed. Onyx is agate with straight parallel black and white bands. Carnelian and sard are reddish-brown from iron oxide. Chrysoprase is apple-green from nickel. Jasper is opaque chalcedony containing more than about fifteen percent foreign material, usually iron oxide and clay. Chert and flint are the sedimentary end of the family. Chert is a hard, dense sedimentary rock made almost entirely of cryptocrystalline silica, and much of it is biological in origin: the opaline skeletons of diatoms, radiolarians and sponges accumulate on the seafloor, dissolve and reprecipitate during burial, and recrystallise to quartz. Flint is the name conventionally given to the dark, exceptionally fine-grained chert found as nodules in the Cretaceous chalk of northwestern Europe. Its uniform texture and complete lack of cleavage give it the crucial property of conchoidal fracture: struck correctly, it breaks along smooth curved surfaces controlled entirely by the propagating crack rather than by any internal plane, producing edges one or two molecules thick. That single mechanical property made flint and chert the dominant raw material of stone tool technology for more than two million years, and it is why obsidian, a natural silica glass, was prized for the same reason. Chert comes in two forms whose difference matters. Bedded chert, laid down as continuous layers on the deep ocean floor beyond the reach of carbonate preservation, forms the striking ribbon cherts of accretionary complexes in Japan, California and the Alps, and is a key marker for reconstructing vanished oceans. Nodular chert grows within limestone during burial, replacing carbonate mineral by mineral and often preserving fossil detail with astonishing fidelity, which is why chert nodules are among the best sources of exquisitely preserved Precambrian microfossils.

sections.heading: Opal and the Amorphous Silicas
sections.body: Opal is silica that never achieved a proper crystal lattice. Its formula is usually written SiO2 with n molecules of water attached, and the water content ranges from about 3 to 21 percent by weight, typically 6 to 10. Structurally, opal is built from spheres of amorphous silica between roughly 150 and 400 nanometres across, deposited from silica-saturated groundwater. Because it is not crystalline it has no fixed density; values run from 1.9 to 2.3 grams per cubic centimetre, distinctly lighter than quartz, and its hardness is only 5.5 to 6.5 on the Mohs scale rather than quartz's 7. Mineralogists divide opal into three families by X-ray behaviour. Opal-A is genuinely amorphous. Opal-CT contains nanoscale domains of disordered cristobalite and tridymite. Opal-C is dominated by better-ordered cristobalite. Over geological time opal tends to lose water and convert through opal-CT to chalcedony and eventually to ordinary quartz, which is why opal older than a few tens of millions of years is rare and why almost all opal comes from young sedimentary or volcanic settings. The play of colour in precious opal has an elegant physical explanation, worked out with electron microscopy by Australian researchers led by John Sanders in 1964. In precious opal the silica spheres are uniform in size and stacked in a regular three-dimensional array, a natural photonic crystal. Light entering this array is diffracted by the regular planes of spheres exactly as X-rays are diffracted by atomic planes in a crystal, following Bragg's law. Sphere diameter sets the wavelength: arrays around 150 to 200 nanometres diffract blue and violet, while rarer arrays near 350 nanometres give red. Because red requires the largest spheres, red-dominant opal is the most valuable. Common opal, or potch, has spheres of irregular size or disordered packing, so it scatters light without diffracting it. Amorphous silica takes several other important forms. Diatomite, also called diatomaceous earth, is a soft sedimentary rock made of the opaline shells of diatoms; it is quarried for filtration media, mild abrasives, absorbents and insulation, and it is the inert carrier that made nitroglycerine safe enough to sell as dynamite. Silica gel, the desiccant in small sachets, is synthetic amorphous silica with an enormous internal surface area, often 500 to 800 square metres per gram. Opaline silica also forms inside plants as microscopic bodies called phytoliths, which are species-diagnostic, survive burning and decay, and are one of archaeology's most useful tools for reconstructing ancient diet and agriculture where no pollen or plant remains survive. Opal presents two practical difficulties that follow from its water content. It can craze, developing a network of fine internal cracks, if it dries out too fast, and dealers traditionally keep rough opal in water for this reason. It is also sensitive to sudden temperature change and to ultrasonic cleaners. Australia has historically supplied most of the world's precious opal, from Coober Pedy, Andamooka and Lightning Ridge in the Cretaceous Great Artesian Basin, where silica leached during a long arid period filled cavities and fossil cavities alike, producing celebrated opalised shells and bones.

sections.heading: Handedness, Twinning, and Piezoelectricity
sections.body: Quartz has no centre of symmetry and no mirror plane, and its spiralling chains of tetrahedra can wind either clockwise or anticlockwise. The two versions, right-handed and left-handed quartz, are mirror images that cannot be superimposed, a property called enantiomorphism. Both occur in roughly equal abundance in nature. When present, small trapezohedral faces on the crystal, set asymmetrically at the junction of prism and rhombohedral faces, reveal the hand: faces to the right of the prism edge mean right-handed quartz. Handedness also shows optically. Quartz rotates the plane of polarised light, right-handed crystals turning it clockwise by 21.7 degrees per millimetre of path at a wavelength of 589 nanometres and left-handed crystals the same amount the other way. This optical activity was discovered by Dominique Arago in 1811 and explained by Augustin-Jean Fresnel, and it was the first demonstration that molecular or structural chirality could be detected with light. Real crystals are rarely single-handed throughout. Brazil twinning intergrows right and left domains within one crystal; Dauphine twinning intergrows two domains of the same hand rotated 180 degrees about the c-axis, and these can form spontaneously as a crystal cools through the 573 degree inversion, which is why natural quartz is so often unusable for precision devices. Japan-law twinning joins two crystals at 84 degrees 33 minutes, producing flat heart-shaped pairs prized by collectors. The absence of a symmetry centre gives quartz its most technologically important property. Squeeze a quartz crystal along the right direction and the internal displacement of silicon and oxygen produces a net electrical polarisation, so charge appears on opposite faces. Apply a voltage and the crystal deforms. Jacques and Pierre Curie discovered this piezoelectric effect in 1880. Because a properly cut quartz plate is also extremely elastic and has very low internal damping, it rings mechanically at a sharply defined frequency with a quality factor that can exceed one hundred thousand. Wire it into an oscillator circuit and it locks the frequency to that mechanical resonance. Walter Cady built the first quartz crystal oscillator in 1921, and Warren Marrison and Joseph Horton built the first quartz clock at Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1927. The AT-cut, discovered in 1934, is cut at 35 degrees 15 minutes to the optic axis and has an almost flat frequency-versus-temperature curve near room temperature, which is why nearly every watch, computer, radio and phone contains one. Natural quartz is too twinned and too variable for this; essentially all device quartz is grown hydrothermally in steel autoclaves. Cultured quartz is grown by dissolving crushed natural quartz in hot alkaline solution at around 350 degrees Celsius and 1000 atmospheres in one end of a steel vessel and letting it recrystallise on seed plates in a cooler zone at the other, a process taking weeks and yielding bars of untwinned material. A typical watch crystal is trimmed to 32,768 hertz, two to the fifteenth power, so fifteen successive halvings give exactly one pulse per second.

sections.heading: Physical and Optical Properties in Practice
sections.body: Quartz occupies position 7 on the Mohs scale of hardness, and that is not an arbitrary placement. Friedrich Mohs chose it in 1812 as a reference precisely because it is the hardest common mineral, and the practical consequences are everywhere. Ordinary window glass has a Mohs hardness of about 5.5, a steel knife blade about 5 to 6.5, so quartz scratches both. Airborne quartz dust is why glass, paintwork and spectacle lenses become progressively hazed. Anything softer than 7 exposed outdoors in a dusty environment is being sandblasted. Conversely, quartz cannot be scratched by a knife, and this single test separates it in the field from calcite (hardness 3), fluorite (4) and feldspar (6), the last of which a good hardened steel point will just mark. Quartz has no cleavage. This is unusual and diagnostic. Most minerals contain planes of weaker bonding along which they split cleanly, but the quartz framework has strong silicon-oxygen bonds in every direction, so there is no preferred plane. Instead it fractures conchoidally, breaking along smooth curved surfaces resembling the inside of a shell, with fine concentric ripples radiating from the impact point. Feldspar, the mineral most often confused with quartz in granite, has two good cleavages at nearly 90 degrees and therefore shows flat, mirror-like faces that flash when the rock is turned in the light. Quartz never does this; it looks greasy or glassy and its broken surfaces are curved. That contrast is the fastest reliable discriminator in hand specimen. Optically, quartz is uniaxial positive and weakly birefringent, with ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices of 1.544 and 1.553 respectively, a birefringence of only 0.009. Under a petrographic microscope with crossed polarisers this gives quartz its characteristic pale grey and white first-order interference colours, one of the first things a geology student learns to recognise. Quartz is also transparent well into the ultraviolet, down to about 150 nanometres for pure fused silica, which is why ultraviolet lamps, spectrometer cells and mercury arc envelopes are made of quartz rather than glass, and why a suntan cannot be acquired through an ordinary window. Its thermal expansion is low and its melting point high, 1713 degrees Celsius, and fused silica glass has an expansion coefficient of only about 0.55 parts per million per degree, roughly fifteen times lower than window glass. A fused silica crucible can be taken red hot and plunged into water without cracking. Two more properties are diagnostic in practice. Quartz is chemically inert to almost every common reagent: hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric acids leave it untouched, and only hydrofluoric acid and hot concentrated alkali attack it appreciably. That inertness is why geologists can safely use dilute acid on a rock to test for carbonate without harming the quartz, and why laboratory glassware is made of it. Quartz is also diamagnetic and a good electrical insulator, with a bulk resistivity above ten to the twelfth ohm-metres, which is why quartz spacers appear inside high-voltage and high-temperature equipment where an ordinary polymer insulator would fail.

sections.heading: Quartz in Igneous Rocks and Pegmatites
sections.body: In a cooling magma, quartz is usually the last major mineral to crystallise. The order in which silicate minerals appear from a melt was established experimentally by Norman Bowen at the Geophysical Laboratory in Washington in the 1910s and 1920s and is known as Bowen's reaction series. Olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase come out first at the highest temperatures, followed by pyroxene, amphibole, biotite, sodium-rich plagioclase, potassium feldspar, muscovite and finally quartz. Because quartz crystallises last, it fills whatever space is left between the earlier crystals and rarely develops good faces. In a granite thin section, quartz is the interstitial mineral with ragged, irregular outlines wrapping around the well-formed rectangular feldspars. Mineralogists call a crystal with good faces euhedral and one without anhedral, and quartz in granite is almost always anhedral. The amount of quartz present is the primary basis for classifying igneous rocks. The standard scheme, the QAPF diagram formalised by Albert Streckeisen and adopted by the International Union of Geological Sciences in the 1970s, plots quartz against alkali feldspar, plagioclase and feldspathoids. A rock with more than twenty percent quartz is a granite, granodiorite or tonalite depending on the feldspar ratio; below five percent it is a syenite or diorite; rocks containing feldspathoids such as nepheline contain no quartz at all, because nepheline and quartz react together and cannot coexist at equilibrium. In volcanic rocks quartz behaves differently because cooling is fast. Rhyolite and dacite often contain quartz as phenocrysts, larger crystals that grew slowly in the magma chamber before eruption, and these frequently show the stubby bipyramidal habit inherited from high-temperature beta quartz, often with deeply embayed, corroded outlines produced when the crystal began dissolving back into the melt as pressure dropped during ascent. Pegmatites, the very coarse-grained bodies that crystallise from the last water-rich residue of a granite magma, produce the largest quartz crystals on Earth. Individual crystals weighing many tonnes have been recorded, and a documented example from Podolia in Ukraine reached about 70 tonnes. Pegmatites also host graphic granite, an intergrowth in which quartz forms angular wedges resembling cuneiform writing, produced by quartz and feldspar crystallising simultaneously at exactly their eutectic proportions. The relationship between silica content and magma behaviour is worth spelling out, because it governs volcanic hazard. Basalt contains roughly 45 to 52 percent SiO2 by weight, andesite 52 to 63, dacite 63 to 68 and rhyolite more than about 69. As silica rises, more of the melt's tetrahedra polymerise into chains and networks and viscosity climbs by orders of magnitude. Basalt at 1200 degrees Celsius flows like thin honey and builds gentle shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa; rhyolite is so stiff that dissolved water cannot escape as bubbles until the pressure release of eruption shatters the melt into pumice and ash. Every catastrophic explosive eruption in the record, from Yellowstone to Toba to Vesuvius in 79 CE, involved silica-rich magma, so the abundance of quartz in a rock records how violently its parent magma reached the surface.

sections.heading: Hydrothermal Quartz: Veins, Geodes, and Ore Deposits
sections.body: Water at high temperature and pressure dissolves silica far more effectively than cold water does. At 25 degrees Celsius the solubility of quartz is only about 6 milligrams per litre; at 300 degrees and the corresponding vapour pressure it rises to several hundred milligrams per litre, and in alkaline or saline fluids higher still. This strong dependence on temperature is the engine of hydrothermal quartz deposition. Hot water circulating through the crust, driven by a cooling intrusion or by deep burial, leaches silica from the rocks it passes through, rises, cools or boils, and dumps its dissolved load into any open fracture. Fill the fracture and you have a quartz vein: the white ribs that stripe so many outcrops and roadcuts. Because growth proceeds inward from both walls, vein quartz commonly shows crystals pointing toward the centre, with the last remaining gap either sealed by a final generation of crystals or left as a cavity called a vug, lined with well-terminated points. Quartz veins matter economically far beyond the quartz itself. Gold is transported in hydrothermal fluids as a bisulphide complex, and the same events that make quartz precipitate, boiling and cooling and reaction with wallrock, also destabilise that complex and drop the gold. Orogenic gold deposits, which have supplied a large share of all the gold ever mined, are essentially quartz veins in metamorphosed belts, from the Mother Lode of California to Bendigo in Victoria to the Ashanti belt of Ghana. Prospectors follow quartz for good reason. The same logic connects quartz to tin, tungsten, molybdenum, silver, antimony and mercury. Geodes are the same process in a different container. A cavity, often a gas bubble in a lava flow or a dissolved nodule in limestone, is progressively lined from the outside in: first a thin chalcedony rind, then bands of agate, then a final generation of crystals growing into the remaining void, sometimes amethyst if iron and radiation are available. The famous amethyst geodes of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and Artigas in Uruguay, some large enough to stand inside, formed in vesicles in the Cretaceous Parana basalts. Chalcedony rather than quartz forms when the solution is strongly supersaturated and crystals nucleate faster than they can grow, so the product is a mass of tiny fibres. Hydrothermal quartz also preserves a legible growth history. Because impurity uptake varies with temperature and fluid chemistry, successive growth layers differ subtly in trace titanium and aluminium. Under a scanning electron microscope with a cathodoluminescence detector, which makes the crystal glow under an electron beam, those layers appear as sharp bright and dark zones like tree rings, revealing dozens of separate pulses of fluid in what looks to the naked eye like one homogeneous crystal. Titanium content is itself a thermometer, since its concentration in quartz varies systematically with growth temperature, so a temperature can be read from a single growth band. Combined with fluid inclusion work, this makes vein quartz one of the richest archives available for reconstructing how hot fluids move through the crust.

sections.heading: Weathering, Sand, and the Sedimentary Cycle
sections.body: When a granite is exposed at the surface and attacked by rain, its minerals do not all fail together. Feldspar hydrolyses, reacting with slightly acidic water to produce kaolinite clay and dissolved potassium, sodium and silica. Biotite and amphibole oxidise and break down into clay and iron oxide. Quartz does essentially nothing. Its solubility at surface temperatures is a few milligrams per litre, and the kinetics are so slow that a quartz grain can survive tens of millions of years of exposure. The result is that weathering acts as a giant sorting machine, steadily converting mixed rock into clay plus quartz sand. Geologists express this with the concept of mineralogical maturity: a sandstone that is almost pure quartz has been through many cycles of weathering, transport and redeposition, while an immature arkose full of fresh feldspar was deposited quickly and close to its source. Physical rounding tells a parallel story. Freshly weathered quartz grains are angular. Every kilometre of transport in a river chips their corners, and after a few hundred kilometres they become subrounded. Rivers are inefficient at rounding because water cushions the impacts; wind is far more effective, because grains in air collide at full velocity. Desert dune sand is therefore often superbly rounded and frosted, the surface pitted to a matte finish by countless impacts, whereas beach sand of the same age is smoother and shinier. Under a hand lens the difference is obvious and lets you tell a wind-deposited sandstone from a water-deposited one in ancient rocks hundreds of millions of years old. Grain size follows a standard scheme. Sand is defined as material between 0.0625 and 2 millimetres, subdivided by the Wentworth scale of 1922 into very fine, fine, medium, coarse and very coarse. Below 0.0625 millimetres is silt, and below 0.0039 millimetres is clay. The silica dissolved during weathering does not vanish. Rivers carry roughly six milligrams of dissolved silica per litre to the sea. Diatoms and radiolarians extract it to build opaline skeletons, and their remains accumulate as siliceous ooze on the deep seafloor; buried and heated, that ooze recrystallises into bedded chert. Silica also cements sandstones: pressure at grain contacts dissolves quartz, which reprecipitates in the pore spaces as overgrowths in optical continuity with the original grain. The result, quartz arenite cemented by quartz, is among the toughest rocks in the sedimentary record and forms many of the world's most durable ridges and escarpments. Not all sand is quartz, and the exceptions are instructive. Tropical beaches beside coral reefs are made of calcium carbonate skeletal debris. The black sands of Iceland and Hawaii are basalt fragments and volcanic glass, too young to have been sorted. The white gypsum dunes of White Sands in New Mexico are calcium sulphate. Each of these occurs where the supply of quartz is negligible or where the sand has had no time or distance in which to mature. Where a continent has been supplying sediment for a long time, however, quartz wins by default, simply by outlasting everything else.

sections.heading: Metamorphic Quartz and the Record of Deformation
sections.body: Heat and pressure change quartz in ways that record the deformation history of mountain belts. A quartz sandstone metamorphosed at moderate grade recrystallises into quartzite, in which the original grain boundaries and pore cement are replaced by an interlocking mosaic of new quartz crystals. The diagnostic test is simple and reliable: break a sandstone and the fracture runs around the grains, leaving a rough, sugary surface; break a true quartzite and the fracture runs straight through the grains, giving a smooth, almost glassy surface. Quartzite is one of the hardest and most resistant rocks known, so quartzite ridges commonly stand above their surroundings, and quartzite makes excellent railway ballast and road aggregate. Under stress, quartz deforms by several mechanisms whose relative importance depends on temperature. Below about 300 degrees Celsius it behaves brittlely, fracturing and undergoing pressure solution, in which quartz dissolves at highly stressed grain contacts and reprecipitates in low-stress pore spaces. Above roughly 300 degrees, dislocation glide and climb become important and quartz starts to flow plastically. The optical signature of this is undulose extinction, in which a single grain viewed under crossed polarisers goes dark in sweeping bands rather than all at once as the microscope stage rotates, because the lattice has been bent. Push further and the grain subdivides into subgrains, then into a fine mosaic of new strain-free grains, a process called dynamic recrystallisation. The size of those recrystallised grains is inversely related to the differential stress that produced them, and calibrated piezometers let geologists estimate ancient stresses in megapascals from a thin section, one of the few ways to measure the strength of the deep crust. Quartz also records the extreme. Shock metamorphism from a meteorite impact produces planar deformation features, sets of extremely narrow, closely spaced planes of amorphous silica cutting through a quartz grain along specific crystallographic orientations. These form only above about 8 gigapascals of shock pressure, cannot be produced by any known volcanic or tectonic process, and are the standard diagnostic evidence for an impact structure. Shocked quartz grains scattered worldwide in the thin clay layer at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, combined with the iridium anomaly reported by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980, were central to establishing that a large impact coincided with the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago, and eventually to identifying the buried Chicxulub crater beneath the Yucatan Peninsula. One more metamorphic behaviour deserves mention. In intensely sheared rocks, quartz grains flatten and stretch into ribbons many times longer than they are wide, and these ribbon textures are the standard field evidence for a mylonite, a rock deformed in a ductile shear zone. The preferred crystallographic orientation the grains adopt while flowing records the direction and sense of shear, so a geologist can determine which way one block of crust moved past another hundreds of millions of years after the event.

sections.heading: Identifying Quartz in the Field
sections.body: Identifying quartz reliably needs no laboratory, only a small kit and a disciplined order of tests. The properties that matter are hardness 7, complete absence of cleavage, conchoidal fracture, a glassy to greasy lustre, density 2.65, and no reaction with dilute acid. Run through them in a fixed sequence and the identification is secure. The three minerals most often mistaken for quartz are calcite, feldspar and, in fine-grained form, various pale cherts and altered rocks. Calcite is easy: it is hardness 3, it has three perfect cleavages that make it break into rhombs, and it fizzes vigorously in dilute hydrochloric acid, which quartz never does. Feldspar is the serious one, because it looks similar and sits at hardness 6, close enough that a careless scratch test misleads. The decisive difference is cleavage: turn the specimen slowly in strong light and feldspar will flash from flat reflective cleavage planes, often showing fine parallel striations on plagioclase. Quartz shows only curved, shell-like fracture surfaces and never a flat mirror. Feldspar also tends to be opaque and chalky white, pink or grey, while quartz in the same rock looks grey and translucent, like grains of dirty ice. For crystals, look at the form. A well-grown quartz crystal is a six-sided prism, usually with fine horizontal striations across the prism faces, terminated by six rhombohedral faces that meet in a point. Those horizontal striations are a strong confirmation, produced by alternating growth of prism and rhombohedron. Cryptocrystalline silica such as chert, flint, agate and jasper will fail the crystal test entirely but still passes hardness and fracture, and its waxy lustre plus a translucent edge when a thin flake is held to the light are the giveaways.
steps: Choose a fresh broken surface, not a weathered one, and clean off soil and lichen with water and a stiff brush.
Drip a little dilute hydrochloric acid, about 10 percent, on it. Any fizzing means carbonate, not quartz. Rinse afterwards.
Try to scratch the surface with a hardened steel point or a good knife blade. Quartz will not scratch, and the steel will leave a grey metal smear that wipes off. Wipe before judging.
Now scratch a piece of glass with the specimen. Quartz cuts glass cleanly. If it does not, it is softer than 7 and is not quartz.
Turn the specimen slowly under a bright light and watch for flat mirror-like flashes. Flashes mean cleavage, so feldspar or calcite. Only curved, rippled, shell-like surfaces mean quartz.
Check the lustre with a hand lens: glassy on fracture surfaces, greasy or waxy on fine-grained varieties, never metallic and never earthy.
If it is a free-standing crystal, count the prism faces, look for fine horizontal striations across them, and check that the termination is a six-faced point.

If still in doubt, weigh it and measure its volume by water displacement. A density near 2.65 grams per cubic centimetre confirms quartz; feldspar is 2.55 to 2.76 and calcite is 2.71, so use this as a last check rather than a first one.

sections.heading: From Flint Knapping to Fused Silica: What Silica Is Used For
sections.body: The technological history of silica begins about 3.3 million years ago at Lomekwi in Kenya, where the earliest known deliberately struck stone tools were made, and runs unbroken to the present. Flint and chert were chosen because conchoidal fracture makes them predictable: a controlled blow at the right angle detaches a flake whose shape can be anticipated, and the resulting edge is genuinely sharper than steel, with a radius of curvature measured in nanometres. Obsidian, natural silica glass, is sharper still and has been used for surgical scalpels in specialist applications. Flint's second gift was fire: struck against iron pyrite or, later, high-carbon steel, it shaves off tiny particles of metal that oxidise so fast they ignite, which is the mechanism behind every flintlock firearm and every traditional flint and steel fire kit. Note that the flint does not spark; the steel does. Glass is silica's other ancient use. Ordinary soda-lime glass is roughly 70 to 74 percent silica, with sodium carbonate added to lower the melting point from 1713 to about 1000 degrees Celsius and lime added to stop the result dissolving in water. Borosilicate glass, patented by Otto Schott in 1893 and sold as Pyrex from 1915, replaces some of the soda with boron oxide to cut thermal expansion by two thirds. Pure fused silica is the most demanding form: transparent from about 180 nanometres in the ultraviolet through most of the near infrared, it is the material of telescope mirror blanks, semiconductor photomasks, and the core of the optical fibre carrying essentially all long-distance internet traffic, where losses have been pushed below 0.2 decibels per kilometre. Modern industry consumes silica sand on an enormous scale. Foundries use it for casting moulds, because it withstands molten metal without melting. Construction uses it as concrete aggregate and in mortar. The semiconductor industry needs quartz twice over: as the source of metallurgical silicon, reduced from silica with carbon in an arc furnace, and as the ultra-pure crucible in which single-crystal silicon ingots are pulled, a role for which the exceptionally pure quartz of Spruce Pine, North Carolina, holds a near-monopoly. Hydraulic fracturing uses graded quartz sand as proppant. Abrasives, water filtration, paint extenders, dental porcelain and ceramics all depend on it. Two constraints shape this whole industry and are worth understanding. The first is that not all quartz sand is usable: foundry and glass sand must meet tight specifications on grain size distribution, roundness and iron content, because even a few hundred parts per million of iron oxide tints glass green. Genuinely high-purity deposits are geologically uncommon, which is why silica sand is traded internationally despite being made of the commonest compound on Earth. The second is energy. Reducing silica to silicon in an electric arc furnace consumes roughly 11 to 13 megawatt-hours per tonne of metallurgical-grade silicon, and purifying that further to semiconductor grade multiplies the figure again. The chip in a phone therefore begins as ordinary sand but arrives after one of the most energy-intensive purification chains in manufacturing.

sections.heading: Silica Dust, Silicosis, and the Limits of What We Know
sections.body: The great hazard of silica is not the rock but the dust. Breathing fine particles of crystalline silica causes silicosis, an incurable, progressive scarring of the lungs, and it is one of the oldest occupational diseases on record; Hippocrates described breathlessness in metal diggers, and Agricola wrote about it in 1556. The mechanism is now reasonably well understood. Particles in the respirable fraction, below about 10 micrometres and especially below 4, reach the alveoli, where macrophages engulf them. The freshly fractured silica surface carries reactive silanol groups and radicals that rupture the macrophage's lysosome and kill the cell, releasing inflammatory signals, notably through the NLRP3 inflammasome. The dust particle is then taken up by another macrophage and the cycle repeats indefinitely, because silica cannot be dissolved or cleared. Each round lays down collagen, and over years the lung stiffens into fibrotic nodules. There is no treatment that reverses it. Silica is also classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as a Group 1 human carcinogen for lung cancer, and it raises the risk of tuberculosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma. Freshly fractured dust is far more toxic than aged dust, which is why cutting, grinding, drilling, chipping and abrasive blasting are the dangerous activities and why cristobalite, found in fired refractories and some engineered stone, is worse than plain quartz. The modern epidemic is engineered stone benchtops, which can be over 90 percent crystalline silica against granite's 25 to 45 percent. Australia recorded hundreds of cases in young fabricators and banned the manufacture and installation of engineered stone from 1 July 2024, the first country to do so. Exposure limits are strict: the United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration sets a permissible limit of 50 micrograms of respirable crystalline silica per cubic metre of air averaged over eight hours, and many authorities recommend 25. Those are vanishingly small quantities, far below the level at which dust is visible. The practical rules are simple and non-negotiable: never dry-cut silica-bearing material, always use water suppression or on-tool extraction, wear a properly fitted respirator rated at least P2 or N95 and preferably a powered air-purifying respirator for heavy work, work outdoors or with ventilation, and never dry-sweep the debris. The honest limits of current knowledge are worth stating too. The exact dose-response relationship at low exposures remains debated, and there is no agreed safe threshold. In mineralogy, the crystal chemistry of chalcedony and the role of moganite are still being revised, and the growth mechanism of agate banding is not fully settled. If you suspect exposure, the correct step is occupational health assessment with chest imaging and lung function testing, because early silicosis is silent and by the time breathlessness appears the damage is permanent. Note also that ordinary handling of solid quartz, agate or a beach full of sand poses no such risk; the hazard is specifically airborne respirable dust generated by mechanical breakage, so the sensible response is control at the point of cutting rather than avoidance of the mineral.

guides.safetyNote: Respirable crystalline silica dust causes silicosis, an incurable and progressive lung disease, and is a recognised human lung carcinogen. Never dry-cut, grind, drill or abrasive-blast quartz, sandstone, concrete, engineered stone or any silica-bearing material without water suppression or on-tool dust extraction, a correctly fitted P2/N95 or better respirator, and ventilation. Do not dry-sweep the debris. Hazardous exposure levels are far below the concentration at which dust is visible, and engineered stone is especially dangerous. Hydrofluoric acid, the one common acid that attacks silica, causes deep, delayed and potentially fatal burns and must not be handled without specific training, calcium gluconate gel to hand and an emergency plan.

guides.title: The Mica Group
guides.summary: A full account of the mica group of sheet silicates — their layered crystal structure and the interlayer bond that produces perfect cleavage, the chemistry that splits them into dioctahedral and trioctahedral families, every significant species from muscovite and biotite to lepidolite and the brittle micas, and where they form, how to identify them, what they are used for and how they weather away.

sections.heading: What the Micas Are and Why They Matter
sections.body: The micas are a family of sheet silicate minerals defined by a single striking property: they split into flexible, elastic, often transparent sheets that can be peeled apart almost indefinitely, down to films a few thousandths of a millimetre thick. Anyone who has picked up a piece of granite and pried a shining flake off it with a fingernail has met a mica. They are not rare curiosities. Micas make up several percent of the continental crust, they are a defining constituent of granite, schist and gneiss, they are the minerals that give a schist its silvery sheen and its tendency to split along wavy planes, and they carry a large share of the potassium, the water and the fluorine locked into crustal rocks. Because they contain potassium, they are also one of geology's most important clocks: the potassium-argon and argon-argon dating of micas underpins much of what is known about the timing of mountain building. The name comes from the Latin mica, a crumb or grain, probably reinforced by micare, to glitter. The group is not a single mineral but a structurally coherent family sharing one architectural motif and a general formula usually written as X Y2–3 Z4 O10 (OH, F)2. In that formula X is a large, weakly bound cation sitting between the layers, most often potassium but sometimes sodium, calcium, barium, rubidium or caesium. Y is a smaller cation in the sheet's middle layer: aluminium, magnesium, iron in either valence state, lithium, and less commonly chromium, manganese, vanadium, titanium or zinc. Z is the cation at the centre of the tetrahedra, almost always silicon with aluminium substituting for roughly a quarter of it. The hydroxyl and fluorine sit inside the structure, not on its surface, which is why micas hold their water to high temperature and release it only when the mineral itself begins to break down. More than thirty-seven species are recognised in the group, but a handful dominate geology and industry: muscovite, the colourless to silvery potassium-aluminium mica; the dark iron-magnesium micas long lumped together as biotite; phlogopite, its magnesium-rich pale-brown relative; lepidolite, the lilac lithium mica of pegmatites; paragonite, the sodium analogue of muscovite; and glauconite, the green mica of marine sediments. Around these cluster the brittle micas, the interlayer-deficient clays and a long tail of rarities. Understanding the group means understanding one structure and then watching what happens as different ions are threaded into its three distinct sites. Humans have used mica for thousands of years. Powdered mica gives the shimmer to pigments at Mesoamerican sites, to Egyptian cosmetics and to traditional Indian preparations; the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan incorporates thick mica layers whose purpose is still unexplained; and across Europe and Asia thin sheets served as lamp, lantern and stove windows wherever glass was scarce or too fragile to survive the heat. That practical career began long before anyone understood what a silicate structure was, driven purely by the two properties an ordinary observer can see without instruments: mica splits into transparent sheets, and it does not burn.

sections.heading: The Two-to-One Layer: Tetrahedral and Octahedral Sheets
sections.body: Every mica is built from the same repeating sandwich, and once that sandwich is clear the rest of the group's behaviour follows almost inevitably. The bread of the sandwich is a tetrahedral sheet. Each tetrahedron has a small cation at its centre, silicon in most cases, surrounded by four oxygen atoms. The tetrahedra link by sharing three of their four oxygens with neighbours, producing an indefinitely extended, essentially two-dimensional net. Viewed from above, that net is a honeycomb of six-membered rings, though in real micas the rings are slightly twisted from perfect hexagons into a ditrigonal shape, with the rotation typically between about 5 and 12 degrees. The fourth oxygen of each tetrahedron, called the apical oxygen, points away from the sheet. The filling of the sandwich is an octahedral sheet. Here each cation sits at the centre of an octahedron with six oxygen or hydroxyl neighbours at its corners, and the octahedra share edges with one another to form their own continuous layer. The apical oxygens of the tetrahedral sheet reach into this octahedral layer and become part of it, which is what welds the three sheets into a single mechanical unit. Because a tetrahedral sheet is bonded to each face of the octahedral sheet, the unit is described as a 2:1 layer, or a T-O-T layer, and this architecture is shared with talc, pyrophyllite, the smectite clays, vermiculite and illite. The whole of clay mineralogy and much of soil science is built on variations of the same motif. There is a subtlety in the geometry that matters. A free tetrahedral sheet and a free octahedral sheet do not have quite the same natural dimensions; the tetrahedral net is usually slightly the larger. The structure resolves the mismatch by rotating the tetrahedra within the plane, which shrinks the effective size of the net without straining the bonds, and it is this accommodation that produces the ditrigonal rings. The size of that rotation depends on what fills the octahedral sheet, so the distortion of the tetrahedral net is a direct readout of the layer beneath it. Substituting aluminium for silicon in perhaps one tetrahedron in four leaves the layer with a net negative charge of about one unit per formula, because aluminium carries three positive charges where silicon carried four. That deficit is the single most consequential fact about mica chemistry, because something must balance it, and what balances it sits between the layers. The thickness of the repeating unit is worth remembering, because it is the number an X-ray diffractometer reports first. A 2:1 layer plus its interlayer occupies about ten ångströms, or one nanometre, and the strong reflection at that spacing is the standard fingerprint of a mica in a diffraction pattern. Talc and pyrophyllite, which have the same layer but no interlayer cation, give about 9.3 ångströms; vermiculite with a layer of water gives about 14; a fully hydrated smectite expands to 15 or more and swells further with glycol. Reading the position of that first peak, and watching whether it moves on heating or glycolation, is the everyday basis of clay mineral identification.

sections.heading: The Interlayer Cation and the Origin of Perfect Cleavage
sections.body: The negative charge left on each 2:1 layer by aluminium-for-silicon substitution is neutralised by large cations that sit in the gap between successive layers, nestling into the hollows of the ditrigonal rings above and below. In most micas that cation is potassium, an ion large enough to be surrounded by twelve oxygens, six from the layer above and six from the layer below. This twelve-coordinated interlayer site is the structural feature that makes micas micas, and its bonding is the weakest link in the entire crystal. The strength of the interlayer bond is a matter of simple electrostatics. Each layer carries a charge of roughly one negative unit per formula, balanced by a single potassium ion carrying one positive charge, and that ion is spread over a large coordination sphere at a relatively long bond distance. Within the 2:1 layer, by contrast, silicon-oxygen and aluminium-oxygen bonds are short, strongly covalent and among the strongest in mineralogy. The result is an extreme mechanical anisotropy: the layer is enormously strong in its own plane and the stack is weakly held perpendicular to it. Applied stress therefore finds one and only one easy plane of failure, parallel to the layers, and micas display what mineralogists call perfect basal cleavage on the {001} plane. No other common mineral splits so cleanly in one direction and so reluctantly in every other. This anisotropy runs through every measured property. Hardness on the Mohs scale is 2 to 3 measured by scratching across a cleavage flake, soft enough to mark with a fingernail on the weakest species, but rises to about 4 measured perpendicular to the cleavage, where the scratch must break the strong in-plane bonds. Thermal and electrical conductivity are likewise directional. Most usefully, the sheets are elastic rather than merely flexible: bend a muscovite flake and release it, and it springs back flat. Chlorite and the brittle micas bend and stay bent, or snap, and this simple field test separates them reliably. The identity of the interlayer cation changes everything about how strongly the stack is held. Sodium in place of potassium, as in paragonite, is smaller and binds slightly more tightly. Replacing the single positive charge with a divalent calcium, as in margarite, doubles the interlayer charge and roughly doubles the bond strength, producing the brittle micas, which cleave just as perfectly but whose flakes shatter rather than flex. Removing some of the interlayer cation, as in illite, weakens the stack towards clay behaviour. Removing it entirely and dropping the layer charge to zero gives talc and pyrophyllite, which have essentially no interlayer bond at all and are the softest minerals known. The mica group therefore sits in the middle of a continuous spectrum of interlayer charge that runs from zero in talc, through about 0.6 to 0.9 in illite and vermiculite, to 1.0 in the true micas and 2.0 in the brittle micas, and almost every property that distinguishes these minerals from one another is a consequence of where they fall on that one axis.

sections.heading: Dioctahedral and Trioctahedral: The Group's Great Divide
sections.body: The single most useful division within the micas is not by colour or by occurrence but by how many of the octahedral sites in the middle sheet are actually filled. Each repeating unit of the octahedral sheet offers three sites. If they are occupied by divalent cations such as magnesium or ferrous iron, all three are filled, because three divalent ions supply the six positive charges the sheet requires. Such micas are trioctahedral. If instead the sites are occupied by trivalent aluminium, only two need to be filled to supply the same six charges, and the third stands empty. Such micas are dioctahedral. This is a strict consequence of charge balance, not a matter of chance. The vacancy has consequences you can see and measure. In a dioctahedral mica the empty site is larger than the occupied ones, the surrounding octahedra tilt and shorten their shared edges to screen the now-unbalanced charges, and the whole sheet becomes distorted. In a trioctahedral mica the sheet is regular and more symmetric. Dioctahedral micas therefore tend to have slightly smaller unit-cell dimensions, higher birefringence, and a different response to heating; trioctahedral micas hold their hydroxyl groups pointing straight out perpendicular to the sheet, whereas in dioctahedral micas the hydroxyl tilts towards the vacancy, a difference detectable by infrared spectroscopy and important to how each behaves during dehydroxylation. Muscovite, paragonite, glauconite and celadonite are dioctahedral. Phlogopite, annite, the biotite series, lepidolite and most of the lithium micas are trioctahedral. Lithium complicates the count, because lithium is monovalent and small enough to enter octahedral sites, so lithium micas sit at intermediate occupancies and are conventionally treated as trioctahedral. Chemical variation within each family runs largely along well-defined substitution schemes. The Tschermak substitution exchanges one octahedral magnesium plus one tetrahedral silicon for one octahedral aluminium plus one tetrahedral aluminium, keeping charge balanced while shifting composition between phlogopite-like and muscovite-like ends. Simple ferrous-for-magnesium exchange runs the phlogopite-annite series without changing charge at all, and because iron and magnesium have almost identical ionic radii the substitution is nearly unlimited, which is why dark micas form continuous compositional series rather than discrete species. Fluorine substitutes freely for hydroxyl, particularly in phlogopite and lepidolite, and raises the temperature at which the mineral breaks down, so fluorine-rich micas survive in hotter environments. Ferric iron, chromium, vanadium and manganese enter in smaller amounts and are responsible for most of the colour variation, including the emerald green of chromium-bearing muscovite known as fuchsite and the pink of manganese-bearing lepidolite. The practical value of the dioctahedral-trioctahedral split is that it predicts behaviour. Trioctahedral micas, holding iron in the ferrous state within a fully occupied sheet, are far more vulnerable to oxidation and to weathering than dioctahedral ones, which is why biotite in a granite boulder turns golden and then rusty and crumbles while the muscovite beside it survives unchanged. It also predicts thermal stability: dioctahedral micas dehydroxylate at lower temperature, typically 600 °C to 850 °C, because the tilted hydroxyl groups adjacent to the vacant site are more easily lost, whereas fluorine-rich trioctahedral phlogopite can survive above 1,000 °C.

sections.heading: Muscovite: The Common Light Mica
sections.body: Muscovite is the most abundant mica in the crust and the archetype of the dioctahedral family. Its ideal formula is KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2: potassium in the interlayer, two aluminiums filling two of three octahedral sites, and one aluminium substituting for silicon in every fourth tetrahedron. It is colourless in thin flakes, silvery white, pale grey, greenish or faintly brown in bulk, with a vitreous to pearly lustre on cleavage surfaces. Specific gravity runs from about 2.77 to 2.88, hardness 2 to 2.5 on the cleavage and near 4 across it. It is monoclinic, though the pseudo-hexagonal outline of the layer means crystals often appear as six-sided tabular plates or stacked books. Its name records an old use. Large clear sheets quarried in Russia were exported across Europe as a substitute for window glass and were known as Muscovy glass, after the Grand Duchy of Muscovy; the mineralogist James Dwight Dana formalised muscovite in 1850. The same property that made it a glazing material — transparency combined with heat resistance and perfect splitting — made it the standard window in wood stoves, lanterns and furnace doors for two centuries, where it was often called isinglass. Optically, muscovite is biaxial negative with refractive indices around 1.55 to 1.62 and a birefringence of roughly 0.036 to 0.049, which produces vivid second- and third-order interference colours in a standard thin section. Under crossed polars a muscovite grain cut across the cleavage shows a distinctive mottled or speckled extinction, often called bird's-eye maple texture, caused by slight misalignments between the stacked sheets. Because its optic axial angle is moderate, typically 30 to 47 degrees, it can be distinguished from the dark micas, whose optic angle is usually near zero. Muscovite is a wide-ranging mineral. It crystallises directly from silicic magmas in two-mica granites and grows to spectacular size in granitic pegmatites, where individual books have been quarried measuring several metres across. It is a defining metamorphic mineral in pelitic rocks from greenschist facies upwards, and its very fine-grained form, sericite, is the pervasive alteration product of feldspar under hydrothermal attack, giving altered granites their dull, soapy look. It is mechanically and chemically tough enough to survive erosion and transport, so it accumulates as glittering flakes on the bedding planes of sandstones and siltstones. Chromium-bearing muscovite is fuchsite, a vivid green; the compact massive variety is sericite schist. Muscovite is stable to roughly 700 °C in the presence of quartz, where it breaks down to potassium feldspar plus an aluminium silicate plus water, a reaction that defines an important metamorphic boundary. Because muscovite is chemically inert, non-toxic, an excellent insulator and available in large flawless sheets, it is also the mica of industry: essentially all high-grade sheet mica, all silver mica capacitors and most cosmetic pearlescent pigment is muscovite rather than any other species. Its platy habit means that milled muscovite behaves as a reinforcing and barrier filler rather than an inert bulking agent, which is why it appears in paints, plastics and joint compounds far out of proportion to its cost.

sections.heading: Biotite, Phlogopite, Annite and the Dark Micas
sections.body: The dark micas are the trioctahedral counterparts of muscovite, and they are far more chemically variable. For a century and a half all of them were called biotite, a name given in 1847 in honour of the French physicist Jean-Baptiste Biot, who in the 1810s studied the optical behaviour of mica sheets and helped establish the science of polarised light. Modern nomenclature is stricter and worth stating plainly: in 1998 the International Mineralogical Association discredited biotite as a valid species name and redefined it as a series, because what field geologists call biotite is a solid solution spanning at least four end members. The word remains in universal field and petrological use, and there is no reason to avoid it, but it names a range rather than a substance. The end members are phlogopite, KMg3(AlSi3O10)(OH,F)2, the magnesium extreme; annite, KFe3(AlSi3O10)(OH)2, the ferrous-iron extreme; and the more aluminous eastonite and siderophyllite. Natural dark micas sit somewhere on the plane between them, and their colour tracks their iron content almost linearly. Phlogopite is pale brown, honey, coppery or reddish, sometimes almost colourless; iron-rich biotite is dark brown to greenish black to opaque black. Specific gravity climbs with iron from about 2.78 for pure phlogopite to about 3.3 for annite, a spread wide enough to be useful. In thin section the dark micas are unmistakable because of their pleochroism, the change of colour as the microscope stage is rotated under plane-polarised light. A biotite grain shifts from pale straw or tan when the cleavage is perpendicular to the polariser to deep red-brown or almost opaque when it is parallel. The effect is strong, diagnostic, and absent in muscovite. The optic axial angle is small, often close to zero, so an interference figure taken down the basal cleavage looks nearly uniaxial. Phlogopite is the mica of magnesium-rich, silica-poor environments: metamorphosed impure limestones and dolomites, ultramafic rocks, kimberlites and lamproites, and carbonatites. Because fluorine readily replaces hydroxyl in it, phlogopite survives to higher temperatures than any other common mica and remains stable in the upper mantle, where it is one of the very few hosts for potassium and water at depth — a fact of some importance for how volatiles are stored and released beneath volcanoes. Iron-rich biotite belongs to granites, granodiorites, diorites, rhyolites and to metamorphosed shales, where its first appearance defines the biotite zone in the classic Barrovian sequence. Two further properties of the dark micas earn them attention. They concentrate the radioactive elements uranium and thorium in tiny included crystals of zircon, monazite and apatite, and the alpha particles emitted by those inclusions damage the surrounding mica lattice, producing the dark haloes known as pleochroic or radiohaloes that ring such inclusions in thin section — one of the earliest pieces of visible evidence for radioactivity in rocks. And because iron-rich biotite oxidises readily, it is the first mineral in most granites to fail on weathering: its interlayer potassium leaches out, ferrous iron oxidises, the flakes swell and turn golden, and the rock disintegrates around them into the coarse sand called grus.

sections.heading: Lepidolite and the Lithium Micas
sections.body: Lithium enters the octahedral sheet readily despite carrying only a single positive charge, because it is small enough to fit and its charge deficit can be balanced by pairing it with aluminium. The resulting lithium micas are among the most visually distinctive minerals in the group and, in the twenty-first century, among the most economically interesting. Lepidolite is the familiar name, given in 1792 by Martin Klaproth from Greek roots meaning scale-stone, and like biotite it has been reclassified: modern usage treats lepidolite as a series name rather than a species, spanning polylithionite, KLi2Al(Si4O10)(F,OH)2, and trilithionite, KLi1.5Al1.5(AlSi3O10)(F,OH)2. Its colour is its signature — lilac, rose-violet, pink or pale grey — and the pink comes from traces of manganese, not from lithium, which is colourless in minerals. Lepidolite is almost exclusively a pegmatite mineral. It grows in the lithium-rich, volatile-charged residual melts of highly evolved granitic pegmatites, in the company of spodumene, petalite, amblygonite, elbaite tourmaline, beryl and caesium-bearing pollucite. The classic localities are Rožná and Rožná-type pegmatites in the Czech Republic, the Tanco pegmatite in Manitoba, Bikita in Zimbabwe, the pegmatites of Minas Gerais in Brazil, and San Diego County in California. It usually occurs as fine-grained aggregates of small scaly plates rather than large books, and typical lithium oxide contents run between about 3 and 7 percent by weight. Zinnwaldite is the iron-bearing lithium mica, named for Zinnwald in the Erzgebirge on the Czech-German border; it is pale brown to grey and characteristic of greisenised granites associated with tin and tungsten mineralisation, where hot fluorine-rich fluids have converted granite into a quartz-mica rock. Its presence is a recognised exploration guide to tin. Taeniolite, masutomilite and polylithionite fill out the family. Lithium micas have historically been a secondary lithium ore, less important than spodumene because their lithium is harder to extract economically. Interest has revived with lithium demand, and processing routes based on roasting with sulphates or on direct acid leaching are being developed; whether lepidolite becomes a major commercial source is genuinely unsettled and depends more on price and on the handling of the fluorine released during processing than on geology. Lithium micas are also a serious problem in ceramics and glass if unrecognised, because fluorine volatilises during firing. They are, incidentally, mildly radioactive in some occurrences, since they concentrate rubidium and caesium alongside lithium and rubidium-87 is a naturally radioactive isotope with a half-life of roughly 49 billion years — the basis of rubidium-strontium dating, for which lithium micas are among the best available minerals. Field recognition is straightforward where the colour is developed: a fine-scaled, lilac-to-pink micaceous aggregate in a coarse granitic rock is lepidolite until proved otherwise, and a flake will colour a flame carmine red from its lithium if held on a clean wire, one of the few genuinely useful flame tests in mineralogy.

sections.heading: Paragonite, Glauconite, Celadonite and the Brittle Micas
sections.body: Beyond the four familiar micas lies a set of species that are locally abundant, diagnostically useful and frequently overlooked. Paragonite is simply muscovite with sodium replacing potassium in the interlayer, NaAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2. It is visually identical to fine-grained muscovite and is normally detected only by X-ray diffraction or chemical analysis, which is exactly why it was named from the Greek for misleading. It is a genuine indicator: paragonite is common in high-pressure, lower- temperature metamorphic rocks such as blueschists, and a paragonite-muscovite pair with a measurable compositional gap can be used as a rough thermometer, because the two minerals become progressively more soluble in one another as temperature rises. Glauconite is the green mica of the sea floor. It forms authigenically — in place, on the sediment surface — in shallow marine settings with slow sedimentation, moderate depth and reducing conditions just below the water-sediment interface, typically over thousands of years. It occurs as dull green pellets, often the infillings of foraminiferal tests or faecal pellets, and rocks rich in it are called greensands. Its composition is variable and interlayer-deficient, roughly (K,Na)(Fe,Al,Mg)2(Si,Al)4 O10(OH)2, with ferric iron dominant. Glauconite matters practically for three reasons: it is a marker of sediment starvation and therefore of major flooding surfaces in sequence stratigraphy, it is a potassium source that has been used both as a low-grade fertiliser and as a water softener, and it can be dated by potassium-argon methods, though its openness to argon loss makes such dates minimum ages that must be treated cautiously. Celadonite is glauconite's close relative, better ordered and forming in altered basalts and in amygdale fillings rather than in sediment, and it supplied the blue-green earth pigment that Renaissance painters used as an underlayer for flesh tones. The brittle micas form a distinct sub-family defined by a doubled interlayer charge. Where a true mica has one monovalent cation between the layers, a brittle mica has one divalent cation, usually calcium, which requires that roughly half rather than a quarter of the tetrahedral silicon be replaced by aluminium. Margarite, CaAl2(Al2Si2O10)(OH)2, is the dioctahedral example; clintonite and bityite are trioctahedral ones. The stronger interlayer bond raises the hardness to 3.5 to 5 and, critically, changes the mechanical behaviour: brittle mica flakes snap rather than spring back. They are minerals of metamorphosed aluminium-rich and calcium-rich rocks, of emery deposits and of contact-metamorphosed limestones, and though never abundant they are common enough to trip up an unwary identification. A handful of further species round out the group and are worth knowing by name even if rarely met. Zinnwaldite and taeniolite are lithium micas; wonesite is a sodium-bearing trioctahedral mica; roscoelite is the vanadium mica of some sandstone-hosted uranium deposits and gives the ore its olive colour; and the barium micas, oxykinoshitalite and ganterite, substitute barium into the interlayer. Chromium, manganese, zinc and titanium-rich varieties exist for most of the common species. The total recognised membership of the group now runs to well over thirty species, which reflects less the discovery of exotic minerals than the steady tightening of nomenclature around what were once broad field names.

sections.heading: Polytypism: The Many Ways to Stack the Same Layer
sections.body: Because a mica layer is nearly hexagonal, each successive layer can be placed on the one below in several orientations that are geometrically equivalent to a first approximation but crystallographically distinct. Rotations of 0, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees are all possible, and the different stacking sequences that result are called polytypes. Polytypism is a restricted form of polymorphism: the composition and the individual layer are identical, and only the stacking order differs, so the unit cell varies along one axis while the layer itself does not change at all. Micas are the textbook example of the phenomenon, alongside silicon carbide and the zinc sulphides. The standard notation records the number of layers in the repeat and the resulting crystal system. The 1M polytype repeats every one layer and is monoclinic. The 2M1 polytype repeats every two layers with a particular alternation and is also monoclinic; 2M2 is a different two-layer arrangement. The 3T polytype repeats every three layers and is trigonal. The 2O polytype is orthorhombic, and 1Md denotes a one-layer structure with disordered stacking, which gives broad, smeared X-ray reflections rather than sharp ones. The distribution of polytypes is not random and carries real information. Muscovite is overwhelmingly 2M1 in ordinary metamorphic and igneous rocks, while the 1M and 1Md forms are typical of low-temperature, rapidly crystallised or diagenetic material. That correlation is the foundation of a widely used technique in low-grade metamorphic and petroleum geology: the proportion of 2M1 to 1M in fine white mica, together with the sharpness of the ten-ångström X-ray peak measured as the Kübler index of illite crystallinity, gives a practical thermometer for the interval between about 100 °C and 300 °C, where conventional index minerals are absent. Trioctahedral micas behave differently: phlogopite and biotite are usually 1M, with 3T and 2M1 forms comparatively rare. Polytypism also complicates identification. Two specimens of the same species may give visibly different X-ray patterns, and a mineralogist reporting a mica should specify the polytype. It has a subtler consequence too. Because stacking disorder is common, real mica crystals are frequently mosaics of slightly misoriented domains rather than perfect single crystals, and this domain structure is what produces the mottled bird's-eye extinction seen down the microscope and contributes to the way large sheets are graded for industrial use, where hidden stacking faults, wedge structures and included mineral films determine whether a sheet can be split cleanly to a usable thickness. The reason polytypes can exist at all is that the energy differences between them are tiny, on the order of a few kilojoules per mole, far smaller than the differences between genuine polymorphs such as kyanite and sillimanite. Stacking is therefore decided as much by the kinetics of growth as by thermodynamic stability, which is exactly why polytype distribution tracks the conditions of crystallisation rather than final equilibrium, and why a crystal can retain a disordered stacking sequence indefinitely with no driving force strong enough to anneal it away.

sections.heading: Identifying a Mica in the Field and Under the Microscope
sections.body: Recognising that a mineral is a mica is easy; deciding which mica takes a short, disciplined sequence. The group announces itself by a single perfect cleavage yielding thin springy sheets with a pearly shine, a hardness low enough to mark with a fingernail across the flake, and a habit of occurring as stacked books or as glittering plates in the foliation of a schist. Once the group is established, colour separates the commonest species: silvery or pale means muscovite, dark brown to black means the biotite series, honey to coppery brown suggests phlogopite, lilac or pink suggests lepidolite. Green needs care, because it may be chromian muscovite, glauconite, celadonite or, more often, chlorite. The elasticity test is the single most valuable discriminator available without equipment. True micas spring back when a flake is bent and released; chlorite and the brittle micas do not. Talc is a third member of the same confusion, but it is far softer at hardness 1 and feels greasy. Two naming traps matter too: biotite and lepidolite are series names rather than species, so neither pins down a composition, and paragonite is optically indistinguishable from fine-grained muscovite. Fine white mica in slates lies below optical resolution entirely and can be named only by diffraction. Colour is unreliable throughout, being dominated by iron content and by surface oxidation films, so judge it in a thin flake by transmitted light rather than in bulk. In the laboratory, X-ray diffraction identifies both species and polytype unambiguously; electron microprobe analysis resolves composition within a series; and infrared spectroscopy separates dioctahedral from trioctahedral by the hydroxyl stretching band.
steps: Confirm the group first: try to peel a flake with a knife point or fingernail. A single perfect cleavage giving thin translucent sheets, with no second cleavage direction, means a mica or a chlorite.
Bend a flake between finger and thumb and release it. If it springs flat it is a true mica; if it stays bent or snaps it is chlorite or a brittle mica such as margarite.
Record the colour in a thin flake held to the light, not in bulk, because transmitted colour tracks iron content directly.

Check the host rock. Granite and pelitic schist point to muscovite and biotite; a marble or an ultramafic points to phlogopite; a pegmatite with tourmaline and beryl points to lepidolite; a green pellet in marine sandstone points to glauconite.
Estimate hardness both ways — across the flake, where micas are 2 to 3, and perpendicular to it, where they are near 4 — since the anisotropy is itself confirmatory.
Under the microscope in plane-polarised light, rotate the stage and watch for pleochroism: a strong straw-to-dark-brown change means a dark mica, no change means muscovite or paragonite.

Under crossed polars look for bright second- or third-order interference colours and mottled bird's-eye extinction, then take an interference figure: an optic angle near zero indicates biotite or phlogopite, 30 to 47 degrees indicates muscovite.

If the distinction still matters — muscovite against paragonite, or a position within the biotite series — send the sample for diffraction or microprobe analysis, because no optical test resolves these.

sections.heading: Micas in Igneous Rocks and Pegmatites
sections.body: Micas crystallise from melts only where water and potassium are both available, which places them firmly in the evolved, silica-rich part of the igneous world and in a few unusual volatile-rich alkaline settings. Biotite is the ordinary igneous mica: it is a normal constituent of granite, granodiorite, tonalite, diorite and their volcanic equivalents, appearing as black hexagonal plates that in a hand specimen of granite give the rock its characteristic speckled look.
